Class Conflict
Exploitation of Poor Countries

Critics of the free market often argue that international trade leads to the exploitation of poor countries; I dare say that—regardless of how desperate the conditions of the poor are—no exploitation is taking place. Why? Trading with us improves their situation compared to a scenario where we did not trade with them (and the same applies to us, otherwise the trade would never take place); if someone, driven by their poverty, gives up mineral wealth, for instance, in order not to die of thirst or hunger, their situation is indeed dire, but it is undeniably better than it would be without such an offer (if it weren't, they would simply decline it and remain in their prior state).
Representative Democracy

From time to time I engage in
a principled, general critique of democracy
(not of any specific variety, but of democracy in general); right now, however, I would like to focus specifically on representative democracy. Who gets elected as a representative in such a system? What are the best qualifications for winning voters' ballots? Naturally, being charismatic, popular, well-known, capable of entertaining people... and similar traits. And what does a "good leader" require? Most likely wisdom, decisiveness, integrity, perspective... "surprisingly" an entirely different set of qualities. Thus, for representative democracy to function even as well as its proponents theoretically claim it should (putting aside that it fundamentally cannot for far graver reasons), one must rely on the coincidence that the darling of the crowds will simultaneously happen to be a capable leader (setting aside that people follow a capable leader voluntarily); how could anyone want to rely on something like that?
Parasitism

Modern liberals (and I don't mean classical liberals, but rather "leftists" in the sense of American Democrats) like to label anyone working off the books or operating in flagrant violation of the labor code as a parasite; conservatives (classic "right-wingers" in the sense of American Republicans), on the other hand, typically label those on welfare benefits, subsidies, and the like as parasites. I believe both groups are mistaken. The "leftists" more so, because someone working under the table is certainly not parasitizing on anyone—they are merely refusing to be robbed by the state; the "right-wingers" are slightly less mistaken, yet anyone taking welfare or subsidies is only picking up what someone (the state) offers them. The true parasite is the entity that deprives us of those resources under
the threat of violence—namely the state
. Inciting hatred against one group or the other is merely a diversionary tactic by politicians to create scapegoats; the one doing the stealing is neither the grey-market actor nor the welfare recipient—it is the state.
Shipping Goods

"We live in crazy times when goods we could produce locally are instead imported from the other side of the planet," some warn. Is that truly wrong? The answer is not so simple in today's distorted (regulated, subsidized, and taxed) market, where outcomes vary; but on a free market, the answer is unequivocal: "No, it is not wrong!" The reason for importing goods that could be produced locally is typically that doing so is cheaper (even including the shipping costs). No, this is not a market failure; on the contrary, it represents the market discovering the most efficient route, which in this instance happens to be importing. People clearly value the resources consumed by production elsewhere plus transportation less than the resources consumed by domestic production (if they didn't, local production would be cheaper); this can happen because people in different locations value their time (and labor) differently, or because conditions for producing certain goods are simply superior elsewhere.
Wars Without States?

When people hear the word "anarchy," most imagine an apocalypse, conflict, chaos, and war; how far removed are these notions from reality? In
historical anarchies
there was certainly no more warfare than in territories usurped by states; many will object that this proves little, as circumstances today may differ from the past. Fair enough, that may be so; nevertheless, I believe a stateless society would be far more peaceful. Why? Because wars are expensive; and when states wage war, the decision-makers do not pay for it—they finance it with other people's money, whereas if a private party wants to wage war, they must pay out of their own pocket. I am not claiming there would never be any conflicts in anarchy; there certainly would be, because sometimes fighting pays off anyway (whether economically or out of malice); yet I am convinced they would be fewer in number, and above all drastically reduced in scale, since society would be decentralized—making something like a world war a highly improbable scenario.
The Free Market Is Only for the Rich

Statists often hold the view that the free market would serve only the wealthy, because there is allegedly no incentive to provide services to the poor since they can pay less; while it might seem that way at first glance, let us think about it more deeply. Suppose that claim were true: we live in a society where all companies compete to offer ever better and more luxurious services to the wealthy, while nobody does anything for the poor. How would you make the greatest profit in such a society? Well, obviously not by squeezing into cut-throat competition in the luxury sector, but by starting to provide goods (naturally less luxurious ones) to the poor; instead of making a million from one customer, you'd rather make ten thousand from each of a hundred customers. Furthermore, if that thesis were actually true, car manufacturers would only build supercars, nobody would construct affordable apartments—only luxury villas, and so on...
Supporters of the Free Market

In conversations with die-hard anti-capitalists, I am often taken aback by how misguided their ideas are about what I—as an anarcho-capitalist—actually believe; they ascribe all kinds of notions to me that I disagree with completely, such as portraying me as a defender of the current banking system, mega-corporations, and the like. Such misconceptions are understandable up to a point, since nobody can understand everything correctly; the situation turns absurd, however, the moment I explain why I don't hold or advocate those positions, to which the debater responds not by revising their assumptions, but by vehemently insisting that I simply must believe that! What does this show? Personally, I think these people have simply slapped the label "capitalism" onto every economic or social phenomenon they dislike; their anti-capitalism simply boils down to treating "capitalism" as a synonym for "bad stuff I hate." Why is that? Another victory for Newspeak?

Corporations and States

Many people (especially those who call themselves "leftists") dislike large corporations and argue that we need states to protect us from them; yet they fail to realize how much this very attitude (particularly when expressed at the ballot box) actually helps those corporations. For it is precisely states that favor mega-corporations over smaller businesses on virtually every front. How? First, the truly massive players can lobby the legislative process and crush their competition; yes, officially they shouldn't, but it happens (and calling upon the state—the very mechanism through which this occurs—for help is absurdly naive). Second, corporations adapt far better to the legislative and regulatory burdens by which states distort the market. Third, large firms secure subsidies far more easily; they maintain entire departments dedicated to chasing them. And fourth, we have the familiar investment incentives; these are likewise out of reach for small players. Does it really make sense to clamor for a big state to "oppose" corporations?
Whoever Does Nothing Wrong...

All manner of totalitarian practices—especially wiretapping, though not exclusively—are often defended with: "Whoever does nothing wrong has nothing to fear." (And so they don't need encryption, secure lines... and above all, privacy.) This premise is nonsensical, first because the state considers things like tax evasion "wrong," which is nothing other than attempting not to be robbed; but even setting that aspect aside, the phrase reveals incredible naivety, since the speaker perceives the state as some immaculate entity devoid of human error or malice (which is far from uncommon). Yet the state is comprised of people; hence it is simply not true that someone doing nothing wrong has nothing to fear, as they may certainly fear the abuse of information collected about them by the state (which may be authorized by legislation or committed in blatant breach of the law). It reminds me a bit of another claim: "People are evil, so we need a state." Hmm... and who is going to run that state? Aliens?
The Complexity of Society

One sometimes encounters the argument that in "primitive societies" a state might not have been strictly necessary because those communities were very simple, but today, owing to the intricate complexity of "modern society," it is essential and "we couldn't manage without it"; few assertions could be further from the truth. Why? Well, small communities are the only setting where socialism can function to some degree, because people know each other and can perform economic calculation "in their heads" (they can intuitively estimate each other's preferences), a prime example being the family; yet the larger and more complex the society we inhabit,
the harder it is to perform economic calculation without a free market
. The reality is thus the exact opposite of what the argument claims: the more complex and complicated a society is, the harder it is to centrally plan, and the more urgently it requires a free market for proper resource allocation.
A Balanced Budget

Many people—often "right-leaning"—call for a balanced state budget; yet I—surprisingly to many—do not. Why not? Because there are two ways to achieve that state: the first consists in cutting spending, but the second consists in raising revenues. A balanced budget can thus be maintained within a minimal state, but equally within an enormous socialist behemoth (for instance, before 1989 the Czech Republic was far less indebted than it is now, but it was hardly paradise). Personally, I consider it paramount that the state should have the lowest possible revenue. Naturally, a situation with both low revenue and low spending is by far the best, but low revenue coupled with high spending is preferable to a conventional big state (even one with a balanced budget). I'm not saying you must share my view, but I believe we should definitely reflect on how important the "fight for a balanced budget" is compared to efforts to shrink the state.
The Burden of Proof
How Can Anyone Fail to Be an Anarcho-Capitalist...

...a pacifist, vegan, Jain, or any kind of anarchist? Pacifists reject violence entirely; if consistent, they must also reject states, while they could hardly prevent anyone from engaging in trade (even if they choose not to participate themselves, but anarcho-capitalism demands no such thing). Vegans oppose the enslavement and killing of animals, often even phrasing it as not wanting to "take away the fruits of their labor"; theoretically they could be consistent statists, but only if they valued other species above their own. Jains are rigorous ascetics who must not lie or kill, but above all, their first vow is "not to take what has not been given"; yet states are founded entirely on taking what has not been given. And finally, all anarchists—many of whom define themselves against anarcho-capitalism—reject the state, but often reject voluntary hierarchy alongside it; yet how can they stop people from forming voluntary hierarchies without becoming a state themselves?

A State-Run vs. a Stateless Society

How does a state-run society differ from a stateless one? In technology? In the management of certain sectors of the economy? In centralization versus decentralization? Perhaps in the end result, yes; but primarily they differ in the absence of a monopoly on coercion. Instead of having an entity that forces people to do what they don't want to do and pay for things that aren't worth the money to them, as exists today, in a stateless society it would be left to their voluntary choice what they wish to participate in and what not. That would be the most fundamental change—all others would
stem
from this one, and after all, nobody can foresee exactly what would occur and how. People often worry that nobody would have things firmly under control; indeed, nobody would, but anyone who wishes to have someone to whom they delegate some of their rights, liberties, powers, or responsibilities can simply hire them... Does that sound absurd? Yes; just as absurd as when applied to the state.
Job Creation

"Job creation" is commonly viewed as something desirable and positive; and indeed it often is—when an entrepreneur hires someone, a job has been created, which typically enriches society. However, we must not confuse creating a job with creating useful value; if we create a job solely for the sake of giving someone work, value is not generated—quite the contrary. If, for instance, the government employs people to dig holes and fill them up again, clearly no value is generated for society; more interesting, however, are the less obvious cases. Whenever the state employs someone whom people would not pay voluntarily, requiring coercion instead,
waste occurs
—people clearly value their money more than the products of that person's labor. The same applies to jobs that do not fall directly under the state, but exist within private firms solely due to subsidies. They are all variations on digging and refilling holes...
Let's Tax Corporations!

Many (especially left-leaning) people rejoice when a politician raises taxes on their wealthy boss; the right question, in my view, is whether they realize that when this happens, they themselves will be among those who have to earn the money to pay those steep taxes. How so? Heavily taxed companies have fewer resources; and since we live in a world of scarce resources, that taxed money will have to be missing somewhere. For instance, in employee wages; and even if not immediately, the taxed entrepreneurs' incentive to raise those wages in the future will decline. Another place where the shortfall may manifest is in the prices of that company's goods and services; ultimately, customers will end up paying those taxes as well (who may well include those very same celebrating, short-sighted leftists). And last but not least, the company might go bankrupt, or be forced to cut costs by laying off workers. So before you celebrate, ask yourself for whom the bell is actually tolling...

What Is the State?

Quite often in discussions about a free society, I find people asking me to define what I actually consider a state; what still qualifies as a state and what no longer does? A state is an entity that (with substantial success) usurps a monopoly on violence over a (substantially sized) territory that it does not own; it is typically funded by involuntary contributions (it has the power to extract them, so why wouldn't it?). Therefore, if someone entrusts certain functions of today's state to a private firm, it does not become a state merely because of that—even if it performs "almost the same things"—so long as it compels nobody to fund it or obey it. From this, it seems quite clear why the state is such an evil: relationships (commercial, personal, professional... whatever) that are worthwhile are founded on voluntariness; if something cannot function on a voluntary basis, it clearly isn't worth much, ergo it makes no sense to enforce it coercively, because someone is losing out (if they weren't, they would participate voluntarily).

Comparative Advantage

Comparative advantage is one of David Ricardo's greatest discoveries; and what does it actually mean? Imagine a successful attorney who is also an exceptional cyclist. It may still pay for him to hire a bicycle messenger to deliver a parcel, even if the attorney could do it better and faster himself—because by focusing on his legal practice, he earns so much more that paying someone else to deliver the parcel is well worth it. This example is hardly revolutionary, and anyone can easily picture it; but what follows from it? That mutually beneficial trade can take place even when one party is in no way more efficient than the other. This applies equally to international trade: even between states where one is "backward" in every respect, trade can remain mutually advantageous. The concept of comparative advantage replaces absolute advantage (according to which trade only pays off when each party does something better than the other), introduced by Adam Smith.
We Know What Was Wrong

Ex post, we can often easily identify what was wrong in the past; we condemn slavery, torture, witch trials, serfdom, racism, Nazi and communist regimes (at least for the most part). Yet all these practices were accepted and even deemed desirable by society in their day; nobody at the time thought of them as atrocities, even though some did sound the alarm. How was that possible? Were people evil back then? I don't think so; I'd say they were more or less the same as today. How could they allow such things? Well, it was simply normal back then, and "everyone knew" that "it's just reality" and "there's no point banging your head against the wall," while no pragmatist cared about "castles in the sky and naive theories" because everyone was "living in the here and now"; the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing. And so I ask: will we allow our descendants in the distant future to see how blind we are to evil today, simply because "everyone knows that
we need the state
"?
Public Broadcasters

Imagine a media outlet owned by a private party that doesn't have to turn a profit; everyone is mandated to pay for it regardless of whether it produces anything of value... and that is essentially what public broadcasting is (its owner being the largest and most dangerous monopoly—the state—which naturally uses it to advance its own interests just like any other owner). The justification for such (typically outrageously expensive) media is that they are meant to carry content that cannot sustain itself commercially; but what does that mean? It means people simply aren't interested in that content—or rather, they value the resources consumed by the broadcaster more; so we "logically" force them to pay. We are also told we need public media to inform us during "crises"; um... when a crisis hits (natural disasters, terror attacks...), do private outlets remain silent? No! On the contrary, they clear their schedules just to report on what people want to know.
Consumer Deception

Misleading consumers is prohibited by law: no one may deceive consumers, specifically by providing false, unsubstantiated, incomplete, inaccurate, unclear, ambiguous, or exaggerated information, or by concealing facts about the true qualities of products or services or purchasing conditions—all under fines of up to fifty million Czech crowns. But how does the state treat its citizens—the consumers of its services? What does it teach them
in schools
? For instance, outright lies that the free market cannot provide certain services (healthcare, social welfare, justice, currency, etc.), ergo the state must (!) provide them. And this is no mere "opinion"; it is a demonstrable falsehood, since the market already provided those services in the past until governments seized control of them. And how would the state treat an entrepreneur who lied to their customers in such a manner? Quite possibly the same way it treats mobsters collecting extortion money—even though the state itself does the exact same thing on a grander scale and calls it taxes.
Evil Banks

People often clamor for state protection against "evil capitalist banks"; such cries would be laughable were they not so tragic. Why? Today's banks are not "evil capitalist" institutions; they are "evil state" institutions. A free-market bank has its own commercial policy, offers services to people, or issues currency at its discretion, and it is entirely up to people whether they choose to accept that money; if it behaves poorly in their eyes, they can simply refuse its currency.
Today's banks enjoy an enormous privilege from the state
, which granted them the monopoly privilege to issue currency that the state then forces people to accept, keep books in, and pay taxes with; it essentially gives them cartel power imposed on all of us by force. It is therefore paradoxical to call upon the state to "protect" us from "evil banks"; it would be more than enough for the state to stop granting them those disgusting, forcefully extracted privileges (control over currency everyone is coerced to accept) and let the free market resolve the issue.
Anarchy and Capitalism

"Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism." In my view, this quote best captures the essence of the life's work of its author—Murray Newton Rothbard. Unfortunately, many (especially anarchists of other schools) fail to understand it; so I would like to offer an explanation. Pure capitalism—that is, an entirely unregulated market—can exist only in the absence of state power, since any tax—no matter how trivial—distorts the market environment; the prerequisite for pure capitalism is therefore a stateless setting, which is to say, anarchy. And the reverse? Under anarchy, there is no central authority to regulate anyone; people can freely exchange their goods and own the means of production, which is capitalism—even if they choose to live in communes and hold means of production collectively (so long as nobody is prevented from arranging their affairs as they see fit, which is the very essence of anarchy, it will always be capitalism).
Interest
Prisons

Imagine someone wrongs you;
what do you do then?
If it wasn't anything too severe, perhaps you would welcome restitution; if it was something unforgivable that ruined your life, maybe you would want to hurt them back (personally, I consider revenge unfortunate, but let's leave that aside for now). But who would spend their own money to build some bizarre zoo on their own land,
lock the perpetrator inside
, guard them, feed them at their own expense, and after some time release them? Virtually no one. Why then do we
treat lawbreakers this way
? It only takes obscuring the payment mechanisms a bit, hiding from people that they are the ones footing the bill, spreading the costs among those who were never affected... and suddenly it stops seeming absurd, and we have prisons: a massive waste of resources, congregating criminals in one place where they learn the "trade" from one another, followed by their release back into society—such is the state.
Price, Cost, Supply and Demand

Most libertarians rightly grasp the subjective theory of value and reject the cost-of-production theory; and indeed, the value of a good is purely subjective, varying across time and place—there is no such thing as "objective value." Price, then, depends on supply and demand; libertarians understand this too and incorporate it into their arguments. Occasionally, however, they internalize these notions so dogmatically that they walk into a logical trap, claiming that price does not depend on costs at all. That, however, is nonsense: although price is not determined solely by costs (and nothing else), it is determined, among other factors, by costs! This does not contradict the law of supply and demand: price does depend on supply and demand, but supply is influenced (among other factors) by costs. This is not contradicted by the fact that a discovered gemstone—which cost me nothing to pick up—fetches the same price as one mined with great toil; however, if gemstones could be found effortlessly in huge quantities, that would immediately reflect in the price.
Peace with Drugs at the Cherubín Teahouse

Today at 19:00 we can meet in person for the first time since the corona crisis—come join the discussion on drug policy and the war on drugs
at the Cherubín Teahouse
. We love returning to this teahouse for its exceptionally pleasant atmosphere; come check it out as well!
Abortion from the Perspective of the NAP

During discussions about the
Non-Aggression Principle (NAP)
, the topic of abortion occasionally arises; a child is the owner of their own body, so it might appear that the mother has no right to terminate its life. But beware! There is a distinction between killing someone (where they would live without me, but through my action they die—a clear violation of property rights over their body) and failing to help someone survive (where they could survive with my assistance, but through my inaction they die—which is not a violation of property rights). I am not claiming it is virtuous to let someone die, but in my view it does not constitute aggression. Stepping over an injured person in the street is something I consider abhorrent, yet inflicting violence on someone who refuses to help is unjustifiable; I apply the same standard to withholding a blood transfusion from a dying person... and likewise to a mother refusing to provide her body for a child's survival. Personally, I find it distasteful and do not support it, but in my view it does not violate the NAP, and no one should force her to carry the pregnancy to term.
The Value of Going Bankrupt

Bankruptcy is generally seen as an unpleasant event (and it certainly is for those affected); in debates about the market, critics often argue that leaving things to the free market would cause some businesses to fail. Yes, that is true; and it is an argument in favor of the market, not against it! When an enterprise fails, it means it is unprofitable; but what does that signify? That people value the resources consumed by the business more than the goods it produces—meaning it is wasteful (it consumes something valuable and yields something of lesser value). The unforgiving market condemns such firms to demise (or to transforming their operations); this is undeniably unpleasant for the owner and employees, but beneficial for everyone else, because someone more capable will fill the gap in the market (otherwise they will suffer the same fate). Bankruptcy is the mechanism that ensures we are surrounded by the best; the rest are forced to do something they are better at.
Social Engineering

Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes accused of being social engineers because they allegedly "plan out their utopia" and then seek to force it onto people; on the one hand, I understand why some think this (in their eyes, anarcho-capitalism may resemble certain utopias drafted by social engineers), but on the other hand, few things could be further from the truth. Anarcho-capitalists often describe how a free-market society might function; they do so not out of a desire to impose that model on anyone, but because they are constantly bombarded with questions like: "And how would this or that work without the state?" They then venture into various predictions that might resemble the blueprint of a social engineer's utopian world; but anarcho-capitalists present these solely as illustrative possibilities and would never force them upon anyone, as that would contradict the core philosophy. We want to grant people freedom and govern nobody; that is the very opposite of social engineering.
Property and Human Rights

Anarcho-capitalists are often accused of caring solely about
property rights (or the Non-Aggression Principle)
while dismissing human rights and "human beings" as such; here, I fear, lies a fundamental misunderstanding of what anarcho-capitalism, the Non-Aggression Principle, and property rights actually mean. It is not just about owning inanimate objects, but also—in fact, primarily—about self-ownership: that a person owns themselves, their body. From this stem various "human rights" (such as the right not to be murdered, restrained, physically harmed, and so forth). Granted, these human rights are not formulated identically to those in the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms—mainly because, unlike the Charter, they are consistent (
the Charter is inconsistent, as it guarantees rights that cannot be fulfilled without violating the rights of others
). Anarcho-capitalists are not indifferent to "human rights"; quite the contrary—they are anarcho-capitalists precisely because they care deeply about them.
Interest in Politics
Lamenting Poverty Over Time

Socialists have always complained about the "poverty of the common man," typically using it to justify redistribution and robbery of the wealthy; however, I find it instructive to examine what they meant by "poverty" across different eras. Initially, it meant people lacking enough to eat; then the definition shifted, and anyone lacking sufficiently comfortable housing was labeled poor; over time, further amenities were added; and today, even someone who has food, shelter, abundant leisure, and can even afford modest domestic vacations from time to time is considered "poor." These are the "poor" the state is meant to help. If the criteria for poverty keep shifting like this, there will always be a pretext to legalize plunder in the name of the "poor" (who live better today than the wealthy of the past). But why are the poor continually better off? Through capitalism, of course: while not based on equality like socialism, it generates so much wealth that today's "poor" have more than yesterday's "rich."
Home Ownership for Young People

A new "problem" has emerged in society: young people lack sufficient means to purchase their own homes, so they "must" take out mortgages. All kinds of socialists lament where the world is heading, what a disaster it is, and what ought to be done (specifically, how the state should fix it); and where is the world heading? Toward prosperity. This "problem" is completely illusory, as never in history have young people had the resources to purchase their own homes—there is nothing new about this. On the contrary, never in the past were the young (or the elderly) so wealthy and secure; in fact, we live so comfortably that we have forgotten that the default state of mankind is poverty and harsh, wild nature. Wealth, homes, and technology are things that accumulate over time; and the world is moving toward more and more young people owning their own homes... only for socialists to whine that young people don't have their own private jets.
Jobs

The doctrine of "job protection" is largely based on the mistaken notion that there is a finite number of jobs in the world (or in a country); this, however, is an illusion akin to the claim that the world's total wealth is a fixed pie. Neither is true: as wealth continually expands (just compare our living standards today with those of a few centuries ago), people continuously develop new needs. Whereas people once rejoiced simply to have food, today they desire entertainment, travel, fine homes, cars... and when the day comes that they have all of that, they will want even more (new forms of recreation, space travel, floating or underwater cities, hovercraft...). Accordingly, new jobs will continually arise (and if machines take over all work one day, all the better: people will not have to labor, their needs will be satisfied without work, leaving them with ample free time).
Let's Regulate X!

X can represent aggressive violence and property rights violations (murder, robbery, rape, property destruction...); let us put that aside for now and consider cases where X is anything else (that is, non-violent, property-respecting activity). What does a call to regulate X actually mean? In practice, it is a call to use aggressive violence against someone who is minding their own business and harming no one. It means: "That person over there is doing something on their own property and with their own resources that I dislike; let us force them to stop and submit to my will." If you stated that sentence plainly to an ordinary person, they would almost certainly condemn it; yet the vast majority of people actively endorse various regulations of that very kind.
Yet it is the exact same thing
, differing only in phrasing. The power of state propaganda is fascinating: thanks to it, one need only rephrase the same premise into words presented to us by the state as "desirable"... and presto, outright rejection turns into enthusiastic agreement.
The Greedy Capitalist

Many people despise ruthless capitalists because they "only care about money"; but what does it actually mean when someone in a free market (that is, without violating property rights) "goes after money" and profits? Such an individual buys (and consumes) something, and sells something (not necessarily producing it, though they may); they are either an entrepreneur who buys inputs (materials, labor...) and transforms them into a finished product, or a speculator (or intermediary) who buys what they later (or elsewhere) sell. In both cases, the value they consumed is lower than the value they provided to others (even in the case of a speculator—let us not forget that value is subjective and changes over time, the cost theory of value having been refuted); their profit reflects how much they enriched society. Granted, a capitalist whose sole value in life is money might not make the ideal life partner; but to those who trade with him, he
clearly brings value
.
Who "Rules" under Capitalism?

A superficial first answer might be that giant multinational corporations rule; but for deeper insight, one must ask what makes those corporations so massive, where their influence actually originates. The truth is that this size, power, and wealth are granted to them by their own customers—that is, "ordinary people"; they are the ones from whom power emanates in a free market, as they
cast their "votes" daily with their wallets
. If customers stop buying from a corporation, it loses its power and wealth; if they patronize it, they empower it. Under free-market capitalism, it is the consumers who truly "rule"; corporations merely serve their desires—which may indeed be tasteless, short-sighted, or shallow (just look at what people buy), but that is a reflection of people, not capitalism. Blaming capitalism for this is like blaming a mirror for reflecting an unflattering face.
Hated Capitalism
Global Injustice

I often hear people earning below-average wages speaking venomously about the "top ten percent" and the like; they view it as a grave injustice that they don't belong among them. I find this utterly absurd. Why? Because typically, they do! Even poor people in the Czech Republic rank among the wealthiest individuals on Earth. We live in one of the richest corners of the planet and live high on the hog; all of us (even factory workers and supermarket cashiers) belong to the global "top ten percent" (and many likely to the top five percent). Even someone living "hand to mouth" here does not starve (unlike multitudes around the globe); unlike the vast majority of mankind, these folks often enjoy free weekends, work roughly eight hours a day, and get by... yet they complain about not having more leisure, more cash for fancier vacations, a better car, and so forth. And once society becomes even wealthier, they will complain about not owning yachts, simply because some people do.
Rule of the People

Imagine a decentralized society where people express their will through market exchanges: what they like and desire, they
voluntarily finance
, while for goods they have no interest in, they simply refuse to pay, thereby clearly articulating their preferences. Projects whose outputs are valued less than the resources they consume simply never get built, because in such a society the means to execute them will be absent, since no one redistributes wealth by force. In contrast, imagine another society functioning more or less like the first... except that some
democratically elected government
subsidizes certain loss-making projects (against the wishes of those whose money is taken to do so) while taxing and regulating profitable ones. As a result of these interventions, some things exist contrary to taxpayers' wishes, while others never materialize even though people desire them (being banned or burdened). The pivotal question is: which of the two scenarios represents the "rule of the people" to a greater degree?
Homo Economicus

Economic man is a theoretical construct used in certain economic models: a hypothetical individual who seeks solely to maximize his (financial) profits, buy as cheaply as possible, sell as dearly as possible, and always behaves completely logically. This construct was sharply criticized by Austrian economists (notably Ludwig von Mises) for its blatant divergence from reality; any conclusions deduced from such assumptions cannot be applied to the real world, because real people simply do not act that way (while they always strive to maximize their utility, this utility is not merely financial, but comprehensive—including emotional fulfillment). The Austrian school of economics, upon which anarcho-capitalism is grounded, works with real human beings; in light of that, I find it utterly absurd how often homo economicus is brought up against Austrians or anarcho-capitalists as a supposed flaw in their reasoning, even though they themselves are the ones who point it out.
Taxes of State Employees

Why do state employees pay taxes? Well... first and foremost, it must be said that they pay them formally, not in reality. The state takes money under threat of violence from everyone who earns it in the private sector; those paid by the state also pay taxes on paper, but that is merely an accounting gimmick: the state gives them X and takes back Y; in reality, it could just give them X minus Y, take nothing, and the outcome would be identical. Why doesn't it? First, to make state employees themselves feel as though they aren't freeloading on other taxpayers (which works wonderfully—witness the famous quote by an unnamed bureaucrat: "If it weren't for us state employees, who would pay the taxes for all those self-employed people?"); and second, to paint these individuals in as "normal" a light as possible. But what ought to be normal is providing services funded through voluntary payments—certainly not being paid with money
seized from someone under the threat of violence
. Stop the state!
How Much Is a Human Life Worth?

In connection with the coronavirus, many have begun discussing the value of human life in the sense of how much money makes sense to spend to keep someone from dying; and two principal schools of thought prevail:
1/ A calculation based on GDP per capita, or the market value of goods and services produced by an individual minus the cost of their education and upkeep.
2/ The value of human life is priceless; and anyone who attempts to calculate it is callous, inhumane, and reprehensible.
I agree with neither approach. The first ignores non-monetary utility; the second ignores reality (its logical conclusion would be dedicating all existing resources purely to saving lives, forbidding anyone from spending time or money on anything else). What, then, is my answer? The price of each of us is different; and to save any given individual, it makes sense to expend precisely as much resources as people (including the person themselves) are willing to contribute voluntarily, but no more than that individual would wish. A universal price for human life is about as nonsensical as claiming that all people are identical.
Individual Failure

Someone shared a third-party text about police harassment in the
Svobodný přístav Forum
. Because it was just the right length for the Sewers, I asked the author if I could publish it here (under her name). She declined, explaining that she did not want to disparage the police over the failure of an individual. I respect her decision; for those interested,
I am merely posting the link
. Yet I ask: how many obvious systemic flaws of the state are people willing to excuse as "failures of individuals"? Yes, an individual committed wrongdoing; but what else can we expect when we confer power upon a handful of individuals selected from those who, under present conditions, actually desire to become cops? Or politicians: when power is handed to individuals who first claw their way through internal party infighting to the top and then run the slickest election PR campaigns, how do we expect them to govern? When a private firm deceives a client, no one blames the specific teller behind the counter where the contract was signed; so why, when it comes to the state, does everyone blame the individual employee, while almost no one faults the entire institution?
Dan Steigerwald at deCentrála: The Talk Is On, We Have a Government Exemption

Dan Steigerwald will be giving a talk at deCentrála today; since Babiš is a huge fan of anarcho-capitalism, we negotiated a government exemption for this event.
However, just in case someone doesn't believe it, the identical talk will be repeated on the first Wednesday of next month, that is, on May 6th.
I Choose You, Prymula!

Because Vojtěch may be a handsome guy, but he's also a singer and a lawyer, Babiš pulled another ace from his sleeve: "I choose you, Prymula!" An epidemiologist might just be the winning horse for handling an epidemic! And words of wisdom are already pouring out of him: first, face masks until there are zero infected, which I understand. But then we have a proposal to, firstly, ban discount promotions. Are you kidding me? Isn't it enough that government measures (some of which I consider reasonable) will hurt the economy and people won't have enough money? Are we going to take away their ability to buy things on sale, too? Moreover, right here I would really worry about how temporary such a measure would actually be.
Far more critical, however, I consider the statement about closing the borders for months or even years. Yes, there was a time when such a measure made sense; that was precisely when Babiš and Vojtěch were telling us that everything was under control and there was nothing to fear. Closing the borders back then could have prevented the infection from reaching the Czech Republic. Now it is already here—and spreading. If we managed to stop its spread and isolate the infected, closing the borders would, of course, make sense again; but either that will happen in the coming weeks (which is questionable), or never (the infection gets out of hand). If the infection spreads worldwide (which it probably will) and the prevalence of infected people in the Czech Republic does not differ significantly from the prevalence abroad, what is the point of keeping borders closed?
Profiting from Someone Else's Misfortune Is...

All my life—and particularly in recent days—I have been hearing that "profiting from someone else's misfortune" is morally reprehensible, pathetic, despicable, and the like. Can anyone explain (logically) why it is wrong for someone to help people in need and charge (perhaps a lot) for it? When I picture myself in distress, I would much rather appreciate someone offering me help for a mountain of money than someone who offers nothing and merely condemns the former. An offer of help for big money can always be turned down. How, then, can it be worse than no offer at all? Why is someone who provides expensive help so often viewed more unfavorably than someone who doesn't help at all? At worst, I won't accept expensive help, which makes it at least as useful to me as no help. And finally, it isn't clear to me why people who so vehemently condemn "profiting from someone else's misfortune" usually hold firefighters and doctors in high regard, whose livelihoods directly depend on the misfortune of others.
National Self-Sufficiency

The doctrine of "national self-sufficiency" has long been quite popular; and like many popular things, it doesn't make much sense upon closer inspection. First, let us ask why self-sufficiency should exist solely at the national level; wouldn't it be even better to be self-sufficient at the level of a city? A street? Or even a family? Or perhaps for everyone to be self-sufficient individually? Such ideas obviously make no sense, as they would plunge us into poverty due to the absence of the
division of labor
. But how does protectionism on a smaller scale differ from protectionism on a larger scale? Only in that on the smaller scale, it is more visible; economic laws apply internationally as well: Production (say, of food) within a country suffers from the same ailments as production (say, of food) within a household; it is more efficient when everyone specializes in what they are good at (and then exchanges the resulting product with others on the free market) than when everyone tries to do everything. For the division of labor means wealth; isolationism and protectionism mean poverty.
Usury

Most people condemn usury; I, however, maintain that it is an unequivocally positive phenomenon. Why? If someone offers a loan with a dizzyingly high interest rate, there are two possibilities: The recipient either declines the offer, in which case nothing happened and the situation is the same as if no offer had been made; or they reach an agreement, which means the borrower himself considers taking the loan preferable to declining it (otherwise he wouldn't borrow). What does this mean? That the creditor offered him a better alternative, thereby
improving his situation
(by the borrower's own standards); this holds true regardless of the borrower's desperate plight or the interest rate. Whoever dislikes this is welcome to compete with the creditor and offer the poor soul a loan on better terms; if he doesn't, criticizing usury is sheer audacity coming from his mouth. Why? Primarily because he did not do even as much for the borrower as the usurer, who at least offered an alternative (albeit a desperate one) to his desperate situation!
Who Would Handle... the Coronavirus Without the State?

Lately people have been asking me how pandemics would be handled in a stateless society; who would keep people in quarantine? Well, security forces, people with guns—much like today. Except they wouldn't answer to governments, but to private security agencies operating in the territory. They would act in the interests of clients—and in the interest of health insurance companies, which would have a direct financial incentive to participate. So what would be the difference? First, in the accountability of all actors: while a politician can screw up anything and bear zero personal responsibility, market actors pay for their mistakes (an unnecessarily extensive quarantine could bring a barrage of lawsuits and damages for restricting personal freedom, while lax enforcement leads to loss of clients, reputation, or money); and second, without the state, no one would come up with such foolish ideas as banning disease testing by private laboratories or price controls on respirators (which reduce the incentive to urgently produce more).
Pavel Ševčík at deCentrála: Bitcoin Anonymity and Its Risks

The topic of the last
lecture on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club
was an introduction to cryptocurrencies, especially Bitcoin.
Today we will follow up directly on the previous lecture; Pavel Ševčík will be talking about Bitcoin anonymity! Contrary to popular belief, Bitcoin was designed as a pseudonymous system, not an anonymous one; however, anonymity can be achieved with a little effort.
You are all cordially invited to the next lecture, which takes place on April 1st; Dan Steigerwald will be speaking. He will explain to us why socialists are right about everything—save for one tiny detail.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 19:00 at the
(de)Centrála club
.
The EU vs. Batteries

The EU isn't just trying to
standardize chargers
; it is trying to force mobile phone manufacturers to produce only devices with replaceable batteries. It might seem that something like this would help us; but is that really the case? First, there isn't actually much consumer demand for it; if there were, manufacturers would offer such phones as a competitive advantage. Most people, however, like to replace their phones frequently and buy new, faster ones with better features; on the other hand, those who put off buying a new phone for years (like me) can buy a power bank for a few hundred crowns. Second, integrated batteries also offer technological advantages: they adapt better to the phone's form factor, saving space or increasing capacity; moreover, they are better sealed against moisture and dirt. Although I belong to the group of consumers who would appreciate replaceable batteries, I don't want to shove my preferences down others' throats; let the market decide, not the EU.
The EU vs. Chargers

For several years now, the EU has been trying to force manufacturers to standardize chargers for all mobile phones and certain other devices. At first glance, this seems like a service to consumers; but what about a second and third look? First, gradual standardization happens on the market even without legislation; USB-C is already a widely adopted standard, so whoever wants it has plenty of good options. And second—imagine if the EU had succeeded in passing such legislation ten or fifteen years ago; what would have happened? Whatever was used for charging at the time would most likely have been mandated as the universal adapter—something over which data typically could not be transferred. If we had frozen development with such legislation, we quite possibly would never have reached what we have today: a single cable for both charging and data transfer. The question is: What will we deprive ourselves of over the next ten years if we freeze technological development at the current standard?
Totalitarianism Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow

Totalitarianism does need an ideology to function, but no specific one—almost any can serve, though some are more suitable. Of course, a totalitarian regime can be based on the divinity of a monarch, racial purity, class struggle, but also on virtually anything else from the practically inexhaustible wealth of possibilities human imagination has to offer. For far more than the specific ideology, what truly matters is the way the state functions and its practices. Totalitarianism does not lie in divinity, racial purity, or the working class; it lies in controlling (nearly) all aspects of people's lives, while it makes no difference what ideology the state uses to justify these practices. In practice, this means, among other things, that every new regulation, every expansion of legislation, every mandatory registry and data collection, every additional control over our lives—these are all steps toward totalitarianism, entirely regardless of how we justify and excuse them.
Unfortunately, this is something most people fail to realize, so individual ideologies of the past are demonized and guarded against, while at the same time we remain blind to the real totalitarian threats we face day in and day out. What are they?
That is what I spoke about
at the
Free Port Conference 2020: Totalitarianism Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow
.
I also
published an article on Mises.cz
that inspired us to host the conference.
How Would the Free Market Solve...?

If I had to say which question I answer most often in my life, it would certainly be variations on the theme of how the free market would solve this or that; the paradox is that I can never answer with certainty. I only give people—better or worse—estimates; not that I cannot imagine various free-market solutions—given my imagination, quite the opposite—but firstly, I can never know which of the possibilities would actually materialize, and secondly, I consider it very likely that millions of entrepreneurs in a free market, striving to enrich themselves by solving any given problem, will come up with something far better than anything I could ever think of. After all... if the free market could be predicted, it could also be centrally planned. You can therefore view my answers as worst-case scenarios; imagine yourselves (or others who actually tried) a hundred years ago attempting to predict the shape of today's capitalism. Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams—and the free market even more so!
Tax Havens

Tax havens are (as a result of massive state propaganda) widely despised; the state (and consequently many citizens) tries to portray people who pay taxes there as pariahs. Do tax havens harm us, then? No! Quite the opposite. First, one must realize that untaxed money is not "stolen" (on the contrary—
taxes are robbery
and not surrendering them is self-defense against it); second, this money doesn't vanish into thin air—it is simply that politicians won't decide how to spend it, but rather those who earned it (which is purely a good thing); third, even a company that pays no taxes at all is undeniably a positive force in the economy as long as it sustains itself (it provides customers with value they appreciate, otherwise they would not pay for it voluntarily); and finally, fourth, tax havens provide competition for tax hells (countries with high taxes risk companies relocating to those with low ones). I am glad for every tax haven and every entrepreneur who pays taxes there instead of here.
Do We Live in Capitalism?

Capitalists and socialists mostly agree on one thing—and Mises already agreed with Marx: Capitalism means that the means of production are privately owned; under socialism, the means of production are owned by the state. So far, so clear. However, many sometimes forget that from this definition, it is fairly obvious that "pure" capitalism or socialism are rather exceptional states; we mostly live in a society that is to some extent capitalist and to some extent socialist (so capitalism and socialism are not binary). Because everyone tends to notice primarily the things that don't work the way they want, socialists love to claim that we live in capitalism, whereas capitalists say the opposite; how do we determine who is closer to the truth? Even leaving aside the fact that—especially nowadays—it isn't entirely clear what constitutes a "means of production," we run into the distinction between who owns something de jure and who owns it de facto.
Imagine a hypothetical state of affairs where the state completely directs the means of production, but de jure the owners of businesses are straw men (who decide nothing); this state of affairs is undeniably de facto pure socialism (Hitler's National Socialism came close to this). In today's overregulated world, while the state may not have exclusive decision-making authority, through its regulations it de facto deprives owners of the means of production of a portion of their ownership (even if not de jure); legislation dictates how they may manage their property, intervenes in prices, wages, and working conditions, and in addition we surrender most of what we create to the state in taxes. To what extent the means of production are owned by the state and to what extent by the formal owner cannot be quantified objectively, as the impact of individual legislative restrictions is often subjective; we thus live in partial capitalism and partial socialism (except for sectors where the state is both the de facto and formal owner; those are purely socialist).
Who Speaks of Market Failure?

Have you noticed what kind of examples people typically cite as so-called "market failure"? Why, precisely those where their own preferences differ from what others want, so the market decides differently from what they would desire. A classic "market failure," for instance, is the demolition of a beautiful building so that a supermarket can be built on the site; but what does that actually mean? Only that people's utility from the supermarket is higher than from that building; if it weren't, those wishing to preserve the status quo could buy the land for more money than the shoppers are willing to spend (otherwise, it is obvious that the shoppers derive more utility from the land). It is called a so-called "market failure" by statists who want the building preserved and are dissatisfied with the outcome of peaceful, voluntary exchanges—where the alleged "rectification" of the situation consists in forcing free people to do what statists compel them to do rather than what they themselves want.
GDP

Many people take this economic indicator very seriously; for some, it is practically an idol. I am not claiming that this figure is entirely useless; in reality, it can be used to compare the wealth of different nations very roughly (seriously, very roughly—at least by order of magnitude; if one nation's GDP is a few percentage points higher than another's, it means nothing, but a difference of dozens or hundreds of percent does); its growth, however, does not necessarily signify anything good. There are numerous problems with this indicator, but the biggest one, in my view, is comparing apples to oranges (often rotten ones): the state adds its own expenditures to the value of goods traded on the free market. Even if the state paid thousands of people to dig holes and fill them back up, GDP would rise despite the obvious futility of such activity (the same applies to all other state waste); conversely, the informal economy, which unquestionably helps people, is not included in GDP... so beware of that.
VAT on Beer?

Alcoholic beer has a 21% VAT; draft beer consumed on premise has a 10% VAT. Non-alcoholic beer has a 15% VAT; on premise it has a 10% VAT. "On premise" means beer served at an establishment with customer facilities, not in a jug to go. Period, that's it. Although I welcome any criticism of Babiš, the government, or even the state, has this really become the most pressing issue of recent days? We live in a total legislative jungle of utterly impenetrable and unimaginably convoluted laws; running even the smallest business entails a mountain of bureaucracy. And nobody really seems to mind—at least not enough to make it a hot topic. Is VAT on beer really our biggest problem? Yes, let's criticize VAT on beer. But isn't criticism of the existence of multiple VAT rates more fundamental? And even more fundamental, criticism of VAT itself? And far more important still, criticism of the existence of taxation? And are taxes truly the primary way in which the state oppresses us?

Excessive Profit

Recently, for the fourth time in my life, a communist (a different one each time) with whom I was having a discussion claimed to me that because of the profits made by every entrepreneur in the production chain (e.g., mining – ore processing – component manufacturing – product assembly), all products are five times overpriced, so if production were nationalized, without those profits goods would be available for a mere twenty percent of today's price (and since they all cited the exact same number, I assume they read it somewhere, though I haven't found where); I won't explain here why that is nonsense, having done so
elsewhere
, but let me ask: If that is truly the case, why don't socialists simply set up non-profit enterprises within the free market instead of nationalizing, producing goods five times cheaper and grinding capitalist competition into dust, if they can deliver goods to people so much better than greedy capitalists?
Revenue Leaks

Yesterday I wrote about
GDP and the shadow economy
; I would like to expand on this topic a bit further. We often hear about how much money "leaks away" from the state due to the shadow economy. First of all, I'd like to point out that the state and society are two different things: while society is all of us, the state is a parasitic entity siphoning resources from the productive among us. Most importantly, however, no money ever "vanishes" as a result of the shadow economy; the state may not be able to dispose of it, but it remains in people's wallets. So when the finance minister talks about how much money "we" are losing due to the shadow economy, what he really means is that those resources are not at his disposal (the parasite), but at ours (the hosts); that is by no means bad, quite the contrary—
we ourselves know far better how to use our own money
than some bureaucrat does. Not to mention that even if we didn't, it is our property, and what we do with it is entirely up to us—everyone the engineer, driver, and conductor of their own fortune.
The State and Ownership

Is the state the guarantor of private property? It certainly proclaims itself to be; and to a certain extent, it truly is. Specifically, to the extent that it strives to enforce for itself
a monopoly on violating the property rights of others
, suppressing other entities when they attempt to do the same; so yes, the state protects people's private property—but only against robbers other than the state itself. As a result of the state usurping this role, many even believe that without it, private property would not exist at all; that, however, is a profound mistake, since people began appropriating things long before states ever emerged (even primitive humans used primitive tools), not to mention that even in times and places where state power did not reach (such as the American frontier or early medieval Iceland), the institution of private property never vanished. Let us not be misled: property rights do not need to be enforced by state power.

Technological Standards

Some people still believe today that we need the state to uphold technological standards; one socialist even told me during our recent discussion that without the state, we wouldn't even be able to screw in a bolt because the thread would have a different pitch, diameter, and thread profile. Why the bolt example is absurd is likely obvious to everyone at first glance: it makes neither economic (nor logical) sense to manufacture a bolt knowing nothing about the thread (I'd rather manufacture both). A Lack of Humility, or an Excess of It?

Libertarians are sometimes accused of being self-proclaimed "know-it-alls" suffering from a lack of humility when they assert that the free market can provide everything the state currently provides better and to greater satisfaction; but does a lack of humility truly lie behind these claims? Personally, I think it is quite the opposite: Libertarians do not believe any central planner can exist (a politician, bureaucrat, or group thereof) who could make better decisions about people's affairs than the people themselves; libertarians—unlike statists—are humble enough not to presume they know what is best for others, and therefore do not feel entitled to use violence to compel others to conform to their own vision of an "ideal world." And so I ask everyone: let us be humble, let people act, for each individual is the foremost expert on how to live their own life; by all means advise people, help them... but without aggressive violence.

Why Did the State Buy a 400-Million E-Shop?

Yesterday I wrote about
the state's 400-million e-shop
. Today I would like to answer the question: how can the state afford such a thing? Well, it's quite simple. The state is not a free-market firm; it does not serve customers. It is a monopoly on violence; and as an organization, it is not accountable to citizens for anything. In the event of major blunders, it may penalize and replace someone from its ranks if that helps PR; but it doesn't have to change anything about the underlying operating principles that cause those blunders, because it holds force, making it easier to ban competition than to serve people. The main problem with the 400-million e-shop is not the price tag; it is the involuntary nature of the entire transaction that allows it to occur under such terms in the first place. And complaining about the price is, as anarcho-capitalist Dan Steigerwald put it: "...like a woman raped in a park complaining that she didn't get flowers and was left lying in the mud."
A 400-Million E-Shop from the Public Purse

The State Transport Infrastructure Fund purchased an e-shop for highway vignettes for 400 million CZK without a public tender; and everyone is up in arms. Why? Well, because it's expensive. And because nobody in their right mind would buy an e-shop with five and a half items for 400 million crowns. Clearly an overpriced contract! And how do we know? Quite simply: we know what e-shops cost on the market. And we assume that government purchases should be in a similar ballpark to market ones. So when they differ by orders of magnitude, media outrage erupts. Just as Americans weren't thrilled when the U.S. Army
bought a toilet seat for the equivalent of 45,000 CZK, or a hammer for 30,000
.
We all know what an e-shop (or a toilet seat or a hammer) should cost; but we know that solely because market prices exist in that industry; if they didn't, we wouldn't have the foggiest clue. Well... and that is precisely what happens in industries where the state holds a monopoly: nobody knows what Pandur APCs should cost, nor services like courts, police, or education. In those sectors, market mechanisms are almost completely absent, prices are dictated more or less by governments, and nobody has any benchmark to judge how realistic they are or how much anyone would willingly pay for services of such quality. We simply trust the state that these surely won't be overpriced—because when such excesses occur right where they are easy to spot, surely no bureaucrat or politician would dare pull the same stunt where detection is inherently impossible.
Surplus Value

Surplus value represents the cornerstone of the communist justification for the revolutionary violence of the "working class" against "exploiters"; and unfortunately, this explanation makes sense to far more than just communists: workers produce goods that possess some value, the capitalist sells them, pays a portion of the proceeds to employees, spends a portion on other production expenses, and retains a portion (which is precisely that surplus value). However, this line of reasoning completely ignores the subjectivity of value: nothing possesses objective value in and of itself; value is imputed to goods by human beings. What does this mean? That nothing like "surplus value" actually exists: the capitalist purchases people's labor at a market price (for the workers, this price is obviously higher than their subjective valuation of that labor, otherwise they wouldn't work for him; for the employer, the reverse is true, otherwise he wouldn't employ them), and then sells the manufactured goods to customers at a market price (because for them, their value exceeds that price).
Not All Evils Are Created Equal

Totalitarianism is a state in which the government attempts to control virtually all aspects of its subjects' lives on a massive scale.
Dictatorship is the rule of a narrow group (or individual).
Democracy is majority rule.
Fascism is a totalitarian dictatorship with significant elements of egalitarianism (collectivism), nationalism, militarism, and a certain form of progressivism.
Nazism is the combination of fascism with racism (the master race theory) and anti-Semitism.
If we proceed from these (generally accepted) definitions, we arrive at the following (generally overlooked) conclusions: Totalitarianism does not have to be a dictatorship; a dictatorship does not have to be totalitarian (though it typically is). A democracy cannot be a dictatorship, but it can be totalitarian (and often is; majority rule may seek to control virtually every aspect of its subjects' lives). Nazism and fascism are not the same thing; fascism does not have to be racist or anti-Semitic (Nazism does). Not every dictatorship or totalitarian regime is fascism. A police state is totalitarian, yet it needn't have a dictator; even a constitutional state under the rule of law can be totalitarian (if sufficiently repressive laws exist). Democracy means majority rule, not liberty—and certainly not "goodness" or "protection of minorities."

,
cartel agreements

A Quarter Century Since the Death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today marks exactly twenty-five years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses—Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"—departed this world just short of his 69th birthday; his life's work was the consistent, logical synthesis and extension to their logical conclusions of two traditions that had seemingly little in common: anarchism and the Austrian School of economics. Anarchists frequently faltered in economics, and proponents of the Austrian School failed to apply their (sound) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and arrived at the brilliant realization: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This insight and its full comprehension fundamentally changed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
What If X Didn't Exist Without the State?

You can substitute absolutely anything for X... roads, schools, charity, research... literally anything. Once you do, two possibilities arise: Either we need X so much that we are voluntarily willing to pay more than the cost of providing X; or we don't, meaning the resources we are willing to sacrifice for X fall short of its costs. In the first case, anyone who starts offering X can make a profit (people will pay him more than what it costs him to produce X, provided the above condition holds); there is no reason to doubt whether X would be available just because providing it without a state might seem tricky—if a profit can be made, someone will step up to provide it. In the event that we are unwilling to cover the necessary costs for X, then X will most likely not come into existence at all; and that is purely a good thing, because under those circumstances, providing it would represent economic waste (people value X less than the resources consumed in producing it).

Aggression or Non-Aggression? That Is the Question!

Although most people support regulations and laws enforced through threats of violence against the innocent, virtually everyone condemns threatening innocents with violence; can you feel the contradiction? When
I argue against regulations based on this very violence
, the responses are like carbon copies: The person first claims that it's absurd; when I explain that state violence against the innocent genuinely does take place, they change the subject and object that "we couldn't manage without it" (even if they were right, that doesn't refute my claim that violence occurs; rather, it confirms it); when I point that out, another unsubstantiated dismissal follows, or more excuses for why it's impossible any other way, or at best a very grudging admission. For most people, however, even uttering such a thing is an ordeal (blatantly obvious though it is); they prefer to pretend it simply isn't happening. That is why I believe most people do not actually accept state violence; rather, they turn a blind eye to it. Let's show them the truth!
Information Privacy

People care more and more about who stores what information about them; many are sensitive about it, some even specifically so that nobody profits from it (targeted advertising, recommended products, and the like—personally, I tend to welcome these practices, though I fully understand why someone wouldn't). The question is: why do the very same people who are so bothered when private entities collect (fairly superficial) information about them have no qualms when the state collects (deeply personal and sensitive) data? And if it were only about themselves... they very often fail to grasp and even trivialize it when it bothers someone else (for instance, arguments against EET [electronic sales reporting] based on the collection of sensitive business data were widely mocked). Wars and Progress
Free-Market Regulation

Most people picture the free market as an absolute jungle where no rules apply and anyone can do whatever they please; to some extent that is true, but not entirely. The free market is naturally not bound by coercive state regulations, but that does not mean we cannot regulate the behavior of others without a state at all. We have the ability
to reward those who act as we wish
, and deny rewards to those who do things we dislike; it is solely up to us whom we choose to do business with. Dislike products tested on animals? Fine, don't buy them; and the more people you persuade to do the same, the more animals you save. If you are successful enough in such efforts, those who do not test on animals will eventually dominate the market. In a free market, regulations emerge naturally: the kind people genuinely care about, such that they can demonstrate that interest through actions, not merely words.

The NAP and Veganism

I have already written extensively about the
non-aggression principle
; perhaps that is why vegans increasingly ask me why I don't apply it to animals. The answer is that the non-aggression principle stems from property rights, which animals not only fail to respect or understand, but are not even capable (and it seems never will be capable) of understanding; thus it makes no sense to me to recognize such rights towards them (if animals capable of understanding property rights were to appear, I would reconsider my stance). I completely understand and fully respect anyone who chooses not to exploit animals for personal utility, and I won't discourage them (in fact, I consider it a certain virtue); however, I believe that choosing otherwise is fundamentally neither worse (nor better). And just as vegans ask why I apply the NAP to humans but not to animals in general, one could just as easily ask why we don't extend the NAP to all living things outright (which would mean starving to death). Does anyone have an answer?
"Our" Resources

"Our" mineral wealth; "our" jobs; "our" land; and sometimes even "our" doctors (who brazenly dare to leave the Czech Republic, which was a huge scandal a few years ago). We frequently run into these—and many similar—phrases where "our" means Czech; ideas and arguments derived from such premises inevitably turn out completely misguided. Why? Well, raw materials have an owner, ergo they are his; claiming them as "our Czech resources" denies that ownership. Land in the Czech Republic likewise belongs to its owners, not to "all of us"; and as for "our" doctors, that is utter absurdity. What is especially insidious about this rhetoric is that it operates on a notion of quasi-ownership that directly violates property rights: whoever says "My country, my rules," meaning the Czech Republic and implying they have a "right" to (co-)decide how others live here, is directly negating the very premise they started from (my property, my rules) with respect to the actual owners of individual plots of land within the country.
