Subjective Theory of Value and Anarcho-Communism

Some time ago I was talking with an anarcho-communist; among other things, we discussed his idea that everyone should "have a right" to an apartment or house, because housing and a sense of security are fundamental human needs. I countered that while most people probably feel that way, someone might prefer other things over housing. He looked at me uncomprehendingly and offered an analogy: it's as if he bought chocolate for everyone and I reprimanded him for spoiling their taste because someone would have preferred a donut; it obviously escaped him that the state and socialists buy people chocolate with their own money. But that's beside the point right now; reflecting on our conversation on the way home, one thing struck me: We both want the same thing. Seriously. And what is that? We want people to be happy. The only difference between us is that while he is an intuitive proponent of an objective theory of value, I understand that value is subjective.
You sometimes ask me why I feel closer to anarcho-communists than to the conservative right; this is precisely the reason: While a different understanding of the theory of value separates me from the anarcho-communist and his notion of "housing for everyone," what separates me from the conservative right-winger and his "defense of the traditional family" (which causes homosexuals to suffer, which he knows and simply doesn't care about) is... I don't know... humanity? When an anarcho-communist tells me "housing for everyone," I understand that my task is to explain that we live in a world of scarce resources and show him Bastiat's "what is unseen"; but when a staunch conservative tells me he opposes gay marriage because "it's unnatural" (which is hardly his real reason, since he wouldn't advocate throwing away antibiotics and dying of infections just because that's natural) and because "marriage between a man and a woman is among traditional age-old values" (yet he wouldn't endorse slavery, which boasts an even longer tradition), what am I supposed to think?
Death to Speculators!

Nobody likes speculators; unsuccessful ones we might forgive because they've already suffered the consequences, but the successful ones are condemned by mainstream society. What do I say to that? These reactions are not only illogical and absurd, but completely inverted: a successful speculator actually helped others, whereas an unsuccessful one caused harm. The market is not a zero-sum game! Prices of goods are subjective and fluctuate over time. When there is a surplus, prices fall; when there is a shortage, they rise. A savvy speculator buys during times of surplus (helping struggling producers by driving prices up) only to sell during times of scarcity (helping consumers by driving prices down); in essence, he "smooths out" price volatility over time. If he makes a mistake, he may cause the opposite, harming others and paying dearly for it himself (as dearly as the damage he caused); paradoxically, only complaints against failed speculators could be deemed justified, yet those have harmed themselves first and foremost.
Business Cycles

People often think of business cycles (periods of rapid boom followed by bust) as something that has always existed, sometimes even as an inherent feature of capitalism; both views are mistaken. Business cycles occur as a result of (state-driven) artificial lowering of interest rates. The market exhibits this fascinating characteristic: when there are sufficient saved resources in a society, interest rates drop as a result of the law of supply and demand, motivating people to invest and produce goods that they then easily sell (as there are ample resources in the economy); artificial depression of interest rates induces entrepreneurs to make identical investments, only for them to find no actual market for the finished goods (society is poorer than the distorted price signals suggested).
I explained this phenomenon in greater detail in my lecture on money.
Yet for those of a practical bent unconcerned with theory, empirical evidence speaks for itself: so long as governments did not artificially suppress interest rates, business cycles did not occur.
A Zero-Sum Game?

Many claim that envy lies behind the hatred directed at the rich; and perhaps they are right (certainly in part). However, I believe that beyond envy, a widespread conviction plays a role that the market is a zero-sum game, meaning that if someone grows wealthy, it must happen at the expense of someone else becoming poorer. Yet that is demonstrably untrue: whenever a
voluntary exchange
takes place between two people, each person subjectively values the good they receive more than the one they give up (otherwise they would never enter into the transaction voluntarily). This is precisely why the wealth of society continuously expands; look at the conditions people lived in a few hundred years ago and compare them to how we live today. Society as a whole grows richer; even the poor become wealthier. In a free market, the person who prospers most is the one who best improves the condition of others. When a company makes loads of money, it isn't "at the expense" of its customers; both parties end up better off.

Che Guevara as a Symbol

Whenever there is demand for something, in our capitalist society it will typically become available sooner or later; and merchandise bearing the image of revolutionary Che Guevara is no exception. Many even perceive him as a symbol of freedom—and I never cease to be amazed. A murderer of hundreds who, alongside Castro, helped establish a brutal dictatorship in Cuba, where he subsequently held senior government positions (serving as a minister), ran the central bank (!), and aggressively centralized all power in society, he clearly acquired a taste for killing (and not just in battle), personally participating in mass executions when he undoubtedly didn't have to. When the powerful had a falling out (el Che with Fidel), he left Cuba for Zaire, then Bolivia; in both places, as a professional revolutionary, he continued harming people and spreading misery; yet he failed to achieve his goals, was captured, and ultimately riddled with bullets from head to toe. Judging by photographs, he was a genuinely handsome man; is that really the reason someone puts him on a T-shirt?
Intellectual Property

Many (though by no means all) anarcho-capitalists (myself included)
reject intellectual property
; this certainly does not mean I have any objection to people voluntarily entering into contracts for whatever terms they see fit—including agreeing not to distribute a purchased book or piece of software (under the threat of any contractual penalty agreed upon). What, then, do I consider unacceptable? For anyone to extend the reach of that contract to third parties who had nothing whatsoever to do with it. If Person A creates a work and sells it to Person B, who contractually pledges not to distribute the content but does so anyway, it makes no sense to prosecute Person C for further distributing it if Person C never signed any contract (and did not obtain the work by violating anyone's property). You might object that in practice it is hard to prove Person B's breach? Indeed it is; but when a crime is difficult to prove, do we prosecute innocent bystanders simply because we cannot track down the perpetrator?
Many wonder why some anarcho-capitalists do not recognize intellectual property even though property rights are sacred to them; the answer is simple: precisely because property rights are sacred to us, we cannot recognize intellectual property, as its very existence infringes upon property rights in tangible goods (if you forbid me from using my own bricks to build a house according to your design, you are restricting my property rights in my bricks). I elaborated on this in more detail in one of
my lectures
; for reading material, I recommend Stephan Kinsella's book
Against Intellectual Property
.

Promises Cost Nothing

Are you familiar with the Czech proverb: "Promises cost nothing"? And do you know where it holds doubly true? In politics!
Why? Because politicians, though they promise the moon, bear zero accountability for their promises; and not only that! To get their snouts into the trough, politicians must out-promise their rivals. The more decent ones promise only what they think they can deliver; the spineless will promise anything just to win elections. And because people tend to fall for alluring promises, political competition inevitably favors the greatest liars and populists. The market, on the other hand, punishes empty promises mercilessly: an entrepreneur who breaks his word loses customers, reputation, and capital. A politician? After losing an election, he merely finds a cushy post in public administration or on a supervisory board. As long as we put our faith in political promises rather than market mechanisms, we will continue to be baffled by the very same disappointments.

Regulating the Damage of Regulations

Many state interventions cause so many problems that they "must" be solved by... the state. How? I must disillusion naive readers who might have thought it solves them by repealing what caused them—it "solves" them with the very same tool that caused them: namely, additional regulations. A quintessential example is socialist healthcare and the healthcare tax (dubbed "health insurance"), which gives rise to further regulations in the name of public health and reducing treatment expenditures. The existence of the first regulation is then commonly invoked to defend preserving the second (dependent) one; this hardly surprises me with statists, yet sometimes even libertarians get trapped in this logical paradox, where although they favor repealing both, so long as the first exists they support the second. Examples: "The state seizes free-market resources from us to handle the migration crisis, so immigration must be regulated." "Vaccination must be mandatory until health insurance is voluntary."
Yet for a libertarian, this mindset is a highway to hell; good luck finding a regulation that can be repealed without causing problems for anyone that wouldn't have arisen in the absence of other state interventions. Example: opening borders is a problem because of welfare benefits; abolishing welfare benefits is a problem because of the labor code (people will struggle to find work); repealing the labor code is a problem because of barriers to entrepreneurship (employees face worse conditions for starting a business when unhappy with their employer); removing barriers to entrepreneurship is a problem because of tax evasion; tax evasion is a problem because of pensions; and so on. If we deem any of those problems serious enough to justify not repealing a regulation, then in light of the interpersonal incomparability of utility, we cannot logically withstand anyone declaring any other problem to be just as serious. The only sound path, in my view, is always to deregulate.
Immature People
Choosing a Partner

A snippet from a movie comes to mind (I don't recall which one) where actress Simona Stašová says: "I certainly won't marry someone who voted for Bush." That line, I believe, was intended to be humorous and hyperbolic, from which I'd deduce that for most people, that wouldn't be sufficient reason; and since my mind seems to work a bit differently, I'd like to ask how you feel about it, dear readers. I'd appreciate it if you shared your perspective in the comments: whether you are a libertarian or not, how essential is it to you that your partner shares these values with you?
Extortion Money

Allow me to quote something written long ago by OC—an anarcho-capitalist whom I hold in high esteem, as he has inspired what I do for over a decade; it is a (fictional) letter you receive after moving into a new home:
Dear neighbor,
Welcome to our quiet and pleasant neighborhood. I, of course, look after its peace and security, incurring substantial expenses in doing so; it is therefore only fair that these costs be shared among the other neighbors as well. Today is Monday; if you do not wire 50,000 CZK to my bank account by Friday, I am afraid my representative will pay you a personal visit early next week to collect 100,000 CZK. If you kick him out, he will return accompanied by a group of armed men who, if push comes to shove and you refuse to pay, will kill you. Should you, against all odds, manage to slaughter them or drive them off, an armed force twice as large and better equipped will arrive the very next day.
Everyone else on your street pays their annual contribution gladly, promptly, and properly; I trust that you will not become a disturber of our peaceful and harmonious coexistence.
Yours truly, M.V. (Minister of the Interior), m.p.
Pretty foul, isn't it? And if I told you that M.V. stands for Minister of the Interior and that this protection money is called taxes... does that change anything? If so, why? Feel free to share your thoughts in the discussion xD

Voluntary Slavery

May I voluntarily sell or donate myself into slavery? There is no consensus on this question among libertarians (neither among renowned authors nor in our community); and with my answer—an unequivocal "Yes!"—I join the ranks of those who are currently in the minority. Yet I cannot answer otherwise; why? It would not be consistent with the Non-Aggression Principle and foundational libertarian tenets. What does it mean to be someone's slave? That I am his property, he owns me, he can issue orders to me, and if I resist, he may even kill me. However, if we accept that individuals have the right to sell their organs (even if doing so costs them their lives), and also that they have the right to loan and borrow things (both of which libertarians endorse), then I can sell all my organs to anyone, and he can loan them back to me for my use for as long as I obey his every command, or as long as he pleases; in that case, I am his slave—he owns me and decides my fate.
Whoever disputes this must challenge either my right to sell my organs or the buyer's right to loan them back to me; yet hardly any libertarian would do so. Ergo, to remain consistent, one must concede the legitimacy of voluntary slavery. Some nevertheless object that even if someone owns my body, he cannot directly control it; but direct control is by no means a prerequisite of ownership—one can own animals without being able to directly control their bodies either. The objection that surrendering the capacity to act freely invalidates the contract upon signing also falls flat: if I sell or donate my heart to someone, I die, thereby relinquishing the ability to act freely far more definitively, yet I would be hard-pressed to find a libertarian who would want to deny me the right to sell or donate my heart. Why, then, could I not voluntarily become someone's slave? Whether we like it or not, it is the logically consistent consequence of the Non-Aggression Principle.

The Evolutionary Argument

People often ask me why, if anarcho-capitalism is so great, it hasn't prevailed in the "evolutionary struggle" against states; I realize that my answer—"What isn't yet, may still come to be"—sounds rather foolish at first glance, so I ask you for a second look. Human society is continually evolving, an evolution that will likely never end; history shows us that people believed in countless absurdities, and atrocities frequently took place in society that seemed entirely justifiable to everyone at the time, yet a matter of decades or centuries was enough to change everything. Slavery, for instance, endured for thousands of years, decisively winning the "evolutionary struggle" against non-slaveholding societies, until suddenly the tide turned—a paradigm in place since the dawn of time collapsed and crumbled to dust in a historical heartbeat. For that to happen, people fighting for the right cause had to refuse to accept the notion that because slavery had existed for so long, it couldn't be all that bad. But it was. It is. And it always will be. Just like states.
What a Wonderful World

Some time ago during a discussion, I was asked an intriguing question: someone asked whether, as a libertarian who views taxes as theft and laws as aggression, I find the world terribly evil and rotten; I'd like to share my answer here. I told him that I certainly do not, for I consider the world an utterly breathtaking and fascinating place. Yes, of course we don't have as much freedom as I'd wish, and we see bloodthirsty robber states all around us, but that is far from everything! We must not forget all the cooperating human beings working together and creating value; we must not forget the tremendous progress (both ethical and technological) that relentlessly drives humanity forward. And things (occasional turbulence aside) are heading toward the better: slavery has virtually disappeared, wars are less frequent, living standards (for both poor and rich) are climbing, and for the first time in history more people suffer from obesity than starvation... and while everything isn't perfectly fine, the world is a wonderful place to live.
Medicine, Drugs, and Double Standards

I find the topic of "drugs" fascinating, as it is shrouded in numerous myths propagated primarily by governments to justify their "War on Drugs"; I have tackled debunking them both
in speech
and
in writing
, and added
something more personal
as well. While some drugs are unquestionably reliable instruments for slow (and sometimes quite swift) suicide, the state portrays every illegal drug this way (starting from our school years through various anti-drug programs, while painting legal ones in a completely different light); many then distrust the government (which is fine) so intensely that they reflexively embrace the exact opposite of whatever the state claims as absolute truth (which is dangerous). Some people—often, coincidentally, the "all-natural" types suspicious of pharmaceutical companies—then underestimate drugs; though skeptical of vaccines and often even antibiotics, they have no qualms about experimenting with completely untested substances or ways of taking them. Please, let's not let the state manipulate us in either direction!
A Parallel with Slavery

As some have astutely noted, I relatively often draw a comparison between the institution of slavery and the state on various occasions; I'd like to pen a few lines about that analogy. It isn't strictly that we are slaves of the state (I probably wouldn't even phrase it that way), but rather about the mainstream public attitude toward the two institutions: Today, almost everyone recognizes slavery as abhorrent, yet just a few centuries ago that was not the case; and it is fascinating to see how people back then viewed those who first began proposing its abolition. It was deemed utterly impossible. It would trigger economic catastrophe. The slaves wouldn't be able to provide for themselves. It was a lovely theory, but unworkable in practice. These were viewed as extremist and radical ideas. The notion that a slave could disobey his master was about as unthinkable as the idea that a citizen could disobey an on-duty police officer. Yet change arrived extraordinarily fast...

Certainty Above All...

How long does it take for someone who has never looked into the subject to think through whether a stateless society could function? It involves an immense range of topics, questions, unknowns, and contemplating alternatives; such an intricate and multifaceted subject requires, in my view, hundreds of hours of reading and reflection—but even supposing one needn't delve quite that deep into everything, we could still anticipate dozens or at least several hours. I cannot imagine anyone thinking it through in a matter of minutes; yet the vast majority of people answer within seconds, without having ever heard anything about it. How is that possible? They are simply indoctrinated by state propaganda: they were taught that we need the state, and that's just how it is. So when we try to convince someone that the state is immoral, we don't start from scratch, but from their deep-seated conviction that we must surely be wrong. What can be done about that?
Separation of school and state is the solution.

Who Writes History?

Although I am not a historian and know next to nothing about academia in this field, I would like to share with you, dear readers, the perspectives of two historians that intrigued me during conversations with them. Both claimed that research grants are allocated by people who already hold a specific conception of historical events, and who are unwilling to fund research whose subject matter sharply contradicts their own narrative. In my opinion, this needn't be any kind of conspiracy (which I'm not particularly fond of anyway, being a great believer in Hanlon's razor)—it makes perfect sense on its own: those people simply consider funding something they disbelieve to be a waste of money. However, the consequence of this—quite natural—approach is that correcting major flaws in the prevailing perception of history becomes exceedingly difficult. If this happens, the root cause is not malice, but rather the socialist subsidization of historical research; the solution, as in so many other fields, would be
free-market funding
.
Without the State It Would Cease to Exist!

When discussing a stateless society, I often encounter objections that something (anything) would disappear without the state, and therefore we need a state; what's interesting is that the counterargument is entirely universal, regardless of the specific service or good in question. The crucial question is: Does the thing in question provide people with greater utility than the utility they would derive from the resources it consumes? If the answer is yes, then the objection collapses: people would acquire it even without the state (either individually or by pooling funds, but they would willingly part with the necessary resources because the final outcome is more valuable to them). If the answer is no, then that thing should not exist and the state should not artificially keep it on life support. Why? Simply because people can put those scarce resources to alternative uses that yield even higher utility; and since we live in a world of scarce resources, we shouldn't squander them.
Two Conversations

Whenever I have to wait somewhere, I read; that's why waiting doesn't bother me. A few days ago, however, I found myself waiting with nothing to read, so I simply sat and thought; I was distracted, however, by two conversations I happened to overhear. The participants in the first appeared to be the owner or CEO of a business and likely his sales manager; they were passionately brainstorming ways to make customers feel welcome and eager to return. The second conversation was between what looked like two nurses; they were jointly railing against patients daring to show up without an appointment, exchanging tips on how to "punish" the offender (making him wait longer than necessary so he wouldn't dare pull that stunt again). Do you see the contrast? While one group fights for customers, the other finds them a nuisance. Why? Well, to the former, clients bring resources, whereas to the latter, they drain them. Do the nurses think about it in these terms? Likely not; they probably aren't even conscious of it.
Hatred of Capitalism

Capitalism is hated by many people (much like anarchy, but let's set that aside for now); why is that? I believe, however, that we shouldn't be asking "why," but rather "what": what is it that these people actually hate? Typically one of two things: either the "unbridled capitalism" of the nineteenth century (relative to modern standards), or today's state-crony corporations. Hating nineteenth-century capitalism because people lived in harsher conditions than today (even though vastly better than in preceding eras) makes about as much sense as disparaging the invention of the steam engine because we possess more powerful machinery today; while branding state-entangled, overregulated corporations (which often draft legislation through lobbying to stifle competition) as "capitalist" reveals a profound misunderstanding of the concept. Capitalism means free markets and voluntary exchanges, not lobbying and bribing lawmakers; and it is up to us to explain that to people.
Respect for Authority

Many often complain that "kids these days" (naturally worse than previous generations—as every generation has felt) lack respect for authority, which they would gladly remedy with compulsory military service, or at least strict school discipline. But what does youth actually learn through such means? To grovel before an authority they did not choose for themselves. How can anyone possibly consider that a virtue? Respect and healthy humility are of course highly commendable, but they must spring from within the individual—he himself must choose who earns his respect, who is worthy of following. When we force upon him whom he must obey, we merely turn him into a puppet, blunt his willpower, and teach him to "shut up and toe the line." Have you noticed how rampant this is in schools, for instance? And it is hardly surprising: raising obedient citizens serves the state's interests perfectly—the teacher can later be seamlessly replaced by a cop, a bureaucrat, or a politician. Is that truly what you want for your children?
Dead Horses and Their Manure

Over a century ago, someone in New York felt there were far too many horses; he observed how quickly the horse population was multiplying and extrapolated future trends: sometime in the second half of the twentieth century, people in New York would be wading through a three-foot layer of horse manure, not to mention an ocean of dead horse carcasses. Does this strike you as absurd? It certainly does to me: for one, the author somehow overlooked automobiles (not that they existed in his day), but more importantly, even without automobiles, people would have resolved the issue long before they had to wade through excrement in the streets. How is it that when it comes to horses, everyone sees how ridiculous such reasoning is, yet as soon as someone promotes "sustainable development" based on equally absurd premises, everyone takes it seriously? When in reality, all models of sustainable development rely on precisely such linear projections and the assumption that human beings will never adapt or react to emerging challenges...

Key Libertarian Moments

During my life, I have spoken with many hundreds of libertarians; whenever we talked about what brought them to this philosophy, it usually came down to specific turning points that they typically remember very clearly and consciously—in my own life, there were two major libertarian "aha moments" (one concerning firefighters, the other concerning law) and several other quite significant ones. A wonderful moment was described to me by Dominik Stroukal, who was convinced by Murray Newton Rothbard and his commentary on the buying and selling of children; in a very brief nutshell: That transaction is good for the seller, good for the buyer, but ultimately and most importantly, good for the child as well! And what convinced you, dear readers? Please share in the comments; I am not just asking out of idle curiosity—I am trying to find the best arguments. I would like to find a strong common denominator across as many stories as possible, which I then want to apply to my rhetoric.
Let's Blame the Freeloader!

A lazy person who doesn't want to work and just latches onto the welfare system is often a favorite target of hatred, especially among right-wing conservatives. Why is that? At first glance, it seems like a fairly understandable idea: "He who does not work, neither shall he eat." (In connection with this text, I especially recommend that right-wingers Google who notoriously used this phrase.) But why should everyone have to work? If poverty or begging suits someone in exchange for a certain freedom and an enormous amount of leisure time, that is purely and entirely their own business; and if someone begs for a living, there is absolutely nothing wrong with that. The moment they come to ask the state for alms, a problem arises; but who is its source? The beggar, who is merely taking advantage of what he was told (by the state) is his "right," or the one who hands out other people's money? Blaming the former makes about as much sense as blaming the recipient of a thief's gifts for the theft instead of the thief himself.

Ancap in Nebe xD

What sentence can an anarcho-capitalist say to infuriate both a left-wing socialist and a right-wing conservative?
"I support the right of married gay couples to defend with fully automatic weapons their shops stocked with freely available drugs of all kinds, sold by minor employees unregulated by any labor code."
While this is a somewhat peculiar way to present the libertarian worldview, it is not for nothing that people say an anarcho-capitalist is someone who never adds the word "but" after saying: "I am a proponent of freedom."
At first glance, drug and gun regulation might seem like relatively unrelated topics; yet upon slightly closer examination, we find that typically, proponents of deregulating one would love to regulate the other with even greater fervor. But why? Logically speaking, the arguments for deregulating both are virtually identical in principle. Disagree? Then come have a chat with Terezka and me; afterwards, you might disagree even more. In any case, you will definitely get the chance to passionately debate these topics and try to convince others of your view—or perhaps learn something new.
We look forward to seeing you tonight at Bar Nebe!
Heaven on Earth

People often complain about how badly off the "common man" is and how his situation keeps worsening, requiring government intervention; honestly, I can think of no popular myth at the moment that is further from the truth (at least in Europe or America). First, the "common man" has never had it better in all of history than right now; we have plenty (often a surplus) of drinking water and food, we live in warm, lit homes, and we enjoy an enormous number of modern amenities. Second, the condition of the "common man" has probably never improved so rapidly; virtually every conceivable metric shows that our lives are getting better and better. Third, never before has so little labor been required of an average person to sustain themselves; we thus have heaps of leisure time (compared to virtually any conceivable period in the past). And finally, fourth, this is happening precisely despite government interventions; those can only make our wonderful situation worse.
Inability to Reconsider One's Views

Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes labeled fanatics, and statists very often insinuate that they are unwilling to change their minds and admit errors; I find such a claim fascinating and, to some extent, paradoxical. After all, almost all of us were raised on statism; nearly everyone originally believed in the state. Anarchists had to go through at least one fundamental change of worldview during their lives and admit a mistake; statists may have done so as well, but not necessarily. How, then, can statists accuse anarchists of being incapable of reconsidering their opinions and thinking critically, when anarchists have already demonstrated this ability at least once in their lives? Of course, it is possible that anarchists are mistaken in their view of the world and statists are right; nevertheless, the likelihood of someone having been fanatically indoctrinated is higher among statists, because they merely believe what was instilled into all of us back in elementary school.
Private Is More Expensive than State-Run!

Across society, there is a very popular, largely unquestioned belief that the private sector is more expensive than the public sector. Yes, higher quality is attributed to it, but in terms of price, almost everyone perceives the state as cheaper. But why should that be? In reality, there is no reason for it; the state is incapable of producing goods and services more cheaply than a private entity. On the contrary, it is more expensive because, in addition to the goods themselves, one must also fund bureaucracy, civil servants, central management, and the like. The difference is that state payments are hidden: while we clearly see the full amount we pay to a private firm, taxes for state services are detached (and, furthermore, split into numerous components to obscure the fact that the state takes roughly two-thirds of what we earn). Above all, however, we have been manipulated with such myths from an early age through the state education system, whose goal is to disseminate propaganda. So let us not believe dogmas, and let us always ask for reasons.
Faith in Socialism

It was not so long ago that many people widely believed the economy had to be centrally planned or else we would starve, because something as crucial as food production and distribution could not possibly be left to the free market. Thus, the state ran both—and it showed. After the revolution, what many had feared came to pass... and lo and behold, things suddenly began working much better! And, to everyone's "great surprise," the same happened to all the other sectors that were privatized; many, however, remained in state hands so their notorious problems could continue. In connection with this, two questions come to my mind: How is it possible that even though everything the state no longer manages thrives better, so many people still object that things would somehow be different for the sectors that remain state-run? And how can anyone believe that a state which cannot even ensure something as basic as toilet paper on store shelves will take good care of education or healthcare?
Anarchists and Other Anarchists

There is rivalry between anarcho-capitalists and anarcho-communists (and not only between these two schools, but also among many others related to them; I take these two as an example). Anarcho-capitalists reproach anarcho-communists for inconsistency, while the latter charge in return that anarcho-capitalists are not real anarchists. In principle, I don't mind this too much, but it strikes me how little each camp actually knows about the opponents against whom they define themselves. Most anarcho-capitalists draw their knowledge of anarcho-communists from fellow anarcho-capitalists who mock and caricature them (and vice versa). It is always sad to see critiques of capitalism along the lines of: "Capitalism is when the state gives privileges to banks." On the other hand, the reverse (the anarcho-capitalist critique of anarcho-communism) is often no better. Therefore, to anyone who wishes to criticize anarcho-communists, I recommend first going and speaking with them directly.
Fluid Gender and Sexual Identity

Lately, we have been hearing more and more often about people who are unsure of their "gender" identity. I don't mean "straightforward" transsexuals who are completely clear about their gender, where that clarity simply does not match their physical body, which can be addressed with surgery; I am talking about people who simply don't know, who alternately feel like women and men, or even beings of entirely different genders. I respect their identity (even if I am sometimes a bit confused about which grammatical gender to address them in—and I only know a few), and I don't feel it is any of my business. That is why I am baffled by the increasingly frequent outcries from defenders of family values about where the world is heading and how this threatens the traditional family. What? How could it? I cannot imagine what fragile state a family must be in if it is threatened by the mere existence of someone somewhere who isn't sure whether they are a woman or a man; I think pro-family warriors should primarily look after their own families and leave everyone else alone.
Taxing Against Work

Interestingly, excise taxes are often defended on the grounds that they reduce consumption: a tobacco tax curbs smoking, an alcohol tax reduces drinking, a fuel tax incentivizes people to conserve fuel (and nature), and so forth. This logic makes sense; taxes can indeed influence human behavior—not that this is a good thing, as it always ends up harming someone, but it works. The question then is: what effect does income tax have in this regard? By taxing labor, we genuinely disincentivize taxpayers from working, since they receive a lower reward for their labor. Combined with various welfare benefits and unemployment support, this is truly a rather effective tool for discouraging people from working. More or less the same can be said about VAT; although it goes by a different name, it has essentially the same effect—only not on employees, but on entrepreneurs. And how much different do you think it is with mandatory social and health "insurance" contributions?
Muh... Roads?

Many people consider it a serious problem for a free society that even the road network would be owned by private owners; why this would be nowhere near such an issue, I explain for example in my series on anarcho-capitalism. It is remarkable, however, that while we frequently hear questions like: "What if someone refuses to lease me their road in the city?", almost no one asks: "What if someone refuses to rent me their apartment in the city?" Why is that? Well, apartment rentals operate more or less on a free-market basis, and there is fundamentally no issue with them. Yet there is no reason why road owners should behave any differently from apartment owners—everyone simply wants to make a profit, and very few people are interested in owning land and doing nothing with it (in which case they can always sell it). Yes, occasionally there will be an uncooperative road owner, just as we occasionally encounter an uncooperative landlord today; however, most of them behave quite normally.

Ancap vs. an Ideal World?

Often in debates about anarcho-capitalism, one encounters a situation where a statist comes up with some hypothetical bad thing that could happen to someone and asks how the market would resolve it; it could be someone failing to pay health insurance and dying of an illness, or a child being abused by parents, and the like. Most free-market advocates then proceed to answer such objections in various ways (charity, etc.). There is nothing wrong with that, but I believe the very first point to make is that even the existence of the state does not prevent such tragedies—many people die as a result of poor medical care in a socialist healthcare system, and many parents abuse their children despite laws against it. For no one claims that anarcho-capitalism represents an ideal world where evil never occurs; yet we allow ourselves to be maneuvered into defending anarcho-capitalism not against the state, but against a utopian ideal world, whenever we accept the premise of the objection: "And what if <unlikely scenario> happens?"

Since I consider lectures in schools to be the most important, I gladly accepted an invitation to the František Palacký Grammar School in Valašské Meziříčí, where I will be debating ancap with students starting at 10:40.
And when the owner of the Tucan CAFÉ heard about it, he invited me for an afternoon discussion at their café. If you are nearby, come join us at 17:00!
Get Used to the Teacher, Accept the Politician

I have already written and said plenty about the direct indoctrination of children in state schools, which they are forced to attend under compulsory school attendance—lest the state kidnap them from their parents and subject them to propaganda anyway. However, I would like to mention another aspect of this monstrosity: because children are forced from an early age to accept violently imposed authorities in the form of teachers, they grow into adults for whom this behavioral pattern becomes completely natural, leading them to automatically accept other unchosen authorities as well—the state, the government, and politicians. The danger of schools therefore lies not only in direct indoctrination, but also in the fact that everyone accepts involuntary authorities as the norm and a "necessary evil." Of course, this does not mean that authority (in general) is bad—I only consider harmful those authorities that are forcibly imposed on someone. I do not believe that involuntary subjugation should be part of "preparing for life"; voluntary acceptance of authority, yes, but that cannot be coerced.
Compulsory School Attendance

Most people perceive compulsory school attendance as something beneficial, without any deeper societal debate about it. It belongs to those things that "everyone knows" and that "are just obvious"... so "obvious" that the vast majority of people do not even realize (and when confronted with this fact, they are surprised, often tapping their foreheads and finding it absurd) that in reality, compulsory school attendance—regardless of its potential benefits—means the state threatening parents that they must either put their child in school or the child will simply be kidnapped by child protective services and forced to undergo that school indoctrination anyway. And what do I mean by indoctrination? Well, for instance, precisely how one-sidedly compulsory schooling is presented in schools: its advantages are discussed, while the disgusting violence it entails is completely hushed up; through schools, the state teaches children how to be "good citizens."
Such a state of affairs is no coincidence, nor is it a conspiracy; it is quite public. Just look at the White Paper, the National Education Development Programme, where it is stated quite openly—teachers of all subjects are supposed to make good citizens out of their students. Imagine if any organization other than the state did something like this—forcing its education onto your children under the threat of forcibly taking them away. What if, say, a church made your children compulsory believers? What if McDonald's turned your children into "good customers" and you were forbidden to refuse? Would that be justified by the fact that children would also learn other things there? And if not, why tolerate something like that from the state? Sure, the state has the power to enforce it; but having power and using it does not mean it is ethical or excusable.
Anarchist Revolution?

Anarchy is (primarily due to the stances of many left-wing anarchists, such as anarcho-communists or anarcho-syndicalists) associated in the minds of most people with (violent) revolution; personally, however, I believe that anarcho-capitalism, at least, simply cannot be achieved through revolution. Why not? Well, even if a revolution were successful and an anarcho-capitalist seized state power, he would basically have two options: give people true freedom; but people today want a state, so the first thing they would do with that freedom is establish a state. The second option is to forbid them from creating a state, at which point he himself becomes the state. People can be coerced by violence into building the brighter socialist future, gassing Jews in the name of Nazism, or guillotining heads for the republic; but freedom cannot be forced upon them—they must arrive at it themselves.
Related to this is a favorite question, a frequent dilemma: sometimes someone asks me in a debate whether, if I had a button that could abolish the state overnight, I would press it (they usually hint that if the state suddenly vanished out of nowhere, chaos and violence would likely ensue). But such a choice is pointless in my view: either people want the state, in which case if I abolish it with a button they will immediately re-establish it, or they don't want it, in which case no buttons are needed. It makes no sense to deliberate whether to "uninstall" the state immediately or not, because the state can only be dismantled as quickly as people themselves desire; if we want to abolish it, let us convince people and demonstrate the benefits of freedom! I do not even believe people would then democratically "vote" for freedom, but rather that if the majority ceases to recognize the state, it will disintegrate regardless of any elections (though, of course, as society changes, it will be reflected in elections as well).
The Dull Masses?

Quite a few people (and years ago, I was one of them) feel that "average people" are not smart or capable enough, cannot take care of themselves, and generally constitute a "dumb herd." Naturally, each elitist who proclaims this considers himself above average (how could it be otherwise; after all, most people consider themselves above average). But where does this conviction that "almost everyone is an incompetent idiot" come from? In my view, it stems from the fact that we all have things in life that do not interest us, which we do not understand and have little desire to, because our priorities lie elsewhere—which means that all of us appear to be idiots in at least some respects. In our own case, however, we understand the reasons, comprehend them, and excuse ourselves, whereas with others we do not, seeing only their shortcomings in areas we personally deem essential.
Virtually every human being is a complex individual with strengths and weaknesses; people develop what they consider important and stagnate in what they don't care much about. And just because we constantly see many people around us behaving unwisely from our vantage point doesn't mean the "average person" is a moron. For one thing, we ourselves will act unwisely in many other matters from their perspective, but above all, we typically don't know the full context of their actions. What might seem stupid to us may simply be the result of their having different priorities, caring about different things than we do (which, by the way, makes it difficult for us to appreciate their qualities). To anyone who sees nothing but idiots around them, I recommend reflecting on whether they themselves might often appear the exact same way to others; I am not claiming people are "equal" or "equally good," but rather that there is really no objective way to judge.
The Path of Reconciliation

I cannot count how many times over the long years I've spent among libertarians I have witnessed anarcho-capitalists calling minarchists socialists, minarchists calling anarcho-capitalists fanatics, and anarchists of all stripes waging their endless war over who is a real anarchist and who is merely posturing; these are simply disputes where ad hominem attacks are never far away. Personally, it always saddens me, especially since I know from experience how easily such unnecessary conflicts can be avoided in the vast majority of cases simply by not wanting to argue and by behaving in a friendly manner. The other side almost always comes around after a while (true, recently an ancom responded to my conciliatory approach by telling me to fuck off with my empathetic act, but that happens only rarely). Seriously, try it sometime: look for common ground, try to understand your debate opponent.
I'm not saying you have to agree; it's enough simply not to treat the person you're debating with like an idiot just because they hold a different opinion. Try instead to look for shared touchpoints; it's possible far more often than it might seem. Then you might surprisingly discover all sorts of fascinating things—for instance, that anarcho-communism is not necessarily inconsistent. Let us ask ourselves the fundamental question of what our goal is: To persuade people, or to blow off steam and tell someone to get lost? In the latter case, anyone can handle that on their own, but regarding the former, let me remind you that picking a fight drives your opponent into an emotional state where they will refuse to accept the views of others, which is counterproductive. Not to mention that, even from the perspective of spectators, a civilized discussion looks much better than moronic yelling. I understand it is difficult at times, but from personal experience, I warmly recommend it.

Detecting Indoctrination

At my first lecture at Polis, I voiced a thought to which many people later returned in conversations with me, as they considered it essential; therefore, I am writing about it today. Exposure to propaganda often results in indoctrination that partially blocks our critical thinking; we then approach matters as if we "know" everything beforehand, seeking arguments and information not to discover the truth, but merely to confirm our preconceived opinions. The bad news is that this doesn't only apply to statists and state propaganda; even after someone opens their eyes, they can fall into the exact same trap on the opposing (or any other) side. Personally, a few years ago I caught myself doing just that in my reflections on anarcho-capitalism: I "knew" in advance where the truth lay, and stopped treating opponents' arguments as something that could actually persuade me. The good news is that to remedy this, simply being aware of it and admitting it fully is enough to change the mindset on its own.
How do you detect such a state of mind? I'm afraid everyone possesses such murky blind spots; it has always fascinated me, I actively work to uncover them in myself, and I am convinced it is a never-ending journey. I consider the simplest method of detection to be our initial reaction to an idea encountered for the first time: if it is complex and we have never thought about it before, one cannot decide offhand whether it is nonsense. If we immediately "know" that something "is completely absurd" and only search for arguments in retrospect, we can be certain we have been indoctrinated in that regard. As an example, I like to use the analogy between a soldier who kills on orders from a superior and an employee who kills on orders from their boss... almost everyone immediately "knows" this is an absurd comparison, and only afterwards looks for reasons why. The point isn't whether the comparison holds, but the mental process itself: "I know how things are right away; only then do I go looking for an argument." I may write about other detection methods sometime in the future.
Child Labor

Child labor is nowadays considered a bad thing in our parts of the world and our civilization; and no wonder, since in such a wealthy society it makes no sense for children to work—firstly, studying allows them to attain far better jobs later on, and secondly, there is an abysmal gap between the value of skilled and unskilled labor. In other eras or parts of the world (in poorer societies), however, this unfortunately does not hold true; children work simply for the family to survive at all—not only does the family lack the resources for their education, but often even for putting food on the table. How can such a situation be changed? Only by that society growing wealthier, and certainly not by imposing a ban on child labor upon them. Working sixteen hours a day in appalling conditions is dreadful; yet the alternatives (such as starvation) are even worse—if they weren't, people would choose them. By outlawing child labor, however, we force them to do precisely that: choose the worse alternative.
Individualism Does Not Consist in Isolation

Libertarians are individualists by nature; however, many people understand the concept somewhat differently, assuming it means isolating oneself from others, and one often encounters people contrasting individualism with cooperation in a human community. I do not wish to argue here about which meaning of the word "individualism" is "correct," as I consider that beside the point—after all, what's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. I would like to emphasize, however, that anyone who criticizes libertarians as people who reject cooperation has failed to grasp the following fundamental distinction: voluntary cooperation—which, by the way, is one of the core ideas of the Austrian School of Economics—is one thing, while violent coercion is something completely different. No libertarian rejects peaceful cooperation; on the contrary, all libertarians fiercely condemn its enforcement through violence.
The Excuse of Authority

If a police officer commits an outrage (such as harassing citizens) within the bounds of the law (or even because the law mandates it), an immense number of people tend to excuse it by saying: "He had to do it; he was just doing his job." I reject such reasoning—partly because concentration camp guards were also "just doing their job," but primarily because each of us is personally accountable for our actions. It is remarkable how everyone understands this in the private sector (everyone agrees it would be absurd to excuse a murder by claiming the killer's boss ordered it), yet so many turn a blind eye when it comes to the state (almost everyone excuses soldiers killing by claiming they were merely following orders). Why might that be? Well, the state simply enjoys better PR; propaganda runs on all fronts, and even the youngest are indoctrinated under compulsory school attendance. Next time you catch yourself excusing someone because they are "just doing their job," ask yourself whether you would excuse them in the private sector.
Whining About "Modern Times"

The grass was greener and girls were prettier; we constantly hear complaints about "the world today," and it is fashionable to lament how everything is going to hell. Yet we live in wonderful times, we live comfortably, and never before have so many people enjoyed prosperity. In the US and Europe, we are swimming in abundance; never before have so few working hours been needed to secure basic necessities, and never before have people enjoyed so much leisure time. Even in the rest of the world, which is worse off than we are, people are growing wealthier faster than ever; there are now more obese people in the world than starving ones. So why all the constant whining about terrible times? There are heaps of reasons, but one in particular caught my interest: imagine five wonderful things that could happen to you within an hour of finishing this article. Got them? Good; now imagine five terrible things. Wasn't the latter easier? For me, both come equally easily, but the vast majority of people conjure up bad scenarios far more quickly. Why is that? Share your thoughts in the comments.
Urza at (de)Centrála: Economic Calculation

The topic of the previous lecture on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club was abortion, euthanasia, vaccination, and other issues concerning the right of self-determination over one's own life; the lecture was delivered by my wife Tereza.
Today we will talk about economic calculation. Unfortunately, it is extremely neglected in today's world; most people are completely unfamiliar with the problem, and a considerable number of libertarians, while familiar with it, struggle to explain it well.
You are all also cordially invited to the next lecture, which will likewise take place on the first Wednesday of the month, June 5; the topic will likely be the property-rights-based constitution I drafted for Liberland.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 19:00 at the (de)Centrála club.
Voluntariness

When anarcho-capitalists oppose the state operating or funding something, they very often face accusations of opposing the thing itself (for example, when they don't want the state to subsidize art, statists claim they are against art as such). Unfortunately, this is not always a deliberate fallacy, as those critics very often genuinely fail to see the distinction between "not wanting people to be coerced into something" and "not wanting that thing." Yet voluntariness is one of the most vital aspects of anything: the difference between a theater funded by ticket sales and other voluntary contributions and a theater funded by the state is roughly the difference between two people making love to express genuine affection, and rape. Naturally, these differ immensely on a moral level, but that is far from everything; even from a utilitarian perspective, coercion poses a massive problem.
Why? Because of the impossibility of economic calculation. Anything funded voluntarily has the property that if it starts consuming resources that could provide greater utility elsewhere than the resulting product itself, it begins generating losses and requires action (reforming, shutting down, etc.). In contrast, when the state runs something, there is no way even to tell whether it represents an outright squandering of resources. People often label it "waste" when the state pays dearly for something that could be obtained cheaper; while true, a far more fundamental question is whether the state should be purchasing that "something" in the first place! How do we determine what yields more utility than the resources required to produce it? Well, very simply: we let people decide whether to voluntarily buy it or not. Whatever they choose not to buy voluntarily clearly does not provide them more utility than the resources they would have to give up for it; and whatever provides them greater utility, they will buy. Laissez-faire!

The entire event runs from 16:30 until midnight; my talk will last 90 minutes and starts at 17:00.
Looking forward to seeing you at Hollar this afternoon!
Not Everything Can Be Converted into Money

The objection that not everything can be converted into money is a relatively sensible response to the tendency of some people to ignore the non-monetary utility of various goods and evaluate only their financial return or price-to-performance ratio. However, it is not at all a logical objection to the conclusions of the Austrian School of Economics, which also evaluates things in terms of money, but never without incorporating non-monetary utility while fully respecting the subjective theory of value for each individual. How, then, does the Austrian School convert goods into money? Well, the price of anything equals the higher of the following two figures: the first is the highest bid anyone is willing to pay for that good; the second is the lowest ask for which the owner is willing to sell it. It naturally follows, among other things, that there can be (and are) things whose monetary price is infinite—namely, goods that someone owns and refuses to sell.
Thus, if someone owns something they are unwilling to sell under any circumstances, it is currently incommensurable in money. On the other hand, all other goods that someone is willing to trade can be "converted" into money in a very meaningful way: the price of a good is the highest bid from potential buyers, or the lowest price at which the owner would sell (whichever is higher). This is a free-market price, and it encompasses absolutely everything—artistic, emotional, sentimental, or charitable value, simply everything. How is that possible? Well, when someone buys or sells something, they factor into that price their knowledge, emotions, humanity, intuition, and everything they are capable of. For precisely that reason, arguing against a free-market economy by asserting that "some things cannot be measured in money" makes no sense: acting individuals in the market convert into monetary terms precisely and only what can be converted, doing so in a way that incorporates all non-financial aspects as well.
Human Preferences

You surely know plenty of people who, on the one hand, support restricting freight traffic in cities, but simultaneously object to paying higher prices for goods (which rise as a result of such restrictions); or people who sign petitions against building a mall or a parking lot in place of a park, but then shop or park there far more than they ever visited the park; or people who protest against polluting factories, yet avidly buy and use their products. They do this because they often fail to realize the underlying connections themselves—which is completely fine, as no one can know everything. But what follows from this? That asking people about their preferences (or having them vote on them democratically) does not yield results reflecting reality. Their true preferences cannot be discovered other than by letting them act in a free market—for it is only through actions, not words, that a person demonstrates what truly brings them utility.
The Icemen

Just a few decades ago, many people made a living as icemen; they harvested ice and sold it so that people could keep their food cold. Then came the refrigerator; and thanks to profit-seeking capitalists, it soon became affordable to almost everyone across Europe and the US, with millions of refrigerators flooding households. But... icemen lost their jobs in droves; today, there is quite possibly not a single one left in the entire world. And it's not much different with elevator attendants; how many people lost their jobs because of automatic elevators? I could go on. But would it have made sense in those cases to "protect jobs"? No! It is a thoroughly good thing that icemen were replaced, that their job became obsolete, and that people can preserve food better. Those workers then went on to do other things instead of trading ice, contributing to society in new ways. In retrospect, almost everyone understands this was for the best; why, then, do so few people grasp the same principle when it comes to the present day?
Advertising

Many of us regard advertising as a necessary evil; some even want to restrict or ban it, arguing that the world would be a better place without it, and complaining that the customer ultimately foots the bill. So why not outlaw advertising? Even leaving aside moral arguments, advertising provides, among other things, informational value to everyone exposed to it. After all, how else would we navigate the boundless variety of goods offered to us by capitalist entrepreneurs? Even the simple copy on product packaging, or any information about a product anywhere, is a form of advertising. So we are merely discussing scale; but how does one determine the proper amount? Well, let firms compete on the free market. Anyone who advertises excessively will also spend excessively, thereby losing competitiveness; the very fact that advertising costs are reflected in the final retail price of goods naturally curbs its volume.
Street Lighting

Sometimes we encounter the claim made by statists that without the state and public budgets, we wouldn't even have street lighting. The truth is that where people pooled funds for it, street lighting would exist, while elsewhere it would not. But is that bad? No; quite the opposite. Where people voluntarily fund street lighting, they evidently derive greater utility from it than if they used the necessary resources otherwise; conversely, where they do not chip in, they make it clear that they have better uses for those resources (otherwise they would voluntarily build lighting), so it is a better choice for them to go without it (and have something else instead). This is where the popular free-rider argument usually comes up: people will be less incentivized to pay when they know they can "free-ride" on what others pay for. That is indeed true—excluding someone from consuming street lighting is exceedingly difficult.
Is that a justification for forcibly extracting resources, however? If it were, one could justify the coercive collection of resources for anything merely because free-riding exists, or because of some other objective (physical or intrinsic) factor where an externality drives up costs. Non-excludability in consumption is simply an attribute of a given good that makes it more expensive—just as a swamp on a plot of land increases construction costs there, free-riding raises the cost of street lighting for those who pay. Yes, if conditions were different (if the soil were dry or free-riding more easily managed), those goods would be cheaper; however, that is by no means a reason to violently coerce people into paying when they have no voluntary desire to do so. That good would still deliver less utility than the resources they were forced to pay for it would have otherwise provided (if that weren't the case, they would pay voluntarily).
Regulations to Protect the Weak

Regulations are usually defended on the grounds that through them, the state protects the weak. Let us set aside for now whether forcibly imposing such protection is morally justifiable, and look instead at its concrete impacts on small, large, and giant corporations. A large corporation has its own accounting and legal departments that can examine new regulations as needed and adapt internal processes to ensure compliance. Giant corporations, in addition to the above, often employ lobbyists and other avenues of influence to sway lawmakers and block regulations that are seriously inconvenient, expensive, or threatening. Small businesses, however, have none of these options, and any new regulation on their business can be potentially crippling or very painful. Thus, protecting one vulnerable group ultimately only endangers other vulnerable ones, often severely. Please, let us not forget that.

The Industrial Revolution

One of the most frequent arguments for state regulation and the welfare state points to the Industrial Revolution, when people worked sixteen hours a day in appalling conditions, children toiled away as well, and life in general was wretched. From this, statists deduce that the free market leads to such outcomes, meaning the state must step in and protect the vulnerable (which, according to them, is what happened and why we are better off today). However, this view is incredibly ahistorical! The reason people worked that way during the Industrial Revolution was not "unbridled capitalism," but the simple fact that society was poor. Factory labor was horrific, yet the alternative (subsistence farming) was even worse; that is why people moved to cities for a better life (yes, factory work represented an improvement for them!). The subsequent rise in living standards and the elimination of child labor were not the result of government regulations (which only appeared once child labor had already virtually vanished), but of capital accumulation and growth in labor productivity, made possible by capitalism itself.

Driver's Licenses: Why?

The very first article on Stoky (aside from the welcome note) dealt with the rationale behind driver's licenses (or rather, state authorizations to operate motor vehicles); in it, I laid out several arguments showing why this amounts to nothing more than pointless bureaucratic harassment. Yet almost everyone takes their existence for granted, considering them proper, justified, and sensible. I would therefore like to emphasize once again the core reason why, in my view, they are completely useless: in theory, they are meant to prevent people who cannot drive from endangering others on the road; but if someone is reckless enough to get behind the wheel and drive out into traffic without having mastered even the bare minimum set of skills taught in driving schools—willing to risk property, health, and human lives (including their own)—how on earth would such a person be deterred by the threat of a police traffic stop, a potential fine, or a license suspension (not that they were legally permitted to drive anyway)?
Democrats-Liberals, Libertarians, Republicans-Conservatives

Dividing the political spectrum into left and right is quite problematic, as these terms have become incredibly debased, distorted by media, and nebulous. In the Czech Republic, it is basically true that wherever a political party classifies itself, that is where the media places it (regardless of its actual program or parliamentary voting record). In the US, the situation is a bit clearer; traditionally, two major political camps operate there: the Democrats (let's say leftists) and the Republicans (let's say rightists). While Democrats champion personal liberties and suppress economic liberties, Republicans operate in precisely the opposite manner. For some reason, most libertarians tend to identify more with Republicans (if forced to choose); and I put this question to the floor for discussion: "Why?" Personally, I find libertarian philosophy equally close to and distant from both camps (we champion both personal and economic freedoms); why do so many libertarians see it differently? Thank you for your thoughts.
Not All "Insurance" Is Insurance

The word "insurance" carries positive connotations in the public mind. When someone is said to be insured, most people picture a responsible person planning ahead for a rainy day. Naturally, the state exploits this, naming the taxes used to fund healthcare and pensions "health insurance" and "social insurance." Yet these levies have precious little in common with insurance—in fact, only the label—since they are not voluntary, and the amount of the "premium" does not depend on risks, the probability of an insured loss, or the coverage paid out by the insurer (should it occur). These payments exhibit all the traits of a tax and virtually none of insurance (in particular, social "insurance" is paid in higher amounts by the wealthy, who are logically far less likely to need welfare benefits, and vice versa). However, because it wouldn't sound very palatable that we are taxed at roughly sixty to seventy percent, the state strives to create an illusion among citizens that this isn't the case by calling a large chunk of taxes by another name—even though Shakespeare aptly noted: "What's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet."
Rational Ignorance

Very often, we hear critics of the free market economy lament alleged market failures caused by information asymmetry or by someone simply lacking knowledge—due to a lack of education, for example—rendering them unable to make an informed decision; hence, according to those critics, the state is needed to fix the situation. Leaving aside that the state fixes nothing and at best wastes a vast amount of resources (and at worst causes harm), I would like to focus on this alleged "market failure," which in my view is not a market failure at all. For it is crucial to recognize that neither information nor education are free goods: obtaining them requires spending time at the very least (and typically more). When someone lacks information, we often see only the downsides of that condition, forgetting that the individual saved resources they didn't have to expend acquiring it.
Before we acquire information, we basically cannot know for sure whether the effort spent obtaining it was worthwhile, because we do not yet possess it; everyone must simply rely on their own experience and make an educated guess, since no one has a crystal ball. And because people are different and our experiences (and temperaments) vary, some simply prioritize information over other things (like leisure time), while others do not. That is by no means a market failure: each person simply chooses what they judge best for themselves. Calling information asymmetry a market failure is akin to declaring the market failed when I missed the bus while someone who jogs every day managed to catch it. Both of us made our choices regarding what was best for us, which brings different pros and cons in different life situations; and if we are dissatisfied with the outcome, we are free to change our lives.
The Balance of Trade

A "positive" trade balance means the value of goods exported from a country exceeds the value of goods imported; the opposite is termed a "negative" trade balance. It is deeply ingrained in the public mind that we should strive for the former; but is that truly desirable? A "positive" trade balance means goods leaving the country have a higher market value than goods entering it. With money it is the opposite; however, if a country maintains a "positive" balance indefinitely, the currency simply gets devalued by inflation because it is never spent—for spending it would require the goods entering the country to exceed the value of those leaving it. It can be compared to earning and saving without ever spending the money, merely letting it dissolve in inflation. This analogy, by the way, explains why arguing that a "positive" trade balance creates jobs is meaningless (yes, it creates jobs, but the objective of economic activity is not labor, but its products).
Is it therefore desirable to aim for a long-term "negative" balance of trade? Well, that is above all a futile endeavor; it would certainly be lovely if others perpetually gave us goods of greater market value than what we give them, but such a state is unsustainable. What is desirable, then? Laissez-faire, of course! The greater the global demand for Czech goods, for example, the stronger the koruna becomes, which naturally drives up the price of those goods and thus cools foreign demand. Conversely, weak global demand for Czech goods leads to a weaker koruna and lower exchange rates, lowering prices and reviving demand. We may track trade balances out of curiosity (provided this does not involve harassing entrepreneurs via customs officers or statistical bureaus), but it is foolish to believe any bureaucrat or economist can decide whether a "positive" or "negative" balance is "correct"—that is something only the market can determine.

Guns Are Bad, Right?

Have you ever noticed how firearms are perceived by most people who have never come into contact with them, have no particular interest in them, and know no one who owns guns and is open about it? Based on years of personal observation, I must note that their attitude toward firearms is typically very negative; however, if they begin taking a closer interest in the topic, or happen to have an avid shooter in their social circle, their views usually shift significantly. This is hardly surprising, considering that firearms are fundamentally the same as knives or clubs—just far more effective—yet essentially tools like any other. And as for the capability to kill as many people as possible quickly and easily, explosives—which are not all that difficult to manufacture at home—serve that purpose just as well; the vast majority of people, however, simply have no desire to do such a thing.
How is it, then, that people who take no interest in the subject are so often biased against guns almost by default? I can see no other explanation than omnipresent state propaganda, which from childhood strives to portray firearms as something inappropriate or inherently hostile that one must beware of, while depicting anti-gun activism as something noble. Why does the state have this incentive? Quite simply because an unarmed citizenry is easier to control, even in extreme situations. We can also observe that, for this very reason, those exact same weapons are neither portrayed nor perceived negatively when held by police officers and the military. Not to mention that the fewer people who own firearms, the less resistance there will be against relentless regulations (especially from the EU, but not only), which unfortunately place an increasing burden on gun owners—even though, in terms of liberty, we have one of the best gun laws in the world. Hopefully it stays that way.
Transparency

A transparent environment surrounding public funds is something that all politicians constantly promise us, and many of them use it as a magic spell to supposedly cure everything. Voters (especially young and left-leaning ones) unfortunately believe them very often and frequently parrot it after them. Transparency, however, is not the solution to our problems, for two reasons: First, our public administration and the state as a whole are already so massive that even with full visibility into every transaction, their sheer volume makes it impossible for anyone to monitor them all (and if someone managed to, it would mean an ocean of wasted time and inefficiency). Second, aside from completely blatant and glaring abuses, even in a transparent environment it is impossible to tell what the state does in the interest of citizens and what it does not, because a directively (rather than market-) driven economy precludes economic calculation. Transparency therefore solves virtually nothing in our situation; the only real solution is shrinking the state.
Everyone Subsidizes, So We Must Too!

I often hear that "we" (meaning Czechs, presumably) must subsidize "our" (Czech) farmers because other countries do so as well, which gives them a competitive advantage. In light of this "logic," I wonder whether the purpose of agriculture is to ensure there is food to eat, or simply to ensure that agriculture exists. What happens if every country except the Czech Republic subsidizes its farmers? Well, people in the Czech Republic will have the opportunity to buy goods subsidized by foreign taxpayers; and the farmers? Well, some will manage to compete (in which case there is no issue), and others will not. But what does that mean? That those farmers clearly consume resources in their business that people value more than the product those businesses deliver; ergo, it is better for them to pursue something else or pivot their business. We will not starve to death (if that were ever a real threat, these farmers would undoubtedly be able to make a handsome living).
