Wasting Food

You know those pictures of heaps of food being thrown away while African children starve? They are often accompanied by some deeply moralistic message about our selfishness and how we should be ashamed of throwing away something that is in short supply elsewhere; I have two fundamental objections to these superficial messages, by which I intend to refute them completely:
1/ Food here and food in Africa are two entirely different goods; the cost of transportation is astronomical compared to the cost of that discarded food, and in many cases it would be cheaper to grow new food locally.
2/ Given how much food our society consumes, it can be considered a (free-market) miracle that surpluses are so small; hitting consumption exactly to the millimeter is simply impossible—so would you rather have surpluses, or starvation?
Besides, who wants to return to the previous regime's meat queues? And even back then, surpluses existed.
Not to mention that there were times when even in Europe people starved; but then came the Industrial Revolution and raw capitalism, which solved this problem. Let us be glad for that and wish the same for Africans; but let us not feel guilty about having those surpluses—on the contrary, let us be grateful for them—it harms no one, and it is a natural consequence of the prosperity in which we live.
Does Alcohol Not Belong Behind the Wheel?

I was just listening to a debate on drugs in which a cop from the narcotics squad was "refuting" the thesis that
drugs are varied
, people are too, and thus the effects of substance use differ, ergo it isn't fair to ban everything across the board; the person used an analogy that alcohol behind the wheel also affects different people differently, yet the law applies equally to all and no one even thinks of questioning or debating it. Well, not only has that occurred to me many times, I have even engaged in such debates before, though I haven't written about it until now; and the fact that this cop took the correctness of such a law as a given prompted me to realize that a short text on the subject wouldn't hurt.
Not only does alcohol affect different people differently, but above all, it doesn't automatically make everyone a bad driver; only past a certain threshold (which is highly individual) does it impair an intoxicated person's capabilities. And there are unquestionably people on the roads who, even with a blood alcohol level of 0.2% (two per mille), will be better drivers than youngsters fresh out of driving school; not to mention that some people begin stumbling after a few drinks, while others with the same amount are only just warming up, with their motor skills and reaction times virtually intact. Alcohol thus not only impairs driving ability differently in different people, but does so from entirely different baseline abilities (some being vastly better drivers than others).
From this perspective, it truly seems absurd to punish people based on their blood alcohol level, since many a completely sober driver is far more dangerous on the road than an intoxicated professional with millions of kilometers under his belt. What is the solution, then? Laissez-faire, I say! Only the free market can deliver an answer. Perhaps private insurers and road owners would ban alcohol behind the wheel entirely; perhaps they would allow a flat threshold, or base permissible intoxication on accident-free mileage, or only factor it in upon an accident, or not at all; and what I consider most likely is that they would come up with something I haven't even conceived of here.
Not to mention that it isn't even clear that the optimum lies where alcohol causes the fewest accidents: we cannot ignore the possibility that road users would willingly accept a slight increase in accident risk in exchange for the utility derived from other things (convenience, enjoying an evening, and so on). Such a possibility is by no means far-fetched, because everyone who leaves home to visit a pub for a beer (even on foot) demonstrates a preference for taking on certain risks to satisfy certain needs; it is therefore hardly unrealistic that people would think similarly regarding driving. The problem, of course, is that
without a free market, we will never find a solution to the problem, because it is simply impossible
.
Let's Buy Local

It is remarkable how often one hears calls to buy "domestic" products, especially food, even though it has been nearly two hundred years since Frédéric Bastiat explained with crystal clarity what nonsense that is; anyone unfamiliar with his work is warmly urged to read "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen" (good news for those who dislike lengthy texts: this one is short and very readable). Patriotism, however, is potent, emotional, and state-subsidized; not to mention that whether someone gets publicity, has influence, and can persuade others has, unfortunately, almost nothing to do with whether they are right or preaching falsehoods.
Supermarkets are even mandated by some new law to flag foods with national flags so that consumers can see which goods they are buying, since the conviction that it is "right" to support "domestic" goods enjoys significant popularity; people are falsely led to believe that they are somehow helping themselves by buying "domestic" goods, as if the prosperity of "their" state translated into personal benefits. Not that this isn't true to a certain (very negligible) extent, but those benefits are utterly dwarfed by the drawbacks resulting from market distortions.
There are many ways to dismantle these fallacies, but I will choose the one that strikes me as simplest: what is the essence of the market? The best producers and suppliers of certain goods make the most money because people voluntarily pay them for those goods; the worst go bankrupt. And it is this very mechanism that is most advantageous to consumers, because it ensures they receive precisely the goods they desire; if we prioritize "domestic" goods over foreign ones instead of looking at other factors, we may well end up giving business to a producer or supplier who, while Czech, isn't as good as their foreign competitor.
I am certainly not saying we should deliberately avoid buying Czech goods; merely that if we choose solely on the basis of quality and price while ignoring country of origin, we will support the best producers and suppliers regardless of where they are from. If, however, we factor country of origin into our criteria, next time we may end up with an inferior Czech product or service instead of a superior foreign one. Personally, when given the choice between Czech and foreign goods of otherwise identical specifications, I pick the foreign ones to counterbalance the patriotic whims of my fellow citizens xD
Students for Liberty: Urza vs. Backa

Few trolls possess the endurance of Mr. Backa; and because I respect tenacity, I will face him tonight at a Liberty Evening organized by Students for Liberty in a duel on the topic: "Is the State Legitimate?" Since Mr. Backa's rhetorical skills certainly cannot be denied (not to mention his passion for making fools of people), I anticipate an intriguing debate this evening from which I may well walk away thoroughly embarrassed, so don't hesitate to come xD
I look forward to seeing you at 20:00 at Café Kampus.
How to Transition to a Free Market?

The goal is a free market, a stateless society—anarcho-capitalism... how do we get there? Privatization? If so, how? Auction off state property? Give it away? To whom, and by what method? All at once? And what about opting out of state "services"? Which ones? In what sequence? Creating parallel structures? I would be keenly interested in your thoughts—and as detailed and well-reasoned as possible, including alternatives you considered and dismissed (and why). Please share them in the comments! For I believe there is no single "right" path; in my eyes, there are only more and less flawed ones. While I am convinced some are better than others, my goal right now is not to persuade, but rather to learn.
If someone is not an anarchist and their aim is a minarchist state (or at least one smaller than the current one), that's perfectly fine; describe the path you would take from the status quo to your ideal system.
People Brainwashed by Advertising

"People don't know what they want, they're manipulated by advertising, we must regulate it to help them!" Such is the common refrain against consumer market society; and I never cease to be fascinated by the thought processes of those who advance it: "I am educated, conscious, unmanipulated, and wise; corporate ads don't work on me; I have seen through what millions of people haven't. So now I will be the savior and help them... even against their will, through violent state intervention." Sometimes, if particularly arrogant, such a person throws in an analogy to parents raising children; then washes down the thought with a sip of latte from their favorite hipster café (marketing has no sway over him, you see—he's a hipster because he chose to be). He lacks humility, respect for people and their wishes, tolerance for different lifestyle choices, and the realization that he is no better than anyone else—and the more deeply rooted these virtues are in a person, the more that person champions
the free market
.
Traffic Jams

Traffic jams seem to be a necessity of our time; and it is quite logical that when there are too many cars, the roads simply clog up and traffic comes to a halt. How to solve this? I have no idea; nobody else knows either, so it is presumably a necessity. There have been plenty of such "necessities" throughout history: for instance, there was a time when traveling around the world in eighty days seemed nearly miraculous, just as it was once considered obvious that heavier-than-air objects cannot fly, that speaking with someone halfway across the globe is impossible, and that a human traveling faster than sixty kilometers per hour would perish. Yet resourceful individuals driven to achieve great things have always managed, through the thorny path of trial and error, to find solutions; and compared to challenges like those, a mere traffic jam looks like child's play. But none of those in a position to solve it have any incentive to risk anything, because they hold cushy positions and everyone has already accepted traffic jams as an inevitability; so why make an effort and risk losing voter favor?
Safe Colors

Cars of certain colors are more visible on the road, while others are less so; imagine—purely hypothetically—a regulation banning "dangerous" car colors: red and yellow are clearly visible, but away with grey. For some time now, I've been probing opinions on such a regulation among supporters of (other) regulations with whom I debate; and guess what? Almost all of them are opposed—even staunch supporters of mandatory seat belts. I find myself wondering why that is: this is a textbook regulation consisting of banning something "pointless and vain" (which nobody strictly "needs," being a mere "whim") in the name of safety (accompanied by the popular argument of endangering not just oneself, but others as well); ergo, opinions on it ought to mirror those on drunk driving or using a phone behind the wheel, yet they don't. Where lies the difference, then? Personally, I think it comes down purely to media barrage and what happens to be "fashionable" to ban nowadays. Do you have a better explanation?
Children of Unschoolers

As many readers know, I am involved with
Svoboda učení [Freedom of Learning]
; and because its members and supporters frequently put their principles into practice (with wonderful results, by the way), their children often do not attend school. This is not pure unschooling—current legislation does not allow for that, as children are required to undergo periodic examinations; and that is precisely where something fascinating occurs. These children simply fail to comprehend why they should have to undergo such a process: they ask whether the examiner doesn't know the answer to what they are asking, offering to help and explain it (which would make sense), but when they discover it is a "test," they cannot grasp the point of the whole exercise. Why should they prove what they know to a stranger from whom they want nothing? You'd be hard-pressed to find such a mindset in an ordinary schoolchild: they have been conditioned to do things simply because they are ordered to—and testing is seen as normal. Yet the question "Why should anyone be testing me?" is a prime example of critical thinking; and that (despite claims to the contrary) is hardly welcome.

Suicides

One possible—if somewhat morbid—way to measure the well-being of a population is to track suicide rates; this naturally has its limitations (it only measures the most dissatisfied segment and is influenced by a host of other factors), but also advantages (the "survey" cannot be skewed by dishonesty). And what does this metric say about the claim, popular in some quarters, that we were better off "under communism"? Well, under the previous regime, an average of 24 people per hundred thousand took their own lives each year (in the five years following 1968, as many as 28); since the Velvet Revolution, we average 16 suicides for the same population size. People committed suicide "under communism" fifty percent more often than today! Naturally, I am not claiming that a person who would otherwise be happy commits suicide solely because of who is in government (I personally don't believe that explanation even in the case of Jan Palach); I am convinced, however, that the political system affects people's lives enough to provide reasons for suicide in some (though not all) cases.
Neoliberalism

Neoliberalism. The new liberalism. What does it actually mean? On Wikipedia, one can find the original definition along with many newer ones, as well as an account of how often its meaning has shifted. Today, the term is used almost exclusively by proud leftists, mostly as an insult. Yet when one asks them for a definition, their answers are either nonexistent or extremely vague (even the panel discussion on "Diagnosis: Neoliberalism," which drew me to visit Klinika, began with an explicit declaration that they would not define the term—a promise they kept). Consequently, when they do manage to articulate something, it is usually a claim that it refers to deregulation, the "free-marketization" of society, and the privatization of state assets; but that directly contradicts their frequent habit of using "neoliberalism" to describe current reality, where the trends are precisely the opposite. So I ask—especially of proud leftists, if they happen to read this: is the word "neoliberalism" anything more than a slur and a cliché?
New Drugs

Some people are horrified by the ingenuity of drug manufacturers, who periodically introduce new narcotics whose destructive effects are often worse than those of the drugs previously on the market; in recent years, one example is the substance krokodil, named because it inflicts damage on users akin to crocodile bites (flesh literally rots off their bodies—hardly surprising given the ingredients). Where does the demand for such drugs come from? Well, they typically emerge as substitutes for more expensive ones (for instance, some turned to meth to substitute for cocaine, or to krokodil for heroin). And what drives the price so high when the production cost of drugs is negligible? The state and its regulations, of course; this entire nightmare was spawned by the
war on drugs
, without which no desperate soul would ever inject compounds of gasoline, paint thinner, and hydrochloric acid into their veins.
Same-Sex Marriage

Virtually all libertarians agree that the state should not interfere in marriage at all (whether heterosexual or homosexual); people should simply arrange their affairs as they see fit. The reality today, unfortunately, is that the state usurps decision-making in this realm (as in almost everything); and the rulers have decreed that only two people of different sexes may marry (two people of the same sex may register their partnership, while other combinations are barred). Some libertarians take the stance that since the state shouldn't be marrying people at all, we certainly shouldn't support same-sex marriage either, as having fewer recognized marriages is closer to "no state marriages." Yet that makes little sense so long as the state disadvantages unmarried couples relative to married ones in numerous ways. From a purely practical standpoint, marriage currently offers relief from certain state regulations; and as long as those regulations exist, we should not deny anyone the option to marry—regardless of gender or the number of individuals involved.
Is Stealing BTC a Violation of the NAP?

One of my readers posed a question to me: when someone steals Bitcoin, does that violate the
Non-Aggression Principle (NAP)
? The "theft" in and of itself (namely, broadcasting a signed transaction that transfers BTC from one address to another) does not, in my view, constitute a violation of the NAP. Nobody can own a private key (it is a sequence of bits, which in principle cannot be owned—only known and kept secret) or prevent others from signing transactions (doing so would itself violate the NAP); ergo, handling "someone else's" BTC is not a violation of the NAP. The real question, however, is how the "thief" acquired the key: in that step, a violation of the NAP almost certainly did occur (even if he didn't break in physically, but hacked a device, that still violates the NAP, as it involves tampering with someone else's property—the device—against the owner's will), though theoretically it might not have (for example, if the "thief" simply saw the key and memorized it).

Costs Versus Benefits

They say that in a blind taste test, wine tastes better to people when they believe it was expensive; well, cheers! In the 1980s, the U.S. military bought a toilet seat for what would amount to forty-five thousand crowns adjusted for inflation, and a hammer for thirty thousand; had they told the soldiers, maybe they would have shit and hammered better. When news of this broke, taxpayers could have lost their shit; however, they had to do so on toilet seats two orders of magnitude (!) cheaper. Some time ago, I
compared the budget of anarchist Wikipedia with that of state-run Czech Television here
; how do you think it turned out? Everyone understands why you shouldn't spend thirty grand on a hammer—because we know the market price of a hammer. Yet there were times when manufacturing a hammer consumed far more resources even on a free market than it does today; toilet seats didn't even exist back then. In light of this, I ask: How do we know that spending on state education, healthcare, the judiciary, and the police aren't just more thirty-grand hammers?
How much are they "supposed" to cost?
We Are Dying Out!

Social engineers have a problem; and as is typical in a state-run society, we have it along with them. The Czech Republic has a low birth rate, the population is aging, the nation is dying out, the apocalypse is nigh; not that there would be any problem at all if the comrades in government hadn't long ago devised an infinitely moronic pension system that presupposes this won't happen (and not that anyone would even notice the whole thing were it not for the Czech Statistical Office and state registries recording every single fart). However, it happened; the state made a mistake (once again); and instead of correcting it by gradually abolishing the pension system, it is trying to salvage the situation with further blunders.
Child benefits, birth grants, child tax deductions, and now possibly even reduced social security contributions for having more children—these are all measures intended to stimulate the subjects to procreate more intensively; much like when a farmer owns livestock and needs more heads of cattle for economic reasons, that is pretty much how our overlords look upon us. They concocted a pension system based on assumptions that held true once upon a time; and as if the plebs were allowed to disrupt their plans now—no such thing, you will pop out babies whether you like it or not!
By the way, what kind of people do you think will actually be swayed by the state's incentive methods? Do you want to increase the birth rate by handing out financial perks to people with children, dear social engineers? Good grief! In the best-case scenario, it simply won't have any effect; in the worst-case scenario, it will mean people start having children because they received state subsidies for it. Surely those will be well-off people overflowing with love, capable of passing on the best to their offspring and raising them into decent human beings. The result will be yet another generation even more dependent on the state than the previous one; and worse still, I highly doubt this is some diabolical master plan—it is merely the normal cycle of things, where moronic state solutions naturally generate and nurture mindless statists.
Another question, of course, is: what is the "correct" number of people in the Czech Republic? Ten million? Eleven? Nine? A hundred? A single million? Although our society would look vastly different with ten times or one-tenth of its current population, living conditions would change, but who really knows how exactly? There is no one who can convincingly justify why ten million people in the Czech Republic is a more "correct" state of affairs than nine million; the only argument for striving for those ten million (or more) is that poorly designed pension system. But why use social engineering to mitigate the consequences of a bad decision when the right solution is to
change that decision
?
Fighting Racism with Collective Guilt?

Every now and then, Romani activist Ivan Veselý enters my radar, commenting from time to time on various events in society; I recall his statements about Germans, whom he distrusts and dislikes because of the Holocaust ("they killed our elites"—meaning Romani elites), as well as about Muslims, whom he would have impaled on stakes if he had to fight them. Let us grant that his second statement might have applied only to those Muslims with whom he would be at war; nevertheless, he distrusts Germans across the board (even without a war) because of what their—long-dead—compatriots did. Isn't that ironic? His lifelong cause is urging people not to judge all Gypsies based on bad experiences with certain individuals, yet he publicly applies the exact same approach himself (albeit toward a different group). Unfortunately, like so many others, he fails to realize that the solution is not to "go to bat" for one's own group against others, but to rid oneself of collective guilt once and for all and lead by example.

I can take care of myself, but others need the state because they are too stupid.

The Abolition of Cash

Lately we occasionally hear talk about restrictions and eventually the complete abolition of cash; what would that achieve? Well, the state would gain absolute control over every single monetary transaction that takes place; whenever you pay anyone for anything, an electronic trail remains for the uniformed apes to follow whenever they see fit. In that case, even EET [electronic records of sales] would basically be redundant, because the state would see vastly more. Of course, it won't happen overnight—people would grumble—yet step by step we are heading in that direction (large cash transactions are already restricted by law); and once some "advanced Western nation" abolishes cash, our politicians will start holding it up as an example worthy of following, because "an honest person has nothing to fear, right?" It is truly enough to make one weep, but what can we do about it? Fortunately, we still have cryptocurrencies; the abolition of cash could open up enormous room for them to thrive.

The EU and Free Trade

Paradoxically, a frequent argument in favor of the EU is the free market; thanks to our EU membership, we are supposedly able to reap the benefits of open borders and a free market, for which we allegedly "must" pay through the bureaucracy that regulates those markets (which is quite a paradox—regulating your way to a free market). It is claimed that without regulation, states could not protect "their" businesses against subsidized and privileged competition; I argue, however, that nothing of the sort is necessary. If other countries subsidize their producers while the Czech Republic does not, Czech producers may indeed become less competitive, yet Czech consumers will be able to buy cheaper (subsidized from abroad) goods; and if someone follows this line of thought further and concludes that all Czech entrepreneurs will go bankrupt, their employees will lose their jobs, and no one will have money for anything, I suggest not stopping the thought experiment there, but thinking one step further (thinking it through thoroughly will explain why even that catastrophic scenario could never materialize).

Private Public Transit

"That could never work," many object; public transit must be subsidized, otherwise ticket sales wouldn't cover its costs. Why? Well... that argument is based purely on the fact that this is how things currently stand: transit companies run deficits and perform terribly despite the subsidies; and when things are a certain way today, people tend to believe they couldn't possibly be any other way. Yet at face value, that makes no sense, since people need transportation and there is no reason why it shouldn't be profitable (and if by some chance it genuinely weren't, that would simply mean public transit isn't worth its real cost to people, ergo forcing them to pay for it makes no sense). At any rate, years ago, the New York subway was private, for instance; today, public transit in Hong Kong is largely private and operates smoothly. Does that surprise anyone? Certainly not me; if we allowed private operators to transport people en masse and without regulation around Prague, for example, I am certain we would be very pleasantly surprised by the outcome.
A Driving Ban—And for What?

Zdeněk Neusar from the Ministry of Transport is threatening drivers with a six-month to one-year driving ban for crossing out the EU flag on their license plates. And do you know what's interesting? Then some monstrosity appears in our legal code from which, formally speaking, crossing out the EU flag on a license plate can be punished with a driving ban. Such an outcome is quite clearly in absolute contradiction to the original justification for the law. But then the statists' favorite argument kicks in: "The law is the law." Badly drafted laws are constantly forced upon us, ostensibly to prevent some evil, but in reality penalizing completely harmless things; and when someone points this out, instead of addressing the poorly written law, we get the usual sermon that we must obey even bad laws. And so liberty dies to the thunderous applause of the crowd...
Everyone Understands Ancap

I make software for a living. I have devoted tens of thousands of hours in my life to programming, algorithms, logic, databases, mathematics, computer networks, hardware, and other related fields, constantly learning along the way; it is a never-ending process during which I make mistakes, acquire information, improve, and become ever more skilled. People typically don't question my professional expertise; at most, another programmer might disagree with me from time to time, holding a different opinion on certain matters that we might discuss—and we don't always agree, but since we both understand the subject, the discussion makes sense. Only once did someone who had spent no more than a few minutes or hours in his entire life thinking about programming start lecturing me on how I was doing it all wrong: it was an aggressive pensioner, and onlookers were tapping their foreheads in disbelief. Even customers, when something doesn't work as intended, don't come around telling me how to code it properly; they know they lack the requisite knowledge and experience for that to make any sense.
I have spent no less time in my life studying anarcho-capitalism, political philosophy, ethics, Austrian economics, praxeology, the free market, and the history of various totalitarian regimes; I have read dozens of books, thousands of articles, engaged in countless debates, and written and produced plenty of material myself, making mistakes, learning from them, and constantly honing my expertise. Yet I face challenges to it on a daily basis—most often from people who haven't spent more than a few minutes thinking about the topic in total.
They don't spend a single second studying historical polycentric legal systems before throwing in my face that they could never work. For some reason, they feel they don't need any knowledge or information here; they fail to realize they are acting just like that pensioner mentioned above. Naturally, I don't rule out the possibility that someone might study everything and still disagree; that happens all the time, just as I don't agree with every programmer on professional questions. But at least that discussion is meaningful.
I can be mistaken and make errors in anything, whether anarcho-capitalism or programming. But in order for someone to point out those errors meaningfully, they must first possess at least a baseline understanding of the subject and familiarize themselves with what I am actually asserting and in what context. When it comes to programming, everyone understands this; yet crowds of people encountering anarcho-capitalism for the first time react with knee-jerk rejection based on some utterly basic, oft-repeated argument like: "Who would build the roads without the state? Besides, justice, healthcare, education, and security would be only for the rich. And the whole thing doesn't account for the average person." Naturally, I could be mistaken in refuting such arguments, but such an error cannot be exposed merely by repeating the argument itself; one must actually research the subject, study it, reflect, and engage in serious debate. Refuting a decades-old school of thought on the first try is about as likely as someone spotting a bug in complex source code just because they watched The Matrix.

The Paradox of Parliamentary Immunity

Members of Parliament (and senators) enjoy immunity, meaning they can only be prosecuted with the consent of their peers (and misdemeanors committed by them are likewise handled solely by their peers); imagine having the same privilege yourself—being subject to criminal prosecution only if your coworkers agree. As an anarcho-capitalist, I see this merely as
the powerful mocking the common subjects
; but what are the "official" justifications used to dupe the public? Supposedly, this exists so that MPs (or senators) cannot be "harassed" by frivolous lawsuits that could paralyze the work of parliament (or the senate); can you feel the mockery? Lawmakers create a legal system while requiring an exemption from it for themselves so that it cannot be abused against them (its very authors)! In other words, they produce an easily abused piece of junk that the rest of us are forced to live under (regular citizens don't have immunity to prevent their businesses from being paralyzed by the legal system), yet they grant themselves an exemption to shield them from the consequences of their own botched work!

Together Against Propaganda!

The battle for freedom begins in the minds of our youngest; and we all know the establishment has been winning across the board so far. Not only does it hold absolute sway over the education system, but also over public broadcasting, funding its own propaganda with our money. Just search YouTube for the video "Demokracie je cool" [Democracy is cool]—little kids singing that anyone who doesn't want democracy is a wimp (funded by the EU and the Ministry of Education); regardless of whether you agree with that view, imagine the uproar and outrage over child exploitation and manipulation if a church or a political party attempted similar propaganda. Yet the state and democracy are sacred idols—anything goes in their name. Worse still, similar propaganda is fed to our children by the public broadcaster ČT [Czech Television]; just look up the show "Bankovkovi," the episode titled "Taxes." Again, it's not so much about whether you agree with the underlying sentiment, but it is anything but "objective and balanced"; when it comes to presenting information about the state, people subconsciously ignore this rule (and the law). Furthermore, the show presents demonstrably false claims.
This time, however, I want us to do more than just point out that this is wrong. I wrote ČT an
open letter, which you can read here
. The problem with open letters, however, is that nobody cares about them because everyone writes them—unless... people start talking about them. And once people talk about them enough on social media, in forums, and on their blogs for the media to take notice (and here I can disclose that I've already arranged coverage with certain outlets, but we need more), the topic will resonate throughout society. And that topic is ancap itself and state propaganda; this is precisely what needs to reach people. It is often said that clicking a button changes nothing and that you need to get off your ass and do something; here, however, that doesn't apply. If you genuinely want to help, you can. It won't cost any money, just a few minutes of your time. Go and spread that letter. Do you run a website? Have a favorite forum? Social media account? Newsletter? Please flood them. Spark discussion and reactions, even dissenting ones. If we do this thoroughly enough, we will capture the attention of major mainstream media as well.
Marksová's Billion-Crown Legacy

Anyone who has read the Sewers from the beginning surely knows which politician is the star here. Yes, that's right: Michaela Marksová-Leninová;
she
does
her
name
justice
(
every
word
,
a
link
). Now, however, she has caught the attention of mainstream media outlets reporting on her IT fiasco that cost us a billion crowns (and is costing another million every day). What happened? The classic: an IT contract four times overpriced and poorly specified, so when faced with hundreds of requests to clarify gaps in the specification, the ministry simply replied that the vendor should propose a solution at its own discretion. If a client replied to me like that as a software engineer, I would definitely push for answers, because I don't just need to technically fulfill a contract—I need a satisfied customer who will pay me again next time; but I don't work for the state, where things evidently work differently. Having watched Marksová for years, I don't even believe she steered the deal to someone to line her own pockets (some of her subordinates might have); rather, she just couldn't be bothered because it's "just IT," while social housing and
worker protection
.
The question, of course, is whether she would have neglected it if it were her own family budget bleeding cash like that. Hardly; but I don't blame her for that—it's completely natural and is a systemic flaw. The problem of incentives under socialism was already described by Ludwig von Mises; it is not an incidental failure of the state, but an inherent feature of it. People talk about the incentive problem; far worse, unfortunately, is the problem of the
impossibility of economic calculation
, which nobody talks about because it is harder to grasp. An overpriced IT contract cost everyone in the Czech Republic about one hundred crowns; it's not pretty, but it's hardly the end of the world, yet the mainstream media gets a sensational story. But how much will all her labor regulations, housing regulations, attempts to overhaul the pension system, and other crusades for "justice" end up costing us? Precisely because of the
impossibility of economic calculation, this cannot be quantified
, but I am convinced it will prove vastly more expensive; while economics paints a clear picture, it isn't as blatantly obvious as an overpriced IT procurement, so journalists will sell it to us as "social reforms" and the like—even though it represents a far greater disaster.

A Pig Farm at a Concentration Camp—Not to Mention the State

I'm watching the Seznam Duel debate discussing the pig farm in Lety; a concentration camp once stood there, and now the state is buying out the site for over a quarter of a billion crowns to build a memorial. This move is defended by Christian Democrat Daniel Herman. How? By invoking reverence, the suffering of the victims, and so forth—against which one cannot utter a single word of dissent, as Nazi concentration camps were truly pure evil; the question is whether that is actually a relevant economic argument. There is certainly a demand for a memorial on that site; on the other hand, there is also demand for a pig farm on that very same parcel of land. How do we resolve this? The owner of the pig farm derives a profit that reflects how much utility it provides to society as a whole (that is, to the people who eat those pigs); on the other hand, there is the non-material utility derived by many people from having a memorial there. How do we compare these two incommensurable values? Quite simply: are those interested in the memorial willing to pool their money and pay the owners of the pig farm enough for them to relinquish it? If not, then they clearly value the memorial less than others value the pig farm.
Unfortunately, nothing like that was heard during the debate. Daniel Herman's opponent was the commie Josef Skála, who could only muster a sort of relativization of the issue by attempting to objectify what cannot be objectified; his entire argument boiled down more or less to claiming that there are other sites where similar or worse atrocities occurred, so we should start with those. In principle, he commits the exact same intellectual error as his opponent: elevating his own wishes and subjective feelings above the preferences expressed by people through their voluntary actions on the market. If people happen to consider Lety more important than other places, it is wrong to force them to build memorials elsewhere first. What is truly sad is that two totalitarians clashed in this debate; while each holds a different idea of how to spend the looted wealth they never earned and off which they parasitize, they agree on one fundamental premise: money must be coerced from people under threat of violence because a bunch of elitist politicians can decide how to spend it better than the robbed citizens themselves. Sadly, no one represented freedom in that debate.

Twenty-Three Years Since the Death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today marks exactly twenty-three years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses—Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"—departed this world at the age of not quite 69; his life's work was the rigorous, logical synthesis and extension to their ultimate conclusions of two movements that seemed superficially unrelated: anarchism and the Austrian School of economics. Anarchists were often economically illiterate, while proponents of the Austrian School failed to apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard resolved both, arriving at the brilliant insight: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This realization and fully grasping it profoundly transformed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

A Robbery Called Taxes

Recently, I was asked to explain an assertion I frequently invoke in my writings—that
taxes are robbery
; allow me to offer a brief and crystal-clear rationale: if you refuse to pay a tax and ignore all notices demanding payment, the state will send a bailiff after you; and if you refuse to deal with him and give him nothing, the police will employ violence against you. In other words, taxes are a payment coerced under threat of violence, making them morally indistinguishable from an ordinary armed mugging. The objection that the state provides citizens with certain services in return cannot stand; does an armed robbery cease to be robbery if the assailant uses a portion of the stolen cash to buy the victim (or someone else) a gift? Nor does the objection hold that anyone who dislikes it doesn't have to live here; that is akin to claiming that an armed mugging in a dangerous park in the middle of the night isn't robbery because the victim didn't have to walk there and could have gone elsewhere.
"Your money or your life"—that is precisely what this comes down to.
Robbery, taxes... what's in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.

The Uninsurable

In debates regarding the redundancy of the state, one frequently encounters the question of what would happen to people suffering from severe, expensive-to-treat congenital conditions—ideally conditions detectable before birth, meaning no insurance provider would want to cover them. And what is my response? Well, naturally no one can predict exactly how the market will look, but I can easily envision, for instance, insurance policies for prospective parents where an insurer offers, for an added premium, an option contract guaranteeing future insurance for their child; I can also envision policies taken out on children prior to conception, alongside numerous other market solutions. You might object that no such services exist today? True enough, but why on earth would they exist under socialized medicine where everyone is nominally covered? Logically, there is no market demand for something the state provides so-called "free of charge"; should the state cease doing so, demand would emerge—and wherever there is demand, supply will follow, because profits are to be made.
My fiancée dubbed this principle "insurance against uninsurability"; I find that term remarkably accurate. Insurance is conceptually similar to a wager: if an event has a low probability of occurring, I can place a relatively small bet on its occurrence, and should it happen, I collect a payout far larger than my stake (because the odds of winning were slim); and so long as people are willing to make bets, there is no reason someone who calculates the statistical odds and designs favorable terms for themselves wouldn't take them. Why, then, shouldn't it be possible to bet that if a child is born to me with condition X, I receive Y crowns, where Y covers the cost of medical treatment? If I am willing to wager noticeably more than Y multiplied by the probability of a newborn having condition X, a wealthy party will gladly take that bet because it is profitable; after all... if people approach you offering 100 crowns for a contract paying out 900 crowns at 1-in-10 odds, would you refuse?
Conscription

You don't have to look far to encounter the opinion that compulsory military service should be reintroduced; yet I am not at all convinced that everyone demanding this truly grasps what they are calling for, as state propaganda has reached the point where many people no longer even reflect on what lurks behind the various euphemisms employed by the government. So what exactly is conscription? First and foremost, it is slavery. Granted, typically temporary in duration, but the core reality remains that conscripts are forcibly (!) compelled to submit to the whims of other men whom the military designates as their superiors. Whether those superiors haze and bully them or treat them reasonably "well" is beside the point; a slave owner who refrains from torturing his slaves and treats them "kindly" within limits does not thereby cease to be a slave owner. So are you advocates of conscription genuinely supporters of slavery? I believe most of you are not; you merely think it's an exaggeration to call military service that. But is it really?
If you tell someone in an African country where female genital mutilation is widespread that it is a sickening, barbaric atrocity, they too will likely view your reaction as an exaggeration, because in their everyday reality it is considered entirely normal; they might very well retort with something like: "I went through it myself as a girl, and at least I don't whore around." That is a chilling parallel to the familiar refrain: "I served in the military; sure, I was hazed, but it built character—at least I'm not a soft wimp like today's youth." What am I getting at? That our emotional perception of an issue is overwhelmingly shaped by how commonplace it happens to be in our environment: once we grow accustomed to something, not even the most horrific practices shock us anymore. In that case, let us set emotions aside and apply pure logic: even if we might not emotionally perceive conscription as slavery, in reality that is precisely what it is (an individual is forcibly compelled to obey another's commands); and what conceivable justification exists for such an atrocity?

Recently, however, while reading a piece on the drug trade inside correctional facilities, another thought struck me: the state cannot even prevent its own inmates from using drugs! Even in maximum-security prisons, where every cell measures just a few square meters, with iron bars everywhere and guards empowered to search inmates' personal belongings at any moment, order them about, dictate their daily schedules, and keep them under round-the-clock surveillance—even there, the state is incapable of "winning" the war on drugs. If it fails even in a virtually sterile, laboratory-like setting ideal for exercising totalitarian control, how could anyone honestly believe it could succeed in the real world, where it has squandered resources for decades without a shred of tangible progress? We can debate whether the stated goal is even worthwhile (in my view, it is not), but that the chosen means completely fail to achieve it could hardly be any more obvious...

I have nothing against biased media outlets; but they shouldn't be state-funded.
Nor, of course, should elections.
So what can we do about it? Let's not lose heart and keep spreading freedom.

The Hell Called Elections

Many people ask me whom to vote for; let me say straight out that I don't know. I have no idea whom you should vote for; I don't even know whether you should vote at all. Although I certainly don't consider abstaining to be foolish or wrong, I personally have always voted; and I will vote as long as the message I would send by not voting is perceived as disinterest rather than disapproval.
I also categorically reject the thesis that casting my ballot legitimizes democracy or the state.
While I cannot tell you whom you should vote for, I dare say that the most dangerous choice is a vote for Babiš; slightly better (though still terrible) in my view is voting for the Christian Democrats or the Communist-Socialist coalition [KSČSSD]; I consider voting for SPD or Úsvit, the Greens, TOP 09, or STAN to be rather foolish (though again, a hair better); I don't judge voting for the remaining parties quite as harshly, because they are either too small to inflict real damage or represent a "lesser evil" (relative to the rest). As for the Pirates, I would merely add that they are a far cry from being "anti-establishment" as they brand themselves (on the other hand, still better than all the parties mentioned above); there are plenty of socialists among them.
Anyone who wants to vote "against the socialists or Babiš"—or "so that the vote doesn't go to waste"—and wants to avoid voting for a minor party, I would probably (with reservations) recommend ODS, as it could perhaps be considered the least bad of "the big ones"; although in the past it sharply abandoned the fight against an oversized state (despite promises), thereby tripping up its voters, lately it seems to be trying to make amends (judging from watching their votes and speeches), though it will take quite some time before they earn even a shred of my trust. However, I regard the "wasted vote" argument as flawed, because your vote will almost certainly be "wasted" anyway (it will only "not be wasted" if the election turned out at least a little differently without it, which is virtually impossible). On the contrary, people overlook one compelling argument for voting for smaller parties: beyond the fact that they can receive state subsidies for votes, it is primarily a motivation for their members, for whom the difference between one and three percent can mean the difference between dedicating their time to that party and to something else.
For that reason as well, I will—with great self-denial—vote for Svobodní. I have an enormous number of reservations about that party; unfortunately, there is no party about which I have fewer reservations. I don't want to detail here everything that bothers me about Svobodní, but given how many libertarians count among our readers, I would like to mention one thing: Two (unofficial) factions are battling within Svobodní—libertarians and right-wing conservatives; and because the former are rather idealists (though many of them engage in practical politics), while the latter are "realpolitikers" (take that as a strong euphemism), unfortunately it is precisely the libertarians who more frequently quit the party simply because they lack the stomach for some of the things that take place there (not that such things don't happen in every political party). What can a voter do about it? Only one thing comes to mind: circling. I'll cast my ballot for Svobodní (even though I don't seriously consider them "my representatives", but that's how democracy works) and try to support the libertarians with preferential votes.
Some want to do the same, but don't know the Svobodní candidates, so they asked me for advice; I don't know whom you should circle, but here is a list of those I would circle myself, as I consider them decent people or libertarians (the list is subjective and incomplete; I do not know all Svobodní candidates): Tomáš Pajonk (not the first by coincidence), Jana Urzová, Zuzana Haberlová, Terézia Mlýnková Išková, Igor Bogdanov, Jakub Cyrani, Josef Káles, Jaroslav Suchánek, Pavel Mises (yes, he legally changed his name xD), Alois Sečkár, Jiří Kubíček, Ondřej Martínek, Michael Kopecký, David Král, Jiří Pánek, Martin Rumler, Petr Pořízek, Jan Šebelík, David Forbelský, Jan Matějka, Jiří Zapletal, Zenon Kuder, Jindřich Pilc, Miloš Bém, David Pokorný, Oldřich Peprla, Roman Bartolšic, Jan Mikula, Radim Smetka, Vítěslav Stanovský, Jaroslav Marsa. I would not choose from the Olomouc or Plzeň regions; I don't know much about the candidates from Olomouc, but unfortunately I do know about those from Plzeň. Do with it as you wish. The choice is yours. I'm not too sure, maybe I'm making a mistake, so take me with a grain of salt.
A Rational Bad Choice

Intellectuals love to express outrage over how terrible it is who people vote for; their votes can be bought for a doughnut, a sausage, a beer, a friendly smile from a billboard... are voters really that stupid? No, quite the opposite; they are smart and know what is best for them. What are the costs of making the "right" (informed) choice? Hundreds of hours of researching party platforms, the credibility of politicians, the basics of economics, predicting the effects of this or that law; assuming you don't have this as a hobby, this is an extreme expense. And what is the gain from making the "right" (informed) choice? Well, none; unless the "right" candidate loses by a single vote (which has probably never happened anywhere), the outcome of the election is exactly the same for each individual regardless of how they voted. So if you don't care about politics, a "sloppy" choice or no choice at all is a perfectly rational solution, not an error. And where is the flaw?
In democracy itself
; it simply doesn't work for real people.

Bad Father? Three Years in the Slammer!

Some idiot encouraged his young daughter to hit a pillow with a baseball bat and imagine she was beating up Gypsies or Muslims; the guy is clearly a lunatic, so he filmed it all and posted it online. And you know what? He's facing charges of inciting hatred and endangering the upbringing of a child, for which he could go to prison for up to three years. I'm not disputing that the father is a brainless jerk for many reasons; but he didn't abuse his daughter, he merely passed on his (admittedly twisted) values to her. If we accept that the state should forcibly dictate to people how to raise their children, we are heading straight to hell. And to anyone thinking they're not in any danger because they aren't such a bigot, I remind them of Martin Niemöller: "When the Nazis came for the communists, I remained silent; I was not a communist after all. When they locked up the social democrats, I remained silent; I was not a social democrat after all. When they came for the trade unionists, I remained silent; I was not a trade unionist after all. When they came for me, there was no one left to speak out."
The point is certainly not that we should approve of or even adopt such a parenting style (I personally find it repulsive); but if the state is the one deciding what is acceptable in upbringing and what isn't, it's not that hard to shift things so that next time, something could be deemed unacceptable that we wouldn't even dream of today and would consider completely absurd (the state could start persecuting parents of children who are overweight, aggressive, religious, or vegan—fill in whatever you like). And the way to prevent this can hardly lie in trying to broadly enforce bans and regulations that suit our personal tastes (because such totalitarian practices always spiral out of control in the end), but in the absolute rejection of letting a police officer, bureaucrat, or politician decide matters for which children and their parents ultimately bear responsibility anyway.
Is Our Country Free?

It could certainly be worse (see North Korea); on the other hand, the state dictates how we must educate our children, what we should guide them toward, which values we must not pass on to them, and which must be drummed into them through the education system; what goods we may sell, buy, and under what conditions; what services we may provide and to whom; that we must register any business we might start, report its earnings, and pay extortion money called taxes in a state-mandated currency that it also forces us to accept; it dictates whom we cannot hire and whom, on the contrary, we cannot turn away, under what conditions people may work for us, and for what reasons we may fire them; what we must not say publicly, and what art and culture we must subsidize; how we are to pay for healthcare, who may and may not treat us, and what medication they may use, and if that fails, who cannot help us die; it also decides what substances we may put into our bodies, from what age we may have sex, and from what age we may watch it on the internet; a bureaucrat inspects what we heat our homes with and what we drive; what vehicles we may own, under what conditions we may operate them, and whom we transport; which weapons we may own and carry; the state determines how and where we may build our own home; what data we may transmit over the internet; which pets we may keep... and that is only a very incomplete list.

Roaming Aftermath

The EU banned roaming, and Eurocrats acted as though we should all kiss their asses for it because they are saving us (with our own money) from evil telecom operators; and at first glance, it really might look that way to some, but as I always say: "You can't outsmart the market." In Norway (which isn't in the EU, but the regulation hit it too), mobile service prices jumped by more than half, in Denmark by an average of 60 euros per customer a year, and the British aren't far behind (depending on the carrier); the Slovak operator Orange, in turn, began charging for "overuse" of services abroad. I was in Belgium in July, where I didn't pay for roaming, but my mobile data didn't work (which could be resolved with the operator, but always only for a few hours; then they cut me off again). So rather than helping anyone, the whole affair was just EU PR; and I wonder how much better or cheaper services operators could have provided us if the money the regulation cost had gone straight to them.
Nocebo: The State Causes Cancer!

Nocebo is the opposite of placebo; while the placebo effect consists of healing based on the patient's belief that they are being treated (even though in reality they are not), the nocebo effect worsens their condition based on, for instance, expecting negative side effects from medication (which they aren't actually receiving). Disgusting images and warnings detailing all the horrifying ways cigarettes can ruin our health are now legally required to appear on every pack of cigarettes; why wouldn't the nocebo effect manifest here? Every time a smoker pulls a cigarette from a pack vividly illustrating the potential negative health consequences of their habit, they are being told that they will fall ill; and if they believe it, their mind can genuinely bring that illness about. Thus, the state not only inexcusably violates the property rights of cigarette manufacturers by regulating the appearance of their packaging, but also actively harms the smokers it ostensibly claims to protect.

The Mafia Called the State

When I talk about the immorality of the state, I sometimes compare it to the mafia; while there are many technical differences between the two organizations, from an ethical standpoint they operate on the exact same principle: within a certain territory, they threaten people with violence to make them pay up. The victim must then either relocate elsewhere, hide their income (at the risk of retaliation), pay up, or be destroyed. The mafia is typically weaker, so it relies on intimidation, has less patience, and quickly resorts to violence; states tend to be stronger, ergo they can afford not to be as overtly brutal, move more slowly, and avoid intimidating so explicitly... at least that's what I usually say; unfortunately, that isn't always true.
Here I am sharing a link to an article that shows what it can also look like. This brings us to another difference: the mafia doesn't have such great PR because it doesn't control the entire school system, so it cannot convince its victims that it isn't actually evil; the state excels at this—its victims feel that a "mistake" was made, that it's "strange" (as a man whose life was ruined by the tax office put it), but they do not reject the state as a whole.
How Much Does Butter Cost?

Recently, the media has been reporting that butter has become more expensive; I didn't notice it myself because I don't look at price tags when buying groceries, but judging by the comments, it caught a lot of people's attention. The chairman of the Agricultural Union of the Czech Republic, Martin Pýcha, proclaimed that people should get used to paying fifty crowns for a quarter-kilo of butter, because that's a normal price; many retailers, however, are reacting by buying cheaper butter from other countries (which, by the way, shows why high tariffs and protectionism in general can be so harmful). But the real problem isn't slightly more expensive butter; it's absurdly high subsidies and the massive level of socialism in agriculture. Nobody has any idea how much butter should actually cost. Mr. Pýcha claims fifty crowns is a "normal price," but he cannot possibly know that, because a "normal price" is determined by supply and demand, which in our case are unfortunately massively distorted by taxes and subsidies. It is sad that nowadays there is no way to determine the market price of butter—or of almost anything else.

Search System at the Czech Post

Everyone certainly has plenty of stories about the Czech Post up their sleeve (myself included), so I won't go into them here; what has fascinated me for years, however, is the search functionality in their information system (one of those programs from the MS-DOS era), which boasts the remarkable feature of lacking the absolute basic function one would expect from such a tool—namely, entering a name and searching for all parcels addressed to that person. Instead, the customer must know whether they are picking up a standard letter, a package, cash on delivery, a registered letter, mail from abroad, and so forth—I don't know exactly how many categories there are—and the postal clerks search through each one separately. Is it really such a problem to write a function that finds any shipment under a given name? It certainly isn't, but why bother when the customer has no choice but to wait? Considering that the entire behemoth is funded by taxpayers who have no alternative, service quality doesn't matter at all, so why make any effort...
Uniformed Monkeys Are Having a Field Day

A guy from Opava drove out to walk his dogs; he left a car window rolled down so the interior could air out in the meantime. And as luck would have it, monkeys in uniforms happened to stroll by; thus began pure, unadulterated police harassment. The man blew them off and drove away. A police spokesperson commented: 'He claimed it was his own business, that he had committed no wrongdoing, and refused to deal with anything. Then he got behind the wheel and insolently drove off. Had he not done so, the situation almost certainly would have been resolved with a verbal warning.' Instead, they slapped him with a fine. And for what? For not being compliant enough; if he had licked the cops' boots and kissed their asses, he wouldn't have had to pay, as they openly admit. In other words: 'Subject, we're going to hassle you, but you must show us due deference that we don't deserve, otherwise we will forcefully make you pay.' And what is the pretext for all this? Well, the law states: 'A driver who intends to leave the vehicle [..] must take such measures to ensure the vehicle [..] cannot be used [..] unlawfully by another person.'
Meanwhile, across the Czech Republic, 279 uniformed monkeys were harassing canoeists; they inspected 606 boats, 93 docks, and breathalyzed 520 paddlers (we've repeatedly addressed the harassment of river paddlers here since last year, including breathalyzer checks). What good is any of this? Here, even the tired old excuse used for cars doesn't work: 'The driver isn't just endangering himself, but those around him!' But whom, other than its own crew, does a canoe realistically endanger? Sure, very hypothetically another canoe, but unless its crew is also plastered and using zero brain cells, at most someone takes an unexpected dip—which simply happens on the river from time to time, and everyone expects it. But this isn't about safety, protection, or help; just like with leaving car windows open, it's solely about keeping the subjects under pressure, stroking the egos of pathetic lowlifes in police uniforms, checking boxes on their activity reports, and looting a few extra bucks for the insatiable maw of the state. Or does anyone seriously believe the police are doing this for our benefit?
Germany as a Corporation

Through German libertarians, I know conspiracy theorists who believe that Germany is not actually a state, but a giant corporation; as is typical with such theories, the clues behind this belief are basically silly—for instance, that German identity cards are called Personalausweis rather than, say, Personenausweis (the former meaning something like an employee ID card, while the latter should logically be an identity card, though it isn't). What intrigued me about this? Both proponents of the conspiracy theory and their opponents (while disagreeing on whether Germany is a corporation or not) agree that it would be terrible if it were true. They live in a country ruled by an entity that operates in a certain way; as long as that entity is called a 'state,' everything is fine, but the moment it turns out to be a 'corporation,' it would suddenly be a catastrophe—even if absolutely nothing about how it operates changed! Can you imagine a better illustration of state propaganda? If an entity does something unacceptable, all it takes is for people to perceive it as a state, and suddenly everything is okay.
"Her Words Killed Him"

Two deeply depressed teenagers in Massachusetts shared their suffering for several years; as often happens with depressed people, they alternately gave each other strength and alternately wanted to die; both were fragile and at rock bottom. The boy then decided to kill himself using exhaust fumes, yet he hesitated and called her; she was seeing everything in black at the time (though earlier they had tried to find solutions to their depression together), so she told him to kill himself. He did; she let him die and didn't call for help. From the perspective of the Non-Aggression Principle, she committed no crime; freedom of speech encompasses even this. From a human perspective, I do not presume to judge; perhaps at that moment she genuinely believed it was the best solution (though I don't know). And from the perspective of the Massachusetts court? Twenty years in prison! Even setting aside the Non-Aggression Principle, I have two questions: In what way is the world supposed to be better after locking her up at taxpayers' expense? And based on this precedent, will someone be convicted, say, for writing a depressing post on the internet if it inspires someone to commit suicide?
Seattle and the Minimum Wage

In Seattle, the minimum wage was raised to fifteen dollars an hour; unsurprisingly, it had the exact negative consequences that Austrian economists have been pointing out for decades. Now, however, a study has come out whose results are deemed 'shocking' because they refute earlier studies claiming to 'prove' the opposite. The authors of the study present conclusions (long known to Austrians) showing that the minimum wage hurts the least skilled workers (who start losing their jobs once their labor cannot cover its own cost); for instance, MIT economist David Autor suggested the study could influence research in the field and completely reshape perspectives on the matter. On one hand, changing that perspective would be great; on the other hand... why is a study needed for this? The laws of praxeology remain valid, and ceteris paribus holds; empirical studies can show virtually anything depending on extraneous factors that cannot be eliminated or isolated, ergo they neither prove nor disprove anything.

Up to Five Years Behind Bars for Six Cannabis Seedlings

What do you think of that headline? Fits right into the libertarian tabloid that Stoky essentially is, doesn't it? Good to hit hard so everyone can see how terrible the state is. But I'm not really that good at coming up with such headlines—I actually lifted this one straight from the official website of the Police of the Czech Republic (I won't link to them, but it's easy to google); the uniformed monkeys are actually bragging about sending someone to prison over six potted plants on a windowsill. Anarchy in Practice: The City of Gurgaon

Gurgaon is an Indian municipal city, yet less than five percent of its territory falls under municipal authority; the remaining ninety-five percent is privately held, and private actors provide all the services we have been taught since childhood the market cannot possibly provide. Economist Shruti Rajagopalan wrote of the city: 'It shouldn't exist, in theory.' Yet exist it does; and it thrives—its population grows by hundreds of thousands of residents every year (already surpassing two and a half million people). Sure, it's in India, so it's hardly paradise on earth, but people are definitely better off there than in other cities, as evidenced by the massive migration into Gurgaon; when people have a choice, they choose the free market over the state. Unsurprisingly, the most horrific conditions in the city occur in the non-privatized sector, where public services and 'social safety nets' are state-provided; the market simply does it better. Want to know more? Martin Pánek translated an interesting article on the subject.
Soundproof Before Demolishing

In Pardubice, a transport hub is set to be built in front of the train station, for which a large subsidy (108 million) is available; one of its conditions, however, is that noise limits must not be exceeded in any surrounding buildings. At first glance, that might seem reasonable, but not when it applies to buildings that have to be torn down as part of constructing that very transport hub! The subsidy grantor didn't consider that, so... Pardubice must first soundproof a building that already has a demolition permit for nearly two million crowns—and only then knock it down. One might be tempted to say poorly formulated subsidy conditions are to blame, but that is only partially true: poorly formulated conditions merely cause the underlying inefficiency to surface so that everyone can see it and laugh at it (as many are doing); without that, the subsidy still wouldn't be efficient—inefficiency is its inherent nature—it just wouldn't be quite so glaring.
A centrally planned economy is doomed to fail...
Křeček's Totalitarian Mindset

Socialist Stanislav Křeček on Airbnb: "The situation is no longer tolerable. Cities must take regulatory action. They must realize that short-term rentals are not a normal way to use an apartment..."
Anarcho-capitalist Urza: "The state is what isn't tolerable! You must realize, Mr. Křeček, that the owner of the apartment should decide how to use it, not parasitic members of parliament living off stolen tax money."
Křeček: "...and it harms the state's housing policy."
Urza: "Then the state's housing policy is flawed! The state is immoral; but if you want to at least pretend it exists for the people, you can't simultaneously claim its policies run counter to their wishes."
Křeček: "Apartments must serve people, not business."
Urza: "And who runs those businesses? Martians? Is that deliberate manipulation, or do you honestly see it that way? Or do you just use the word 'people' as a synonym for your own interests?"
Křeček: "They also violate tax laws; the vast majority of entrepreneurs do not report this income. Such activities should be monitored."
Urza: "And now the truth comes out! No more talk of 'people versus business' and similar garbage; it's simply that someone makes a profit without handing over extortion money to the state to fund your salary, Mr. Křeček, and all hell breaks loose."
Štěch Stepped in Shit...

When we step in shit, we wipe our shoes and move on; not so socialist Štěch, who stepped right into a pile, but instead of wiping it off, decided to wallow around in it a bit more. Instead of keeping his mouth shut after his remarks regarding the utility of the self-employed and their contribution to GDP, he decided to 'improve' things by urging us to snitch on our neighbors: "In Denmark, for instance, if someone is unemployed while working for themselves on the side, the neighbor will simply report them, because they are being robbed of the money they put into the system." Dude, seriously? For one thing... what kind of parasitic monster is this, why is he the President of the Senate, and why do I have to fund this parasite... but above all, what kind of twisted logic is this about 'robbing'? The state forcefully takes someone's money and claims a neighbor was responsible, so the robbed citizen should rat out the neighbor because the state didn't manage to fleece the neighbor out of as much. That this is the logic of a leech feeding on extorted money is obvious; the sad part is how many citizens manipulated by propaganda buy into it.
Wikianarchy

Wikipedia is not operated by any government; it is funded by volunteers. Anyone can write there without needing any license, without having to prove expertise, and without needing anyone's permission. Nobody has an entitlement to it, it is not guaranteed by any law; it is not protected by copyright and has no regulatory agency. When it started, everybody 'knew' it would be complete garbage and that everyone would just troll or post nonsense. Yes, sure, occasionally someone does troll and you can find some nonsense on there, but it remains an amazing project that brings immense value to tons of people. That is how anarchy works in practice—even when everyone 'knows' that 'it could never possibly work.' And how much does the whole thing cost? About sixty million dollars, or a billion and a half crowns a year; which, by the way, is many times less than the budget of Czech Television. How is that possible? Well, Czech Television doesn't have to—and cannot—be efficient, because it doesn't earn its own keep and people are forced to fund it—it's easy to spend other people's money; unlike Wikipedia, which has to sustain itself somehow.
More Regulations!

"The Airbnb application in Prague 1 has completely transformed the dynamics of the housing market. The phenomenon of shared accommodation, if left unregulated, poses a severe danger to every city," declared Prague 1 councilor Ivan Solil of the ČSSD; Mayor Oldřich Lomecký of TOP 09 (singing the exact same tune as ČSSD) concurred: "We cannot allow the Prague 1 district to lose its residential function, which is why we are calling for regulations." Why can't you allow it, you arrogant bigwigs? Do you claim to know how people in Prague 1 ought to live? Where do you get the smug arrogance to believe you know what is good for Prague better than the property owners themselves? Even if every single resident of Prague 1 decided to rent out their apartment, what business is it of yours? None whatsoever!
You are nothing but parasites; you should be grateful we feed you. Lomecký continues: "Tens, hundreds of apartments are flooded with people we don't know the first thing about." And why should anyone (other than the owners) care? If you can't make an honest living like decent people, at least stop posing as saviors.
Štěch: The Self-Employed Parasites v2

How dare this brute judge working people who pay his salary? Second, it is a typical populist Social Democratic attempt to smear the self-employed and pit them against salaried employees, but this time extraordinarily brain-dead: very few things will hurt employees more than tens of thousands of tradespeople being forced to become employees and compete with them on the labor market. Holy shit, if only his voters could grasp this!
Tax Freedom Day

Tax Freedom Day is the date dividing the calendar year into two parts: from the start of the year until that day, people work for the state; only from that day until the end of the year can they work for themselves. For instance, if the state took half of what we earn, Tax Freedom Day would fall right in the middle of the year. Because every person pays slightly different taxes, the date depends on the methodology used: for example, according to Deloitte, Tax Freedom Day is tomorrow, while the Liberal Institute set it for May 29 this year. I try to factor in everything the state costs us, so my Tax Freedom Day doesn't arrive until August; it falls on different days for different people depending on how much they pay in excise taxes and the like. Whether that date lands in May, June, July, or August, the concept is horrifying: just think about how many months from the start of the year we slave away exclusively for a parasitic state... and if someone happens to cut that short, politicians (and sadly, many citizens too) brazenly label them a thief.

Cryptocurrencies and the Economic Crisis

The state forces its non-market currency upon us, thereby causing economic crises; the question isn't whether another one will come, but when. And as an anarcho-capitalist and holder of several cryptocurrencies, I can't help but wonder: when the crisis hits again, what will happen to the exchange rate of Bitcoin (and others)? I can envision two major opposing forces: pure speculators will start panic-selling, since their sole motivation for buying was a quick profit; conversely, those who hold crypto out of distrust of the state or opposition to fiat currency will, in my view, buy more. But which group is larger? People clearly buy cryptocurrencies for both reasons, and I doubt anyone knows which factor outweighs the other. I believe an economic crisis will test this very question. What do you think, dear readers? In which direction will exchange rates move during a crisis? And do my thoughts on the drivers of price increases or drops make sense? We aren't quite there yet, unfortunately; but will we get there before states wake up?
Squirrel Bridge for Four Million

In Sokolov, there is a bridge for squirrels; yes, you read that right, it is literally an overpass over a road, built in 2012 at a cost of four million crowns (seriously, I'm not making this up). I cannot imagine who would defend such a thing or agree with it, but if any hardcore environmentalists are reading this, know that over the entire lifespan of the bridge, exactly five (yes, really five) rodents have crossed it (cameras are installed, so the count is precise). That comes out to about eight hundred thousand crowns per crossing—awesome, isn't it? For that kind of money, I'd gladly carry the squirrels across the road by hand; then again... who wouldn't? Yet the absurdity doesn't end there: the officials at Sokolov town hall are uncompromising champions of bureaucracy to the end. When confronted with the reality of the project, their response was (wait for it): "We are convinced that this animal protection project makes sense." What more is there to say? Well, another one of those things that would be hilarious if it weren't so tragic.
Fined for a "Like"

Once upon a time in Switzerland, there lived a vegan named Erwin Kessler; he objected to Jewish ritual animal slaughter and compared it to the Holocaust (not that I agree with him—I start from different axioms—but I appreciate his logical consistency). A court sent him to prison for that (because "freedom of speech"). A few years later, some people insulted Kessler on social media, calling him an anti-Semite and a racist. Kessler failed to grasp the life lesson on freedom of speech and sued them. And guess what? Not only did he win (even though the defendants attacked him for the very opinion the state had locked him up over), but someone who merely "liked" the post was also convicted! Awesome precedent, right? Normally I'd say this would be funny if it weren't so sad; but this is so absurd that it makes you laugh and cry at the same time: a vegan gets locked up for a "wrong" opinion; he fails to understand why that's problematic; an anti-vegan gets punished for having the "right" opinion; and a random passerby gets convicted for a misclick xD
Lock Up the Nudist!

A guy from Vizovice likes doing yard work on his (!) property naked; he doesn't harm anyone, doesn't trespass on anyone's property, and is even willing to put clothes on when his neighbor asks (not permanently, but when requested, he puts clothes on for the day in the spirit of being a good neighbor). Because he mowed his own (!) lawn naked, and because neighborhood snitching is in full swing.
