Marksová, of course, did not disappoint—she repeatedly affirmed that it was a matter of pride and that she understood them completely. Through what kind of propaganda did the state convince these people that social housing apartments fall from the sky? What exactly does their "pride" consist of? I used to think that rebranding tribute into taxes or social and health taxes into "insurance" wouldn't have much real-world impact; but when I hear this and see people whose "pride won't allow" them to accept housing benefits yet who demand state-subsidized social housing, I have to reconsider: what things are called has a tangible impact in the real world. When people refuse housing benefits but accept a social apartment out of conviction, declaring with a straight face that they "don't want to burden the state" (evidently completely blind to the fact that someone has to pay for that social apartment too), it is probably worthwhile addressing seemingly absurd questions like whether state employees pay taxes. And I now consider it even more crucial to emphasize that taxes are merely extortion money with a new name, that state laws are enforced at gunpoint, and that every single regulation inherently involves aggression. Let's fight newspeak; let's not make it easy for the state!

Uber, Airbnb, Zonky, Doginni, and numerous other platforms that compete with "official" businesses often operate on the fringes of the grey economy (or beyond it); yet (or rather, precisely because of this) they thrive, consistently outcompeting traditional players in open market competition, leaving governments at a loss as to what to do with them. Sometimes states ban them, other times they regulate them, though occasionally a judge will agree with them and rule in their favor. Traditional competitors in these industries typically despise them because they struggle to compete—which in itself speaks volumes about what consumers actually want and don't want. Today at 16:00, I will be discussing this topic in a panel discussion at Polis; fellow panelists will include Daniel Tarljovski, chairman of the Taxi Concessionaires Association, whom I very much look forward to debating. Come check it out and, above all, join the discussion. I look forward to seeing you at Paralelní Polis.
We Don't Work for the State!

"Ethical hacker" and crypto-anarchist Palo is launching both Slovak and Czech versions of the initiative "We Don't Work for the State" (Nepracujeme pro stát / Nepracujeme pre štát); companies (or individuals selling goods or services) can join if they do not work for the state, do not receive subsidies, and ideally also compete with the state or accept cryptocurrencies. Anyone who registers sets the discounts they want to offer to other members (three discount tiers are available: for refusing subsidies, for competing with the state, and for accepting crypto) and can in turn enjoy discounts from other members. The minimum requirement is simply not working for the state and not taking subsidies; sign up, spread both websites, and promote the idea of independence from the state—it matters! The aforementioned discounts are really just a byproduct; the true objective is to build a community of people who actively reject the state, compete against it, promote cryptocurrencies, and cooperate economically.
Another Glimpse of the Power of Propaganda

More and more often, dear readers and listeners, you write me emails discussing libertarian topics; thank you for them—they are usually rewarding discussions. Recently, in response to my lectures, an insightful female listener wrote to me espousing the concept of the so-called "Zen State"; I won't delve into that concept here (you can google it), as I'm not a fan. In the course of that—very interesting—discussion, the lady stated that while she identifies with the ideas of anarcho-capitalism, she doesn't want to call herself an anarchist because anarchy has had violent periods in its history (sic!). This very thoughtful woman (I'm not being sarcastic) endorses the Zen State, yet recoils from anarchy because of its violent history. But what about the bloody nature of states (founded on coercion), which have slaughtered some three hundred million people in wars over the past century alone? Given how our debate has developed so far, I expect she will reconsider; yet that deep-seated subconscious aversion to anarchy is omnipresent...
Cops on the Streets!

Today is World No Tobacco Day; and a totalitarian law comes into effect restricting the freedom of pub owners to decide whether smoking is permitted on their premises or not. Most of the arguments used to defend this amendment boiled down to the premise that since we already live in a totalitarian system anyway, we might as well tighten the screws a little further (pub owners are already burdened by countless regulations; due to socialized healthcare, we all bear the medical costs of smokers; the state ought to look after the population's health; "state, provide me a non-smoking pub in my village," and so forth). In a similarly totalitarian spirit, certain town halls intend to tackle the problems created by the ban (people stepping outside pubs to smoke): Prague 1, for example, hired cops for anti-smoking patrols to go around hassling smokers (about how loud they are, where they discard cigarette butts, and so on). If you run into them, please give them an earful (non-violently) so they might seriously think about what they do for a living.
When the EU Kills Freedom of Speech...

Ministers of EU member states approved a plan to force Google, Facebook, and Twitter into stricter censorship; they are supposed to censor the advocacy of terrorism, hate speech, and incitement to violence. At first glance, that sounds like a good thing, doesn't it? Who would want hate and violence on the internet? But think about who gets to decide what constitutes terrorism, hate speech, or violence: the state! And how does the state define them? As whatever threatens its power and interests, of course. Today it's terrorists; tomorrow it could be anarcho-capitalists or anyone who fundamentally challenges the legitimacy of state power. Furthermore, pushing extremists underground won't eliminate them; it will only radicalize them further, because they won't be exposed to counterarguments, and their followers will view them as martyrs (as will their audiences). And while the ministers were at it, they tacked on another harassment measure for video streaming services (like Netflix): European films and series must make up thirty percent of their content. You can't even comment decently on this anymore, because those people have completely lost their damn minds. The absurdity of this regulation speaks for itself.
Toy Trains for 650 Billion

Transport Minister Ťok wants to play with trains (and the government approved it in its plan for the coming decades); it's going to cost 650 billion crowns (please appreciate the magnitude of that number: it's not just "a lot," it's more than half the annual state budget), and we will be the ones footing the bill. Naturally, something will be delivered in return—very fast trains will run here. The problem is that it is not at all clear who actually wants this and how much they want it, which is typical of state decision-making burdened by the impossibility of economic calculation. What does that mean? It means that if we let a bureaucrat, minister, or whichever Ťok decide whether to build trains or something else, he has zero chance of getting it right (even if he had the best intentions); he cannot determine the subjective preferences of all taxpayers. The only way to avoid getting it wrong is to let people decide with their own money: if a railway line is financed solely by those who want it, it can only come into being if it is truly worth the cost to those paying.
How to Rob a Post Office?

You won't believe this! A thief phoned a post office, introduced himself as a police officer, and said he was coming to disinfect the cash following a chemical attack, so the manager should lock up the post office and let him in through the back door. This clever lady actually complied, brought out all the banknotes to him, and the man (wearing a hazmat suit so cameras wouldn't capture his face) sprayed them with a spray bottle and asked the postmaster to go rinse the coins in the sink. She did just that, leaving him alone with the money and... surprise, surprise, he was nowhere to be found when she got back. Several questions come to mind: Would something like this ever happen in a private business? Say, at a gas station... would the branch manager react the same way? I wouldn't completely rule it out, but if I were a thief picking a target, I'd pick the post office too. And what role did blind faith in the state—and its uniformed monkeys, whom a 'decent citizen' is supposed to never question and always obey—play in this entire fiasco? I suspect it was far from negligible.
The Tax Office Rip-Off

Today we pay taxes on practically everything (there is even a tax on dying, called inheritance tax); buying and selling real estate is no exception, and the state lines its pockets on that as well. Why? Primarily because it can: it is stronger, carries a 'bigger club,' and we have no means of self-defense. A few years ago, the tax office altered the rules so that the real estate transfer tax was paid not by the seller, but by the buyer; this went into effect, and the law also provided for certain exemptions (for new apartments), which citizens naturally had to humbly apply for. Applications poured in and were approved, until one fine day... the tax office decided that it had actually botched the approval of some of those (already approved) exemptions. So what now? The law is the law, and the subject must pay up (often hundreds of thousands of crowns)—including late-payment interest and penalties (!). Yes, you read that correctly. Our rulers are merciful, however: if the subject files a formal plea (!), they will waive the penalty (though not the interest). Can you imagine the (entirely justified) uproar if a private company pulled something like this?
Gift Markets

In a conventional market, you purchase goods; it works roughly like this: you enter into a sales contract with the seller (note: a contract is not a signed piece of paper, but an agreement; the paper is merely evidence that an agreement took place), you pay them money, they hand over the goods... and then they must report this transaction electronically to Babiš. In a gift market, you don't buy—you exchange gifts; that works entirely differently: you enter into two donation agreements with the stallholder (not a seller)—the subject of the first is your gift of money to the person, and the subject of the second is that this good man gifts you his goods... and that's it, because nobody has introduced electronic records of gifts yet. Gift markets have already been successfully held in Hradec Králové and Letohrad; another fifty towns are interested in hosting similar events. Fantastic so far! What do you think will happen next? Will it be declared illegal tax evasion? Will an 'Electronic Records of Gifts' (EED) system be introduced? Or will the state just not bother with small fry?

Alza Accepts BTC!

Urza in Polis: Who Would Build the Roads Without the State?

Everyday Micro-Racism

Oxford University sent out new guidelines to students in its regular newsletter aimed at reducing racial intolerance; is that really needed there? And if so, how will these rules help? Let's take a look at them. For instance, students are forbidden from asking a student of color where they are originally from; but even 'better,' they aren't allowed to avert eye contact either! That's supposedly 'micro-racism.' So if a man glances at a woman of another race, she must return his gaze, whereas if he were of the same race, she has no such obligation. That isn't micro-racism anymore... that's colossal, full-blown racism! Don't all these politically correct geniuses realize that measures like this only highlight racial differences? Don't they understand that this is how you turn people who never cared about race into racists? One can only hope other institutions don't follow the University of Oxford's example.
Sobotka Divides the Loot

Although elections are still some time away, they are steadily approaching; and Sobotka needs to buy votes, but why would he do so out of his own pocket when he has everyone's stolen money at his disposal? So he wants to raise public sector salaries. It's not unlike a pirate captain divvying up what they plundered; after all, those getting raises (aside from firefighters) are primarily police officers, customs officials, and prison guards—the executive enforcers of violence who form the frontline of state oppression and resource extraction through robbery. Furthermore, this move marks another step in the 'fatal cycle of democracy' that I lectured on at Polis some time ago: politicians promise to take care of people (at others' expense); when they deliver, the number of people dependent on the state (and public employees) swells; an increase in state dependents means more votes for politicians who promise to take care of them (at others' expense). The circle closes: democracy inevitably leads to socialism.
The Pope on the Libertarian Invasion

Among foreign libertarians, I occasionally see a joke that goes something like: "Libertarians are diligently plotting to take over the world and leave you alone." (You can google 'libertarians diligently plotting leave you alone' in images.) Guess who took that quip seriously? Pope Francis. He warned the world against an invasion (sic!) of libertarian values into our culture and education system. The danger of our misleading paradigms supposedly lies in the fact that we don't care about the "common good," and in our conviction that "only individuals assign value to things and interpersonal relationships, ergo only individuals decide what is good and what is evil"; he actually articulated that surprisingly well—maybe I'll quote it sometime... I understand why he doesn't like it much, because he would prefer to hold the monopoly on what is good and evil; and his church has always gotten along far better with the state than with libertarians xD
I am a Christian, but not a Catholic, as I cultivate a personal relationship with the Lord, for which I don't need a mediator in the form of a priest, let alone a pope; at moments like this, I'm glad of it, because the Pope's address doesn't cause me a dilemma, but immense joy. Why joy? Ladies and gentlemen, the head of a church with over a billion followers is talking about us! That means what we are doing, we are doing right! As Gandhi said: "First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win." And this speech by the Pope is the first harbinger of that third stage; had the late Murray Rothbard lived to see this, he would surely have been thrilled. So let us press on with our efforts: write, speak, spread the word, explain, strive to understand people without being rude, and give it our best. For that is the road to freedom; I don't believe I'll live to see a free-market society, but I will do everything I can to bring it closer... get involved too!
The Right to Children

Who decides whether a woman longing for a child is denied the possibilities of modern medicine? The state, who else... and the rulers have decreed that if she isn't married, she's out of luck. MP František Adámek of the left-wing ČSSD tried to change this—unfortunately without success. The fiercest opposition came from Jitka Chalánková of the supposedly right-wing TOP 09; she herself is married, has four children, wants to impose her values on everyone else, and the state hands her the power to do so. Her justification: "The right to a child is not among fundamental human rights." And so what? Does that mean anything not deemed a 'fundamental human right' should be banned by the state? She and other lawmakers agreed that this is not a medical issue, but an ethical one. Well, of course! The question is whether people are free to enter into voluntary transactions, or whether the state will step in and prohibit them; the real ethical question is: "Is it legitimate for Mrs. Chalánková, together with other lawmakers, to decide from a position of power who is allowed to reproduce and how?"
Máte slovo: The Cyber-Snooping State

Almost every episode of the show Máte slovo is a disaster (aside from the boring ones about diets and the like); statism runs rampant and the fruits of state propaganda indoctrination are on full display, but in the recent episode on state cyber-snooping, the usual platitudes ("If you haven't done anything wrong, you have nothing to fear") were joined by dishonest manipulation on such a scale that even I was startled (and I think anyone who knows even the basics of network security was too). An advocate of government wiretapping of citizens' internet traffic argued that foreign hackers could attack our power plants, chemical works, water treatment facilities, and other strategic targets; an audience member and the host chimed in that of course that's possible, because everything nowadays is run by "those computers." In short, it was a typical "expert" panel where all technical knowledge was drawn from Hollywood hacker movies; I don't blame anyone for lack of expertise, but the problem is that in a democracy, everyone gets an equal vote.
No matter how skilled a hacker is, they can only attack systems over a network if they can physically connect to them. If a computer isn't connected to the internet, the hacker is out of luck; as one of my teachers used to say: "The best firewall is a meter of air." (That saying may not be quite as neat in the era of Wi-Fi as it was in his youth.) Naturally, the people handling nuclear plant security know this; critical systems run offline. Sadly, this wasn't brought up for a long time, until finally a rather pathetic representative of the Pirate Party tentatively piped up and awkwardly mentioned it; but his technical hesitation was so palpable that his opponent brushed him aside with the Stuxnet virus (which targeted Simatic industrial systems)—a completely irrelevant argument, since monitoring internet traffic doesn't protect against a virus carried on a USB flash drive into an offline machine. But the Pirate was so unconfident (having already been shut down by that opponent earlier) that he simply dropped the topic.
If You Don't Snitch, You Haven't Lived (EET Edition)

You can't teach an old secret police agent (StB) new tricks, but he can certainly teach the youth. Take a twenty-three-year-old man from Domažlice who dialed emergency line 158 because he couldn't find a fiscal identification code (FIK, proof that the sale was registered electronically) on a receipt for a twelve-crown transaction (!). Can you imagine what goes through such a person's mind? How do they think? What did he feel during that episode? Why on earth did he do it? Several possibilities come to mind, though I can't relate to a single one; and I would genuinely love to know how many people like that walk among us... unfortunately, even one feels like far too many. Yet I won't file this story under things that would be funny if they weren't so sad; why not? Because in the end, it was downright hilarious: the uniformed monkeys showed up, found the fiscal identification code right there on the receipt, pointed it out to the snitch, and he slunk off in utter disgrace; this story was almost worth the tax money it cost me xD
An Illegally Open Shop

Back when Stoky was still in its infancy, we discussed the proposed law banning holiday retail sales; back then it was just a bill, but as expected, it passed. And now it's bearing fruit! The Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) had a field day on Easter Monday, inspecting nearly three hundred stores, three of which were 'illegally open' (we'd better start getting used to this bizarre phrase, which would be hilarious if it weren't so pathetic). Those shops now face fines of up to one million crowns (and five million for repeat offenses). And you know what? Someone snitched on all three of them; I really wonder what kind of scumbag a person has to be to do that, and I hope their identities eventually leak. At any rate, the state introduced this law under the guise that families should be together during holidays, because politicians know best what is good for them. Sure, it's easy to boss other people around... but what if the state started with itself? For instance, with those snooping inspectors from the Trade Inspection Authority...
Urza in Polis: Public Space and Freedom of Speech

Two weeks ago, I gave a lecture on weapons; even die-hard gun opponents showed up, which I greatly welcome, and I found it very surprising that their views shifted so significantly over the course of the evening. That pleased me immensely, of course; and tonight I will try for something similar with public spaces and freedom of speech.
What connects these two things? In short, when the state regulates public spaces, streets, squares, parks, transport infrastructure, and public areas, it thereby directly limits who may speak where, gather, promote their opinions, and express themselves. We will also discuss the preservation of historical monuments, statues, and the like; and we'll touch on the issue of roads. If you're interested in the topic, definitely come; and if you know someone who might find it interesting, don't hesitate to bring them along!
The next lecture, to which you are all cordially invited, will exceptionally take place not in two weeks, but in a month (May 17 at 20:00); its topic will be: "Who would build the roads without the state?"
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at Paralelní Polis.
I Have a Right to a Pub

Unfortunately, the smoking ban in pubs has passed and there's nothing we can do about it now; in practice, laws are constantly added but virtually never repealed, ergo we solemnly join the "developed" EU countries that are so frequently cited in arguments. Even more common, however, is the argument I informally call "I have a right to a pub," often elaborated with: "There's only one pub in our village." The best response came in the comments on Stoky from user TaxationISTheft: "So what? If I go to a bookstore and they don't have the book I want, should I start demanding the state make sure it's there?" That is precisely how nonsensical the demand is in the case of pubs; not to mention a rather accurate summary of the currently expanding state that I read recently (I don't even remember where): "I wouldn't want to run a pub. The thought that someone gets drunk, lights up a cigarette, and I kick them out before handing them a receipt is an absolute nightmare."
The Best President Is a Bad President

In my opinion, the office of the President of the Czech Republic boasts a wonderful ratio of prestige to actual power: the head of state is a figure with high media exposure, yet wields relatively little actual power (not that he has none at all—for example, he appoints members of the CNB Bank Board)—in other words, considering how visible he is, he cannot inflict all that much damage. That is why I believe that from a libertarian perspective, it's not such a bad thing when the president is an obvious, complete jerk; why? Because he alienates and infuriates people, making it much easier to explain the absurdity of democracy and state propaganda to them. Someone like Zeman represents, from this perspective, a president who constantly does exactly what I want him to do: embarrass himself and make a mockery of the office. But his term is slowly drawing to a close, and I really wouldn't want to see some Karel (the same evil, just appearing more respectable on the surface). According to my information, however, a candidate will soon be announced who should effortlessly outdo Zeman in making a disgrace of himself... and whoever thinks that's impossible, keep an eye on the news xD
Discussion at Polis: State versus Labor

Today at 16:00, I will take part in a panel discussion at Paralelní Polis; the topic will be recent events at Rohlík.cz, where on March 10, foreign police raided on suspicion of illegal employment and detained 85 people without charge, thereby paralyzing the company's operations. Come along, everyone is invited regardless of your views; in addition, you can enjoy coffee or beer paid for in Bitcoin (and if you don't have BTC, you can buy some right on the spot) with the certainty that the transaction will not be electronically registered.
Step outside.
Urza in Polis: Weapons

Two weeks ago, I gave a lecture on drugs; the hall was packed again, for which I thank all of you who came. I am truly glad to have the opportunity to share the ideas of a free society with others; I am grateful to everyone who listens and at least reflects on what I say. And I will continue to do my best not to disappoint you xD
Tonight I am lecturing on the topic of weapons, which follows up on drugs quite nicely; unlike the previous lecture, however, we won't analyze weapons from a technical standpoint—which will be made up for with plenty of fascinating statistics and hard data. But that is far from all! We will explore the psychological impact of weapons on decent people as well as criminals; we will discuss the differences between an armed and an unarmed society, without omitting their relationship to the government. Finally, we will address the topic of heavy weaponry (very heavy: combat aircraft, battleships, tanks, and artillery) and its role in a stateless society. Definitely come and discuss—especially if you support gun regulations; and bring your acquaintances along, ideally those who have never heard of anarcho-capitalism but might find the topic interesting.
In addition, you are all invited to a lecture taking place in two weeks (April 19 at 20:00); its topic will be public spaces and freedom of speech.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at Paralelní Polis.
The Aftermath of the Mironet Raid

The year is May 2000; uniformed monkeys forcefully (and in violation of the law) raid the company Mironet, seize computers and accounting books, and charge the owner with software piracy—only to conclude two years later: "Sorry about that, a little oopsie occurred, you're innocent, sir, so long." But the man is no sheep and tries to defend himself against this tyranny: he sues the state for 626 million crowns. To which the High Court in Prague effectively responds: "Fuck off, you get 23 million and you should be grateful; keep quiet and shuffle your feet, lowly subject." The saga continues: lawsuits, dismissals, statute of limitations, appeals—it can all be found online (including hateful comments). But do you know what I find most interesting about all this? Absolutely nobody questions the absurdity of a situation where an entity (the state) harms someone and subsequently that same entity (the state again) presides as the judge in the case; if a private company judged its own disputes, there would be an almighty uproar!
State propaganda is powerful indeed...
2017 Elections: Another Assault on Property Rights

For the first time this year, the election campaign will be governed by the latest amendment to the electoral law; Vojtěch Weiss, head of the Office for the Oversight of Political Party Finances, declared that anyone wishing to put up their own (!) political poster on their own (!) fence, shop window, or home window (which includes not only promoting a political party or movement, but also criticizing one) must register in his office's surveillance database—anyone who fails to do so will be fined between 10,000 and 100,000 crowns. That registration is no picnic either: one either needs a transparent bank account, a dedicated website, and other formalities, or must be registered by a political party; this especially penalizes those who want to run an anti-campaign rather than a campaign (such as various Babiš detractors). I wonder whether this applies to Stoky too—while certainly not a poster or large-format billboard, I don't know if it qualifies as a 'communication medium' under the law... what do our resident lawyers think?
And now, once again on Stoky, we enter territory filled with things that would be hilarious if they weren't so tragic: Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Jan Bartošek (KDU-ČSL) stated: "Interpreting the law to mean that anyone hanging a banner on their fence must register as a campaign supporter strikes me as odd." Jeroným Tejc (ČSSD), head of the parliamentary constitutional and legal committee, added: "You cannot interpret the law ad absurdum and prevent people from voicing their opinions. [..] But it is up to the oversight office how to interpret the law." And you know what? Those two geniuses voted for that moronic law in the first place (along with their parties, plus ANO and Úsvit—let's point them out). That is how lawmaking works in this country (and sadly not just here): a bunch of incompetent idiots pass something with a vague idea of how it will work, but when another incompetent bureaucrat enforces it differently, they merely sigh that it's up to him because 'the law is the law' (yes... and where did that law come from, exactly?).
Internet or Electricity Are Optional, EET Is Mandatory

Because the majority of people have an internet connection, Babiš instituted a blanket mandate to electronically register all sales (EET); unfortunately, this also applies to the minority who must somehow figure it out. Take the ruins of Cimburk Castle, situated deep in the woods where there is not only no internet, but not even electricity. Yet the state barked an order, so the subject has no choice but to comply. Connectivity itself isn't such an insurmountable issue, but electricity is: so a generator had to be purchased for the castle ruins, along with fuel canisters hauled up there, bringing the total cost of the cash register setup to around sixty thousand crowns—the subsequent increase in entrance fees was surely pure coincidence, as the two things are obviously unrelated. In connection with such cases, I always find it amusing when Babiš shouts about how the cost of implementing EET is negligible; sure, for the vast majority of people it might be, but that is zero justification for brutally harassing the minority—even if that is what democracy is built on.
Urza in Polis: Drugs

Two weeks ago, I gave a lecture on the topic of education; I consider it very successful, as probably the largest crowd to date showed up (definitely over a hundred and fifty people), so not only did chairs run out, but even floor space was filled, and the livestream (which was exceptional, normally there isn't one) was watched by thousands of people. Thank you all for your attention—especially those who came, and above all those who took part in the discussion.
Tonight I will be lecturing again; the topic will likely spark controversy once more, as we will be talking about drugs. We will cover drugs themselves—their effects, dangers, and risks—because while public schools teach us that drugs are bad, they teach virtually nothing about the substances themselves, resulting in numerous myths circulating in society (some demonizing drugs, others downplaying them; these two phenomena are closely linked in my view, and at the lecture you can find out why). But naturally, I will also examine the state's stance toward drugs, toward our personal freedom, and the drug war that has been raging for decades without visible results, having ruined countless lives along the way.
I also cordially invite everyone to the next lecture, which will take place in two weeks (April 5 at 20:00); its topic will be weapons in a free society.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at Paralelní Polis.
Enforcing Inclusion Through Terror

The state decided that it is simply beneficial for many disabled children to attend mainstream schools; some parents, however, have the audacity to believe they know their own child better than a bureaucrat, and therefore refuse to integrate them. And it is precisely these brazen parents that child protective services targets. Why? Because refusing inclusion is supposedly 'contrary to the best interests of the child'... and who determines what the child's best interests are? Yes, exactly—the state, who else. Not that I consider inclusion bad in all cases; however, it should under no circumstances be decided by the government, but rather by the children, parents, and schools. Education should be voluntary—in every respect (nobody should deny anyone an education, nor force anyone into it; and the exact same should apply to educational institutions), while the absolute last institution that should interfere is a gang of robbers—called the state—living off extortion money.
Let us prevent the indoctrination of our children however we can.
The New Svoboda Učení Website

At Svoboda učení, we have finally launched our new website; and I would like to use this opportunity to recommend that readers of Stoky familiarize themselves with the fascinating ideas we promote at Svoboda učení—you can start, for example, with the manifesto, in whose creation I participated and with which I fully identify (especially its fourth point). Why do I consider the concepts of freedom of learning (now with a lowercase f) so crucial? Because state-run schooling is, in my view, one of the key—and arguably the single most important—foundations of state power; yes, of course, that power is executed by police and courts, but the reason it is so widely accepted by the public lies squarely in the propaganda we are all subjected to from early childhood, when our minds are still forming, making it immensely difficult to resist later on. Let us not subject our children to the same, and let us strive to prevent the state from indoctrinating them!
The State Crushes Rohlík

The company Rohlík.cz delivers groceries ordered online to people's doorsteps; every day in Prague, it receives and fulfills three to four thousand orders (I saw an ad on one of their vans stating they had already delivered over a million orders in total). Such an enterprise is undeniably a fantastic initiative: customers receive groceries on favorable terms (otherwise they wouldn't order), employees earn the best living they can within their options (otherwise they would work elsewhere), and the business owners make their profit; as long as they harm no one, it is unequivocally beneficial—regardless of what politicians or bureaucrats think about the conditions under which people work there, provided they do so voluntarily (and naturally regardless of whether they pay taxes or abide by other regulations, as long as they harm no one). Why should this bother anyone? Why would anyone object?
Yet the armed fist of the state decided to crush Rohlík.cz because it disapproves of foreigners working in their warehouses under conditions that bureaucrats deem contrary to the law. Much has already been written about why the cops behave as disgustingly as always (first they detained dozens of people, paralyzing company operations, and only then did they check their IDs and determine who actually broke the law and who didn't—thus depriving even the innocent of their liberty). However, criticizing the state merely for being overly heavy-handed strikes me as inadequate: the real issue is that such actions happen at all, and that people peacefully cooperating for mutual benefit without harming anyone are persecuted by the thugs who parasitize on their productive efforts—all justified by the excuse that something is written in the law. That should never be an acceptable argument for using violence against someone who has harmed nobody and is, on the contrary, providing a valuable service.
LibertyCon

March 17–19 marks LibertyCon, an annual event organized by Students for Liberty; registration closes on March 12, so if you are interested, don't forget to register. We can look forward to a whole range of interesting talks and people; more information can be found on the
event's website
– in my opinion, attending it is definitely worth considering.
Urza in Polis: Education

The lecture two weeks ago
on the topic of democracy was very successful; a lot of people showed up (maybe a hundred and fifty) and the feedback was great. Thank you! Once again, there was a very interesting discussion, especially because rejecting democracy is quite a controversial issue in today's society; many people also came who had never attended any before, which I am very glad about.
The next lecture takes place tonight, and I consider it the most important of the entire series; the topic will be education, which in my opinion is the main reason why people so widely accept the state without really thinking about it. We will talk about the aforementioned state propaganda, but also about various educational models, most of which are not legal in the Czech Republic; and finally we will talk about the separation of school and state and education in the free market. The lecture is truly crucial, so please come and bring your acquaintances (ideally non-libertarians – it's already working quite well and the majority of people I lecture to know nothing about anarcho-capitalism).
In addition, you are all invited to the lecture that will take place in two weeks (March 22 at 20:00); its topic will be drugs (both the drugs themselves and the state's approach to them).
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at
Paralelní Polis
.
We Bought a Lift for a Disabled Man

Kevin Preiß is a young German libertarian confined to a wheelchair; however, because his home is not wheelchair-accessible, for years he has only been able to get outside if his loved ones carry him out and back. A wheelchair platform lift that would solve the situation costs a quarter of a million (in Czech crowns, that is); and although the state presents itself as an entity that takes care of disabled people, it didn't give a damn about Kevin (well... it would have paid for his lift if it cost half as much, which would be possible, but only in a different building; this way, it won't even pay that half). When my ex-girlfriend (who lives in Germany and knows many libertarians there) found out about the situation, she got the idea to organize a fundraiser... most of the required amount was raised within three days, a quarter million within a week; Kevin will get his lift, problem solved.
Although libertarians are often accused of callousness and an unwillingness to help others, I think the opposite is true; when you live in the belief that the state should help, you logically lack as much motivation to do so personally (of course, it's individual and there are many such motivations), whereas if you live in the belief that solidarity should be voluntary, you simply tend to be voluntarily solidary (again, not without exceptions). However, this isn't just the case for libertarians; if solidarity is not enforced by the state, people will feel greater responsibility for the state of the world around them... when there is no option of calling a politician to solve problems, the tendency to solve them oneself will increase.
Let's Subsidize... Golf?

We have over a hundred golf courses in the Czech Republic, and more are constantly being built; the number of players, however, is declining, which logically puts golf resorts in financial trouble. Whoever thought that the solution would be to let the unneeded ones go bust while the popular ones thrive is probably a bit old-fashioned; current politics naturally dictates: "Tax the successful and subsidize the failures!!" That's what motivates people, after all; and so the EU pours hundreds of millions of crowns in subsidies into these unsuccessful golf course operators. Remember this the next time you hear someone talk about how the balance of money we pay to the EU versus what we get back is favorable for us; yes, in accounting terms it works out that way, but on the outgoing side you have money collected through taxes
under threat of violence
, while on the incoming side, nonsense is being funded. It's like someone taking a thousand crowns from you to buy you something for two thousand that you absolutely do not want, do not need, and cannot sell; would you thank him?
Gore-Tex? Ban It!

Most of us are probably familiar with Gore-Tex; an amazing (and fairly expensive) material for clothing that is waterproof yet breathable, allowing air to circulate – absolutely priceless for hiking and camping trips (similar fabrics are used not only for jackets and pants, but also for shoes). I wore quite a bit of it myself; and I was lucky, because back in my tramping days, the wise, almighty EU wasn't here yet to ban it. But now the situation has changed, and a ban is on the table; well, finally – what on earth would we do without it? The reasons? Toxicity (so now I'm seriously worried about what all those years of wearing Gore-Tex will do to me) and ecology – it takes too long to decompose. Well, even if so, I really wonder what banning this of all things will accomplish; we produce an unbelievable amount of glass and plastic that decomposes... well... maybe never, whereas banning Gore-Tex and similar materials, the production of which is a mere drop in the ocean compared to the above, will totally save the day. Logically...
The State Destroyed, the State Will Subsidize

Small grocery shops are dying out; tens to hundreds of them close down every year in the Czech Republic. Why? While there are undoubtedly multiple reasons, one undeniable factor is regulations that intolerably drive up operating costs – sanitary regulations, occupational safety, employee protection, VAT control statements, and many others, plus all the resulting bureaucracy; you can't just open a shop and start selling, the law forbids it. Naturally, the same laws apply to supermarkets, but they have entire accounting, legal, and HR departments to handle them; as a result, the exact same regulations hit small players far harder, because the burden of associated obligations is certainly not linear with respect to profit or turnover, so larger entities are favored by the state (small shops simply cannot afford to assign even a single person to handle these matters).
The current solution? The state subsidizes these small shops; just as Ronald Reagan said: "If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And if it stops moving, subsidize it." A sensible solution? Abolishing regulations (
ideally taxes as well
) and the bureaucratic burdens associated with them; small shops can then
compete freely on the free market
and we'll see what people actually want. And what does Miloslav Hlavsa, director of the Konzum cooperative retail chain, have to say? "I don't like subsidies." Great so far; but unfortunately, he continues: "Running grocery stores in small municipalities is not a business and should be enacted into law as a public service." As an entrepreneur, he doesn't want subsidies; yet he longs for the good old pre-1989 practices. What can one say to that? The whole thing is so absurd that I don't even know; but if the state didn't distort the market, who would politicians actually save?
More Aggressive Cops...

Uniformed monkeys Ondřej Bína and Přemysl Rückl pulled over a van driver in the Česká Lípa region because his taillight was out; they did so during heavy snowfall in a completely moronic spot (downhill along serpentine curves) where the driver was afraid to stop lest someone rear-end him. He slowed down and turned on his hazard lights, making it clear he intended to stop, but that wasn't enough for the cops; Přemysl Rückl justified it like this: "A car is supposed to stop immediately, not after two minutes. And where we choose the spot for it." They overtook him and pulled him over; the driver asked the cop if they couldn't move forward to a safer spot, for which the cop screamed at him. When the driver wanted to call 158 [the police emergency number], the uniformed thug dragged him out of the car, pepper-sprayed him, threw him to the ground, and kicked him; the official explanation is that they were afraid he was reaching for a weapon, suspected he might be a robber, and besides, he should have stopped immediately. Scum! Compared to that, I
got off pretty easy recently
.
The End of Cheap Calls?

Some time ago, the regulatory authority forced telecom operators to expand LTE coverage for high-speed internet; awesome? Uhhh... sort of. Surprisingly, it cost money, which was reflected in prices; supposedly, said authority does not agree with that. What can one say? It would be laughable if it weren't so tragic. But now Minister of Industry and Trade Jan Mládek is really raising hell; he's setting his sights on discounts. He wants to legally prohibit operators from offering discounts to clients (which, by the way, most of them enjoy); WTF? Yes, just raise prices in the name of the law so it's fair. Motivation? For once, I'm not betting on the usual do-gooderism combined with stupidity; I consider it far more likely that one of the big operators dislikes the current market situation and wants to get rid of discounts, but if they did it on their own, customers would leave for the competition, so they pulled strings to get it banned across the board. Thank goodness we have the state to protect us from those evil corporations!
Urza in Polis: Democracy

Two weeks ago, the topic of my
lecture in Paralelní Polis
was culture and art, and we also touched upon the preservation of cultural monuments and works of art; since the exam and flu season was over, over a hundred people showed up again. Considering the topic, I was very pleased to see how many of the attendees were artists who engaged in a lively discussion with me; many of them came to my lecture for the first time, so I had my hands full re-explaining the basics of the Austrian school of economics while trying not to bore those who already knew them.
Today I'm lecturing again, and the topic (of both the talk and the subsequent discussion) will be democracy; how do people perceive it? Why is it so often considered synonymous with freedom or even good? We'll also talk about protecting the "weak" from themselves; in connection with this, I will also attempt to prove the thesis that democracy inevitably leads to socialism. And at the end, I'd also like to say a few words about elitism. Because today's topic is quite broad and general (and controversial to boot), I think it could interest virtually anyone; this lecture is definitely very suitable for bringing someone whom you'd like to see start asking questions related to libertarianism.
Furthermore, you are all cordially invited to the next lecture, which will take place in two weeks (March 8 at 20:00) and which I consider the most important of the entire series; its topic will be education.
I look forward to seeing you tonight at 20:00 at
Paralelní Polis

Four-Day Workweek

TOP 09 has launched a debate about when and under what conditions the Czech Republic will be ready for a four-day workweek; Kalousek makes it conditional on improving labor productivity, while the unions primarily demand that the reduction of working hours be applied across the board for everyone, with their biggest concern being if it occurred only in certain industries. But furthest along, of course, is the Sewers' favorite, [Minister] Marksová, who long ago set up a working group called Work 4.0 for this purpose and is preparing to visit Germany, where debates on this topic are supposedly further ahead. For now, I'm just shaking my head and asking: why should these hotshots decide this? What if we instead abolished the entire Labor Code and left working hours and all other particulars to agreements between employers and employees? At least then unions would regain their original purpose and stop being merely a group advancing its interests through legal (yet illegitimate) violence.
We Don't Cook for Refugees!

The Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) has for the second time fined the Grand Italia pizzeria in Hrušovany nad Jevišovkou in South Moravia (with an amount in the high tens of thousands of crowns) because the owners dared to put up a sign stating that they do not cook for immigrants. On that note, I would like to make several remarks (starting from the least important and proceeding to the most important): First, I consider the restaurant owners' actions to be quite foolish, and as a patron, I would probably go elsewhere; second, many of their customers see it differently, support the restaurant, and even want to chip in to pay the fine; third, I'd be quite interested to know whether the people in question actually broke the law, given that technically, by putting up the sign, they only threatened to break it—which is probably also forbidden now; and finally, fourth, regardless of whether the law was broken, I consider it utterly immoral and unjustifiable for the state to forcibly compel someone to serve and cook for someone they do not want to.
The real problems associated with migration in the Czech Republic (especially given the actual absence of any significant number of immigrants) are paradoxically caused not by immigrants, but by the state, which interferes with people doing what they want on their own property and with their own money; let anyone who doesn't want to serve immigrants not serve them—there are plenty of others who will gladly serve them (and naturally, let's not interfere with them either). Let everyone freely decide whether they want to be a xenophobe, a racist, an Islamophobe, or an Islamophile; as long as no one initiates violence against others, it is fundamentally their business and theirs alone. What will come of forcing people who clearly do not want migrants here and hate them to cook for them? Will they start liking them or respecting them more? Not a chance! Quite the contrary—they will be all the more resentful that the state is forcing migrants upon them. Even leaving aside the fact that those fines are outrageous (which they are), they will not bring about anything positive on a practical level either.

By signing the petition, you are not committing to agreeing with every single word in it; you are simply signaling that you want this topic to be discussed and that you want politicians to take note of the fact that there are people who desire more freedom in education. add your signature

The State Has Noticed BTC

The state has noticed that cryptocurrencies exist; and it responded in its typical fashion – with the first regulation concerning their purchase and sale. Exchange offices and other service providers that accept virtual currencies (there are over 80 such places in Prague where you can pay in Bitcoin for food, lodging, tuition, or veterinary care) are now required to identify the people with whom they transact in cryptocurrencies. The next planned step is to hold the buyer (!) liable for VAT if they bought in cryptocurrency and the seller failed to remit the tax. Bitcoin and other virtual currencies are, of course, a royal pain in the ass for the tax office because they can easily mask financial trails, meaning the state no longer has all the property of its subjects in the palm of its hand; and the more popular these currencies become, the more the state will push back against them. So let's get ready for Bitcoin to be portrayed as the currency of child porn traffickers and the like; we're in for quite a ride.

School Financing

Until now, Czech schools were funded based on the number of pupils; however, MPs voted that starting in September, money will be distributed based on teaching hours taught (incidentally, the introduction of the bill was accompanied by hysteria featuring topics like the humanist tradition, the genocide of Native Americans, European values, the Thirty Years' War, Christian atrocities, the harms of multiculturalism, and chocolate – the bigwigs really covered everything from top to bottom). What will this change bring? Does anyone know? No. Everyone has an opinion, but the actual results are unpredictable; it might help or harm, depending on who and what. The declared goal is to help rural schools with few pupils, which will probably happen, but assuming overall costs remain unchanged, quite logically at the expense of schools with large numbers of students (the extra money for small schools will have to be missing somewhere). The question, of course, is: Is that desirable? And the answer? Unfortunately, nobody can even know; and what's worse, we won't even find out in the future.
The only way
to find out what is desirable
is to leave the choice free to the people – let everyone decide which school (and whether to a school at all; we also have
unschooling
) they want to send their child to and how much they want to pay for it; until we leave these matters to the free market, where everyone can best decide how they wish their resources to be used, we are completely blind and unable to perform an effective economic calculation. Not to mention that funding is one of the smallest problems when it comes to education; the state education system primarily deforms our children through indoctrination, exposes them to massive pro-state propaganda, and instills in them from an early age the feeling that
submission to imposed authority is desirable

subject the children of the rest of us to it as well

Twenty-Two Years Since the Death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today marks exactly twenty-two years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses departed this world just shy of his 69th birthday – Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"; his life's work was the consistent and logical culmination of two traditions that seemingly had little in common: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often mistaken in economics, and proponents of the Austrian school of economics failed to apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and arrived at the brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This realization and the full understanding of it profoundly changed my life; thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Go Elsewhere!

Not far from where I live, there is a hospital; this hospital is notorious for being terrible, not to mention that the personal experiences of my loved ones point to the same thing (visibly drunk doctors and the like). Fortunately, I personally almost never use doctors' services, but recently I found myself in a state (food poisoning) where a hospital visit was necessary; for obvious reasons, my girlfriend drove me about 30 kilometers to a better hospital (which is practically any other one). Patching me up took the doctors about eight hours, so quite a few medical staff rotated around me; without exception, however, their first question after glancing at my chart was not about my health condition, but why I wasn't at the hospital where I live (I don't think they always ask this, but this time they were severely swamped). Every time, I was told that this simply wouldn't do, and they wrote on my discharge papers (with exclamation marks) that I must go for my follow-up check-up in my local area.
Can you imagine this at a private company? Can you imagine employees reproachfully asking customers why they didn't go to the competitor? Hardly, of course; entrepreneurs are thrilled to have customers, compete for them, strive to accommodate them, and when they have lots of them, do everything they can to keep them. Hospitals
in our socialist healthcare system
, however, have no such incentive; patients represent nothing but a hassle and the nuisance of having to work. I believe those repeated urgings to go to the competition vividly illustrate and symbolize something much deeper; the entire mindset is reflected in them. If you tell an entrepreneur that their competitor disappointed you and that's why you came to them, they will typically be delighted, but a socialist thinks differently. Now consider how deeply the incentive to turn customers away permeates everything; unfortunately, it's not the fault of the individual doctors—they are acting rationally; the flaw lies in the entire state leviathan that more or less forces them to behave that way.

Internet Censorship: Change, or Freedom?

In my efforts to show people the benefits of a free society and the inherent evil residing in states as such, I run primarily into propaganda and indoctrination on the theme of "the state is necessary", where this deeply rooted thesis often completely overrides any logical arguments, which are then swept off the table a priori; besides that, however, there is also the favorite and ubiquitous "that wouldn't work" argument, which I have mentioned many times before and would now like to dissect in a bit more detail.
Before I dive into that, I cannot help mentioning one observation I have made over long years of debating freedom: In stark contrast to people's general distrust of freedom in the real world stands the rather substantial trust those same people place in the freedom of the Internet in the virtual world. Have you noticed that? When politicians come forward with regulations offline, they are frequently supported even in actions that restrict freedom of expression (and far from only that); yet as soon as it comes to Internet censorship, most people are far more sensitive. Why do you think that is?
One explanation occurred to me – while the physical world is so over-regulated that nobody can even imagine it without regulations anymore, the Internet is currently relatively free and everyone sees that no doom ensues and things function even without a central authority. The volume of offline regulation has exceeded all bounds, forcing people to integrate it into their lives to such an extent that the majority of the population likely cannot imagine life without it; or rather, doing so requires a massive dose of imagination and the willingness to accept that the outcome cannot really be predicted, since the free market is unpredictable, meaning even the boldest ideas will only ever be one of many hypothetical versions of the future.
In connection with this, a nagging question arises: To what extent do people, as a consequence of state propaganda, fundamentally reject freedom, and to what extent do they reject change? In an unfree world, these two things can easily merge – someone opposed to change may appear to be an opponent of freedom, and of course the reverse is also true. What role does fear of the unknown play? Everyone sees that a free Internet does not mean the collapse of civilization; yet many are convinced that a stateless society would bring about the end of civilization. Do you think that if these people were able to visualize alternatives, it would change their attitudes?

Murray Christmas 2016!

So another year has rolled by and Christmas is here; holidays that nearly everyone celebrates and likes in their own way, yet very often complains about at the same time (complaints about consumerism, hustle, hectic pace, and so forth). Personally – as a Christian and an anarcho-capitalist – I love Christmas because I appreciate both the spiritual and material aspects of these holidays; and without exception, I always enjoy them to the utmost, completely stress-free. How to pull that off? Well, I spend the holidays with my family and loved ones, and we couldn't care less about what one is "supposed to" do at Christmas; nobody is forced into anything. Whoever feels like getting a Christmas tree gets one; whoever feels like baking cookies bakes; whoever feels like making dinner cooks; whoever feels like buying presents buys them; someone usually ends up doing most of these things... and what nobody feels like doing? We simply don't have that year; but we always come together, everyone is content, loving, and loved. I cannot recommend it enough xD
Even this year, I don't want to forget to hold up (us) Christians as an example in PR for (us) libertarians: Christmas was, by all accounts, originally a pagan festival that Christians managed to transform into the day we commemorate the birth of the Lord Jesus, whom the Lord sent into this world to redeem us from sin through the suffering He endured for our transgressions – at least that is what I believe, and I am immensely grateful to Him for this help on the path to salvation; regardless of what you believe, isn't such a feat fascinating? And I'm not speaking now of Jesus' sacrifice, but of changing the meaning of pagan holidays into Christmas despite the fact that none of the notable astronomical phenomena around year zero that could have been the Star of Bethlehem (whether Halley's Comet or not) occurred in winter; that's something akin to turning Czech Statehood Day into Tax Abolition Day... and there's still a long road ahead to that.

The Spirit of Freedom

I thank the libertarian Robert Higgs for the inspiration to write this text.
Dear readers, have you ever heard or used any of the following arguments?
1/ Look around you, there is a state in every society; do you know of one that doesn't have one?
2/ The state is an institution thousands of years old, existing since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why don't stateless societies emerge?
3/ Without states, people would behave like animals, be dangerous, and unable to care for themselves; they need their rulers!
4/ Without states, economic collapse would ensue; the economy stands and falls with laws.
5/ Abolishing states would cost great bloodshed; then they would simply re-emerge at the cost of even more blood.
6/ Free people in various parts of the world are even worse off than citizens of our state; and citizens should be glad for what they have.
7/ Conditions in states can improve; rather than abolishing states, let's strive to reform them.
8/ A world without states is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to everyone except a few naive fools.
Let's step back a few hundred years in time and look at several arguments against the abolition of slavery:
1/ Look around you, there is slavery in every society; do you know of one that doesn't have it?
2/ Slavery is an institution thousands of years old, existing since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why don't non-slaveholding societies emerge?
3/ Slaves without masters would behave like animals, be dangerous, and unable to care for themselves; they need their slaveholders!
4/ Without slavery, economic collapse would ensue; the economy stands and falls with slavery.
5/ Abolishing slavery would cost great bloodshed; then it would simply re-emerge at the cost of even more blood.
6/ Free people in various parts of the world are even worse off than our slaves; and slaves should be glad for what they have.
7/ The conditions of slaves can improve; rather than abolishing slavery, let's strive to improve their living conditions.
8/ A world without slaveholders is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to everyone except a few naive fools.
These are real arguments by real people (A. Lincoln, G. Washington, T. Jefferson, G. Fitzhugh, T. Carlyle, and many others).
How "strong" do the first eight arguments look compared to the second eight? And how many years must pass before people find the former just as absurd?
Cops and Speeding

If you drive slower, you have more time to react to the situation around you; that certainly holds true if you drive that way by your own choice. But what if you are forced to do so under threat of a fine? An Australian study conducted under the leadership of Dr. Vanessa Bowden shows that voluntariness matters here too: eighty-four drivers (unaware of what was being tested) drove in a simulator through areas with a 50 km/h speed limit—in one scenario knowing they would be fined for exceeding the limit by just 1 km/h, in the second by 6 km/h, and finally by 11 km/h. The result? The more restrictive limits forced drivers to watch the speedometer more and their surroundings less, ergo they demonstrably failed to notice what was happening around them much more often; and what good is a shorter braking distance if you don't even see that you need to brake? But uniformed monkeys don't care about that; their job is to collect tally marks for fines...
The order was clear: They must not pass at any cost!
The Berlin Truck Massacre

Some maniac drove a truck loaded with steel into a crowd of people at the Christmas markets in Berlin, injuring about fifty and killing twelve (hopefully the death toll won't rise further); by all accounts, it was deliberate, a terrorist attack, and I'd wager the perpetrator was an Islamic radical. I am deeply saddened that this happened, just as I am saddened for all other murder victims; worldwide there are about half a million of them each year, and in Germany hundreds every year. What can we do about it? Most likely keep an eye out for ourselves and our loved ones, and accept that the world simply isn't completely safe and we constantly live with some degree of risk; I consider it advisable to arm oneself and prepare for defense against criminals. But so that we don't make the world even more dangerous, let's assess individual tragedies rationally, in context, and without hysteria; let's defend ourselves against aggressors and
not initiate violence against the innocent
.
"That Wouldn't Work!"

The central focus of most debates on anarchy tends to be a discussion of what could or could not function without state power; anarcho-capitalists try to predict (though admitting themselves that it is impossible to say with certainty) how the free market could theoretically replace individual functions of the state, while statists raise various objections as to why that wouldn't actually be possible. However, I believe that the world (and the free market) functions in a far more fascinating way than anyone could ever imagine (including anarchists who realize this); I would like to offer two examples here.
Let's imagine there was a law requiring a policeman to be present in every restaurant to ensure that nobody ran off without paying or refused to pay after a meal; how would statists defend such a law? Well, they would probably argue that if he weren't there, everyone would inevitably abuse it, doom would follow, and all restaurants would go bankrupt; patrons would walk out en masse without paying, pretend after eating that they had no money, or deliberately leave it at home – and what could poor waiters do about it then? And now, anarchists, hand on heart: how many of you would invent some elaborate construct for how the market would solve this "problem"? I certainly would; I'd argue, for instance, that restaurants could demand a deposit from unfamiliar patrons while only regulars would pay after their meal. Yet... in reality, it is simply and plain unnecessary; barring rare exceptions, it works just fine without any special measures.
Now let's assume that the Internet were not anonymous; that anyone's online activity was publicly attributable to their real identity. E-commerce shops would certainly begin using this to verify their customers' identities. How would statists defend this? Here they would likely claim that an e-shop simply cannot function on an anonymous Internet because anyone could order goods cash-on-delivery under someone else's name, stores would be spammed with bogus orders and forced to demand upfront payments; but then everyone would start launching fake e-shops en masse, cashing out money, and never shipping the goods. Thus it would be "obvious to everyone" that on an anonymous Internet nobody would ever buy or sell anything, because users couldn't trust one another; and now – in a world with a non-anonymous Internet – try refuting those statists (or e-shop owners)!
I believe that many problems for which we currently struggle to imagine solutions without the state actually have far more straightforward and unbelievable solutions than we could ever anticipate.
The State vs. Landowners

The agrarian lobby is trying to push through a law that would prevent owners of farmed agricultural land from freely disposing of their property; specifically, the tenant farmer leasing the land would have the right of first refusal, followed by the state, and only then could the owner sell it to whomever they wish. If such a law were actually to pass, it would constitute an enormous infringement on the property rights of many people; after all, they own the land, so they should have the power to dispose of it as they see fit, such as selling it to anyone, rather than being
forcibly compelled
to favor certain buyers in the name of
yet more protection for Czech farmers
. Landowners will be harmed by this law because they will be unable to sell their property to whoever they want (typically whoever offers the highest bid; instead, they must favor a buyer that is worse for them); so let's sound the alarm, spread this news, and complicate the lobbyists' work by informing as many people as possible about their vile intentions.

Banning Reincarnation?

Did you know that the Chinese government has been regulating reincarnation for several years? Until recently, I didn't; and when this news reached me, I couldn't believe it, but after about an hour of Googling, it became clear that this is indeed true. In China, there is an agency called the "State Administration for Religious Affairs" (which is terrible enough in itself) without whose permission reincarnation is prohibited; or rather, if a monk wants to establish who he was in a past life, before meditating and performing all those religious rituals, he must first fill out a form, go to the government office, and wait for approval—otherwise, he is acting illegally. The essence of the law is presumably harassment of Tibetans, since reincarnation is vital to their culture; nevertheless, it is one of the most absurd laws I have ever encountered (alongside, for example, Iowa, where kisses lasting longer than five minutes are allegedly banned, or North Carolina, where the only legal sexual position was missionary).
A Useful Bike Path

What is shorter – a bicycle or a bike path? In some cases, that's not entirely clear; take a look at what kind of bike path you can encounter in Zelenč near Prague – to view the photo,
click here
. Now isn't that wonderful and above all useful? How much could that have cost? The sign, transport, labor (someone had to deliver the sign and install it there), bureaucratic loafing (someone had to wisely decide on the whole thing), well... my guess is a cool ten thousand crowns; can you imagine anyone who could spend that money better? I know, it's hard. But how does this government project differ from others? Really only in that the inefficiency here is blatant and visible at first glance; due to
the impossibility of economic calculation
, it simply isn't in the state's power to do things efficiently in the long run, because by forcing people to pay for a good,

The Town of Cherán

In the Mexican state of Michoacán lies the small town of Cherán, with a population of about thirteen thousand; these residents are characterized by definitely having balls (even though most of them are women xD), which they proved in 2011 when they kicked the mob out of their town. But they really did a thorough job, because it wasn't just the illegal mafia in the form of drug cartels—they also dealt with local politicians and cops, simply running them out of town by force. Political parties were abolished, and each of the town's four districts now elects its representative to the town council. The town is now defended against external aggressors by a community militia composed of local residents who originally didn't even know how to hold a gun, but can now defend against both legal and illegal criminals; residents also provide their internal security (almost) entirely on their own—they fine petty criminals or make them work off their offenses, while handing over those who commit serious crimes to the central government.
Crime in Cherán has dropped significantly since then; for instance, over the past year there wasn't a single murder or kidnapping there, which by our standards wouldn't be unusual for a town of thirteen thousand, but in Michoacán (which has under 4.5 million inhabitants) over a thousand people are murdered each year (in the entire Czech Republic with ten million people, we don't have even a fifth of their murder count, so we don't kill each other even a tenth as often). Thus, by local averages, Cherán should statistically see several murders per year (and previously it really did). I am not claiming Cherán has full-blown
anarchy
—after all, they still cooperate with Michoacán to some degree—yet expelling the agents of state power brought greater peace, tranquility, and order to the town than had ever been there before; so only one question remains: do you think that, if it came down to it, the people of Cherán could even build roads?

Heroes of Paralelní Polis

Ludwig von Mises' motto was: "Tu ne cede malis sed contra audentior ito."
Translated, this means: "Yield not to evil, but proceed ever more boldly against it."
I am convinced from the bottom of my heart that the greatest sources of evil in the contemporary world are states; fighting them is very difficult, because they are powerful monopolies on violence equipped with amazing PR and relentless propaganda. Nevertheless, people can be found who, for diverse reasons, fight their battles against them in many ways: the black market, civil disobedience, raising awareness, and debunking myths, but also trying to reform the state from within... whatever I may think of individual methods of struggle, I am grateful to anyone who does something against the state. Yet few stand up to it directly...
...and that is why I call the libertarians of Paralelní Polis heroes; they defied harassment by the state via the EET—a disgusting and immoral system designed to make the state's plundering of citizens more efficient, defended by absurd rhetoric claiming that anyone who doesn't let the state rob them is a thief themselves—and

to stop by Holešovice for coffee and cake or something to eat for Bitcoin

Mother and Son

Thirty-six-year-old Monica Mares, the biological mother of nineteen-year-old Caleb Peterson, discovered a passionate love for her son as a woman to a man; he reciprocated her feelings, so they began dating. Well, it's bizarre, but that's their business; unfortunately, courts in New Mexico, where both live, do not share this view. In addition to the state banning Monica from contact with all (!) of her children, both lovers face prison time; yet despite the persecution, they want to be together and are determined to find a new home somewhere where they won't be prosecuted for their relationship... which shows how much sense it makes to
punish incest – whom does it help?
Absolutely nobody; they don't plan on breaking up because of it anyway, and besides, they aren't harming anyone with their relationship; on top of that, taxpayers will have to pay for their imprisonment, not to mention the destruction of a family whose mother was taken away by the state.
It doesn't surprise me how many people condemn such a thing, as I understand they find it disgusting; what I find remarkable, however, is how few simply say: "It makes me sick, so I don't wish them well," but instead try to rationalize that feeling with arguments like: "It's unacceptable because if they have a disabled child, taxpayers will pay for it." isn't a sufficient reason
for them, and they want to ban incest out of other motives. Personally, what I find utterly disgusting about the whole affair is state interference and the destruction of the lives of people who are guilty of nothing more than loving each other; while their relationship is heavily aberrant and deviant, I wish them good luck, understanding from their community, and peace from the state.

The "Emergency" State

In November 2015, terrorists attacked in Paris
; the French government declared a "state of emergency" back then, which translates to a (theoretically temporary) police state. We had a chance to see the effectiveness of this measure for ourselves
in July in Nice
; the cops failed; an armed populace would likely have stopped the maniac in the truck, but weapons are bad (and therefore regulated), riiiight. While the "state of emergency" keeps being repeatedly extended (always by several months), French Prime Minister Manuel Valls announced that in January 2017 it will be extended again by several months, because (quote): "It is difficult to end the state of emergency now. Especially in a presidential campaign with meetings and public gatherings. We must protect our democracy. The state of emergency allows arrests and searches, which is effective. Therefore, without a doubt, we will live with this state of affairs for several more months." And thus freedom dies; who remembers what Benjamin Franklin said about trading liberty for security?

Murderous Uniformed Monkeys

Two cops from Pilsen, and I will name those bastards – Jan Pergl and Lukáš Zahradník, were dispatched in October 2012 to handle a grave situation: a homeless man was tapping on the window of a dormitory hostel. Ritual Burning of Ivory

The director of the Dvůr Králové Zoo, Přemysl Rabas, has a penchant for multi-million bonfires; in 2014 he organized a ritual burning of horns in Dvůr Králové, and this year the boys (accompanied by Jan Stejskal, head of international projects) flew to Vietnam to fool around in the exact same manner. my article that I published on this topic back then

private breeding farms (without which bison, for instance, would have gone extinct long ago)
