I have already written tons of arguments demonstrating what nonsense this whole thing is, but here the proponent proves it best himself: because nobody needs to be coerced into what actually pays off.
On Attitudes Toward Refugees

My view on immigrants is currently very "out"; basically, I think roughly this: "No one should force anyone to support refugees. No one should prevent anyone from supporting refugees." The first sentence irritates the bleeding-heart "sunshiners," because after all, that's horrible discrimination, and since we already have a welfare state, why not expand its scope (and when I mention that the whole welfare state is wrong, they clutch their heads); the second sentence enrages the Islam-bashers, to whom anyone wishing to care for people in need on their own property and at their own expense is a plain traitor deserving severe punishment who needs to come to their senses.
As usually happens when I express my opinion in this vein (essentially saying the same thing over and over: laissez-faire, let everyone mind their own business on their own property at their own expense, let others do the same, and let the state stay out of it on either side), everyone always singles out the part that irks them (while one side interprets it as opportunistic xenophobia, the other as opportunistic treason) so they can beat me over the head with it; neither side typically pulls punches, since—despite my futile protests—they automatically lump me in with their opponents for failing to share their orthodox view.
Why am I writing about this? Lately, I often see various Islam-bashers lauding public demonstrations against refugees as acts of heroism; as someone who constantly enjoys criticism from both camps, I can assert that the exact opposite is true (speaking of expressions within the bounds of law; when the thought police get involved, the situation reverses). If any publicly voiced opinion on immigration comes close to heroism, it is standing up for refugees: first, the overwhelming majority of the population holds a more or less opposing view, escalating the risk of confrontation; but above all, Islam-bashers are far scarier than bleeding hearts. While bleeding-heart disapproval manifests (online or in person) typically as grumbling, Islam-bashers can be far more aggressive (I've received numerous profanities and threats from them, virtually and in person, a few times bordering on physical assault).
I wouldn't want this text to sound as though bleeding hearts are the good guys—it is precisely they who typically tap into various subsidies, collaborate with the state, and seek to censor their opponents, which I consider far more dangerous than the aggression of Islam-bashers; I simply wanted to point out that howling with the crowd while posing as a dissident is pretty cheap. True courage lies in saying things that the majority does not want to hear, even when facing the threat of getting punched in the face for it.
Pohlreich in a Bureaucrats' Pub

Zdeněk Pohlreich is a very skilled chef who—despite his strongly statist views—understands the workings of the market on a basic practical level, which probably has to do with being a successful entrepreneur and star of a television show where he teaches other restaurant and pub operators how to succeed; and today I'll write about one episode of that show: the chef visited a hotel restaurant run by municipal officials who described the property relations (literally) like this: "It's not a municipal hotel; it's a private hotel, but owned by the city." I don't know why, but that reminds me of the Stork's Nest. Other gems of explanation include: "Economically it makes no sense, but it's necessary," or: "We offer soup and a main course for 75 crowns because many city hall employees eat here." If you want to see more, look up episode 15 of season 6 on the internet.
And what intrigued me most about the spectacle? Well, even though Ano, šéfe! ("Yes, Boss!") had been filmed with all kinds of desperate characters, at least everyone understood that the goal of their business was to make money; this was the first episode featuring people who didn't even grasp this foundational premise, making up all sorts of "necessary economic nonsense" instead. Only a politician, a bureaucrat, or their subordinates could seriously come up with something like that; after all, how else can one know what is good for people other than letting them pay for it? Everyone pays for what they want and find useful; conversely, nobody voluntarily pays for things they do not deem beneficial. The market operates on this principle, whereas politicians and bureaucrats are typically characterized by misunderstanding it entirely, or at least ignoring it. Delusions in the form of "economic nonsense that is necessary" unfortunately permeate throughout society because they are propagated by the (state) educational system.
Pelikán's Whining and Tax Evasion

On Friday in the Sewers, I wrote that Robert Pelikán had actually done something positive; so today, let's remind ourselves once again what a bastard our Minister of Justice is. A few days ago, the Chamber of Deputies passed his amendment to the Criminal Procedure Code, under which not only tax evasion is a criminal offense, but preparing to commit it is as well; in practice, the law primarily means further expanding the powers of cops, who will now be able to initiate wiretaps and surveillance merely on the suspicion that someone is getting ready to evade taxes. All entrepreneurs with police connections who aren't ashamed to use them to eliminate competition are surely very grateful to Pelikán; far more sensitive data (originating even from people who did nothing wrong, just perhaps preparing to shield some property from robbers) will fall into the hands of cops, who will surely manage to monetize at least part of it. Plus the state plunders more money, so win-win; and canis familiaris defecates upon the taxpayers.
Kuwait: The Dream of Czech Politicians

Czech Islam-bashers and surveillance lovers have another model paradise on earth (like Angola, for instance) that we must strive towards as fast as possible: in Kuwait, the government bought a DNA database of all citizens and permanent residents for hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars; anyone who refuses to provide a sample pays a hefty fine and does a year in prison, while anyone who submits a fake sample goes behind bars for seven years. The reason? Defense against terrorism; logically, what else. When someone blows themselves up somewhere next time, uniformed monkeys will gather up the pieces and immediately know who it was... that is... if any pieces of him remain... and if they don't get mixed up with pieces of the victims... and if the suicide bomber willing to sacrifice his life was terrified of prison and didn't give the government fake DNA... and if he was a citizen or resident... and if he wasn't there illegally... and if he wasn't using a fake identity... and if...
...so if the suicide bomber was a law-abiding citizen who snitched on himself to the government, his identity will be known ex post, which is useful for... uh, what? Oh right, exposing his terror cell... assuming it hadn't accounted for the universally known national DNA database; overall, this sounds like a textbook state tool for fighting terrorism. Most importantly, it cost a ton of money, activity was logged, people can be locked up over it, and hefty fines collected; and of course it rests on every government's notorious premise that criminals obey laws—doesn't this ring a bell for anyone? What about domestic (and even far worse in other EU countries) laws on civilian gun possession? Gun-free zones? All of these are ingenious ideas for rendering defenseless the decent people who obey these laws; conversely, criminals, who by definition are unbothered by breaking laws, gain an upper hand over everyone else.
Did your parents raise you poorly? Don't despair, the government will fix it!

A few months ago, you could read in the Sewers about the violation of the inviolability of the home in the name of boiler inspections; the state can simply send an inspector to your house based on an anonymous tip-off, whom you must let inside and allow to rummage through your boiler, otherwise you will be forced by violence to pay fifty thousand crowns. There isn't much to add to that piece of filth itself, yet interesting things are starting to unfold around it: first, it has been sharply criticized by the ODS (and this is not the first time over the past year that the ODS has tried to block totalitarian laws, since in opposition they act as a more or less right-wing party; what a pity that once they take power, they turn into socialists); and second, in response to this criticism, Minister Brabec's deputy Peštová showed her true colors when she proclaimed: "We want to teach people not to burn trash and poison others' lives. We want to educate them." When parents raise their children, they provide for them at the same time; but when parasites from government ministries "educate" us, we are the ones forced to feed them.
Freedom and homosexuals

Justice Minister Robert Pelikán, whom the Sewers haven't left a single shred of credibility in the past, is now proposing an amendment that I view as positively as possible; yes, you read that right, I am essentially praising a minister. What is it about? Homosexuals will be able to adopt their partners' children (heterosexuals already can). What is that good for? For instance, if a biological parent dies, the child won't be carted off to an orphanage, but can stay with the surviving partner; and not only that, the person simply becomes the child's legal parent. Of course, it isn't entirely ideal—the state naturally shouldn't regulate relations between parents and children at all, which would make such adoptions completely unnecessary; however, as long as the government brutally interferes in people's lives like this, it is undoubtedly positive when the option of adoption (which allows bypassing some of the legal hurdles thrown under people's feet by the state) is available not only to straights, but also to gays.

What is interesting—and deeply sad—is how many people (often calling themselves advocates of liberty) are completely losing their shit over this proposal. Reading a sentence in Vlastenecké noviny like: "Czech homosexual deviants living in unions will be able to [...] trample upon the human rights of children by denying them a life in a non-deviant environment," is not all that surprising, because anything called Vlastenecké noviny is 99% sure to be pure garbage; nevertheless, the reactions of many conservatives, who stomach state bullying in the name of their homophobia, disgust me. I always used to wonder what the four-percent minority is marching for at Prague Pride, given that in the twenty-first century practically everyone (perhaps except old grannies on small village greens) doesn't care who is attracted to women and who to men. But clearly I was wrong; there is still a crowd of young, uptight prigs who mind someone being gay so much that they take joy in seeing them harassed by the state.
Are you a good taxi driver? An official will be the judge of that.

Liberec entrepreneur Pavel Svoboda has a problem: although he found fifteen people who wanted to work as taxi drivers for his company, not a single one received a permit from the authorities, because none of them passed the local topography exam. So Mr. Svoboda took the exam himself, unable to let it go—and he flunked it too. Where's the catch? Well, there are errors in the test, so correct answers are scored as wrong (and this isn't some minor semantic quibble: an aspiring taxi driver might be asked to list all streets crossing another street, and the only "correct" answer includes a parallel street that doesn't cross it at all). Pavel Svoboda therefore asked city hall to cancel this absurd exam, but the response was: "Passing the exam is the sole requirement established by law to ensure qualified drivers providing taxi services." Thus, qualified is someone who answers questions incorrectly.

We can, of course, speculate whether the errors in the test were caused by bureaucratic ineptitude or placed there deliberately so that the only way to pass was to purchase the "correct" answers from someone at city hall; in any case, the biggest scandal in the entire matter is the very fact that mandatory bureaucratic quality control for taxi drivers exists in the first place. The entire premise is utterly wrong, because the only party that should be making such assessments is the customer. An official simply cannot know what matters to whom: How important is it for the driver to be polite? Good-looking? Talkative? Quiet? Cheap? Knowledgeable about topography? Who other than the customer can decide how crucial it is whether the driver knows the city by heart or uses GPS navigation? The greatest outrage, of course, lies in state coercion, where a group of people violently forces individuals to provide their services to others only under certain dictated conditions.
Keep calm; the mass graves are ready

The Prague Cemetery Administration, together with the city magistrate, is drawing up a crisis plan for where to bury people in the event of major catastrophes; officials have identified three sites for mass graves capable of holding tens of thousands of corpses, so you can sleep soundly. Why are they doing this? Well, to quote: "Such situations are completely improbable, but we must be prepared." Sure enough, bureaucrats paid with extorted loot are fussing over nonsense because "we must be prepared." Interestingly, the public mostly buys it and finds it reasonable, even prudent; and to all those people, I ask: How much of your time, money, and land have you already invested in devising procedures for what to do if a large portion of your family suddenly drops dead? Absolutely none, I assume; because you hate to squander scarce resources preparing for scenarios with a miniscule probability of occurring. But bureaucrats don't do it for free either (and furthermore, those plots could be used for other purposes).

This is another widespread paradox: public administration frequently squanders resources preventing various improbable disasters, and people accept it with gratitude only because they don't perceive the spent resources as their own; typically, none of those who praise bureaucrats for foresight would willingly surrender their own funds to insure themselves against such eventualities. And this doesn't apply just to disasters; in general, "planning ahead" (mainly in the field of ecology) is viewed positively because people intuitively feel that it happens for free. If such planning were truly worth the consumed resources, people would do it for themselves, on their own dime and on their own property—which typically does not happen. In their personal lives, everyone intuitively accounts for opportunity costs, but as soon as public affairs come up, they lose sight of them entirely; after all, we did take away something from those (state) schools.
A disarming police state

Do you own a legally held firearm? Then you'd better stay on the cops' good side, because the government has granted them a new power: seizing weapons from any citizen. If the owner doesn't hand it over "nicely," they can seize it by force—either directly from them, or even by kicking down the door and breaking into their home to get it. And the biggest shocker for anyone who hasn't grasped the full horror of the above description? No court order is required. The uniformed ape acts as accuser, judge, and executioner all at once; and they need no evidence, nor essentially any special justification, because it's enough for the authority to feel that the gun owner isn't mentally sound—something a cop can either deduce on his own, or receive via a malicious tip-off from a neighbor. Especially in the latter case, I wonder how many apes will take the responsibility of not confiscating a weapon and risk that the person actually does something—leaving the media to tear them apart.

Because the law is supposedly designed to "solve" situations where a shooter passes the tests but becomes unstable over time, cops can theoretically force someone to repeatedly prove their mental fitness and take their weapon again and again, claiming the person has become dangerous since the last test. Another aspect, of course, is establishing abhorrent conditions under which the state can disarm anyone it sees fit. Not to mention yet another breach of the inviolability of the home. And that, dear friends, is how totalitarianism is forged—stiffer and stiffer by the day.
Warning for drivers: Not all roundabouts are created equal!

Ťok and his minions at the Ministry of Transport are either going berserk again, or the comrades made a mistake and didn't think much while drafting yet more laws; in any case, the result is the same—once again, they have redefined something for us: A classic roundabout, as we know it, must now mandatorily be marked with both the roundabout sign and a "Give Way" sign, which is fine enough; the problem is that the law now also permits a "roundabout" without a "Give Way" sign, meaning in that case approaching traffic has right of way over vehicles already in the circle—in other words, the standard priority-to-the-right rule applies, just as it would if there were no signs at all (their sole function being to confuse the enemy—the driver—by giving the impression of a classic roundabout). I don't know whether the goal was to cause more accidents, collect more fines, or if the law was simply drafted by an idiot; either way, watch out!
News from Liberland

I assume all readers of the Sewers know what Liberland is; anyone who doesn't can go ahead and google this libertarian microstate founded by Vít Jedlička. Although the president of Liberland has not yet succeeded in convincing other states (especially Croatia, which has blocked Liberland off with a wall on its side and arrests its citizens) to recognize Liberland's sovereignty, the first company has registered in the new microstate—which, by the way, has pledged to pay voluntary taxes. Another new development is that Liberland now has its own currency called the Merit, which in my opinion is somewhat unfortunately pegged to the US dollar. Whatever my reservations about Vít Jedlička's actions may be (and I do have a few), I welcome his initiatives: while I don't really believe the Liberland project can succeed, even if it doesn't, it represents massive promotion for libertarianism in the Czech Republic and abroad; and if it should happen to succeed, something far greater than a mere tax haven will be born. What do you think?
A hundred-year weather forecast

According to a new study from the University of Oxford, climate change could (!) cause fruit and vegetable shortages by 2050, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths from cancer and cardiovascular disease; crop-devastating heatwaves, which have so far occurred approximately once every hundred years, could (!) occur every four years starting in 2100. What is there to say? Well, according to Urza's new study, Klingons could (!) arrive tomorrow; not that I've spotted their ships anywhere, but then Oxford scientists can't even predict the weather a month from now, yet they know what it will be like in a hundred years? Or rather, what it could (!) be like, which isn't very different from my Klingon prediction. You might object that weather forecasting is different from climate change? Fair enough. Show me someone who can flawlessly predict climate trends (heatwaves, severe winters, droughts, rains...) ten years in advance; until then, I refuse to take seriously those fortune-telling heatwaves in the year 2100.

Not to mention that if it were merely about fortune-telling itself, I'd have nothing against it—I don't mind tarot readers either (though I don't believe them); the problem, however, is partly that a charlatan predicts the future more cheaply (and for a client who voluntarily pays for it, not using money looted by the state), but above all that the consequences of various climate pseudoscience studies are devastating even to those who want nothing to do with it. Based on climate crystal-ball gazing, governments enact various laws and regulations that cost insane amounts of money on one hand and, at best, produce no effect on the other—or at worst, lead to social engineering and state harassment of citizens. And when time exposes the charlatan's error? No matter, another "expert" will be found; just look at the global warming affair—when it turned out that leading "scientific" figures had manipulated data, the fight against global warming was simply rebranded as the fight against climate change, and the circus goes on.
L'État, c'est moi

To amuse himself, the ruler invited actors to the town to perform a play; however, he didn't like it, so midway through the performance he sent a maid right into the middle of the stage to stop it—the actors leave humiliated, the audience disperses, and the ruler makes his displeasure known. A scene from a fantasy or historical novel? Not at all; Slovakia, Brezno, year 2016. Starring the governor of the Banská Bystrica Region, Marián Kotleba, and an official from the department of education, Marianna Kemková; straight up, plain and simple: "End the play, or we will have the curtain drawn." And as she said, so it was done. Does anything more need to be added? In my opinion, no.
Babiš, ruler of the virtual world

ANO and the ČSSD are jointly pushing another law through parliament (while sweeping all amendments off the table) that will hand Babiš even more power; specifically, the Ministry of Finance is to be granted the legislative authority to block any website. And the reason? Fighting illegal gambling on the Internet. Not that such a fight isn't already a massive outrage in its own right, but this upgrade means that the decision as to whether a given website operates illegal gambling rests solely with Ministry of Finance bureaucrats, whose word will be law—ergo, in practice, this allows unlimited virtual censorship. So whenever a website pisses Babiš off too much, it will simply be axed. "He could never get away with that"? Oh, come on! The Stork's Nest? A completely blatant fraud that everyone just laughs at, while in reality nothing of consequence happens; and people will vote for him again anyway—he's the crowd favorite, and in a democracy that's all that matters.

The Ministry of Finance's defense? Utterly hilarious: "We won't abuse it, though. Blocking will only be applied as a last resort." Sure, of course, we all believe that, makes total sense; that's why ANO and the ČSSD are brushing aside every amendment that would prevent such abuse at least legislatively. Not to mention that a law already exists allowing the Ministry of Finance to block incoming payments to illegal gambling operations, which effectively shuts them down entirely; with that mechanism, they can already eliminate any virtual casino today. But that isn't nearly as sexy for Babiš, because it doesn't allow him to block the websites of inconvenient people, or blackmail them with the threat of a shutdown. I'd really love to know what all those self-proclaimed "right-wingers" who voted for Babiš in the last election—because he's a businessman who will run the state like a firm, and so forth—have to say about this; probably nothing, because such people don't care about deeds, only cheap talk.
Whoever doesn't close on holidays, we'll lock up and he'll be locked up

Labor unions are trying to push through a law mandating the closure of large retail stores on public holidays. I watched the TV debate show Máte slovo on this topic... and dear friends, it made me want to puke; not just from the bill itself, but the "arguments" presented there were extreme. Right at the start, someone had to explain the glaringly obvious (because sadly it was necessary): that retail employees' wages come from the money customers spend in those stores. To which an affected saleswoman replied: "That isn't true! The reality in retail chains is that we employees get nothing from those revenues." I sat there staring with my mouth open; I understand she's totally dense, but this borders on legal incompetence. All the socialists had their mouths full of talk about Western countries—because if Germany implements totalitarianism, we must too; and on top of that, a Christian Democrat started rambling on about national values... I only regret I wasn't there in person to metaphorically shit all over his national values!

On the flip side, the arguments of their opponents... made me clutch my head in despair as well, because hardly anything substantial was said: just endless polls, Western countries (an evergreen: once Germany bans reading, books will be burned in the Czech Republic), statistics, urban lifestyles... but for anyone to say a single word about violent coercion, property rights, freedom, or voluntary exchange? Not a chance. The absolute peak was: "It's social engineering; why should the state dictate to citizens when they can shop?" Damn right! But a far more accurate question would be: "Why should anyone be violently forced not to trade their goods with others on certain days? Why does a herd of demented or violent thugs—including that dim-witted saleswoman—initiate aggressive violence against merchants while the general public pretends it's legitimate?" If someone had ripped the necklace off that cow's neck during the broadcast, there would be an uproar; but violently robbing someone of millions? Perfectly fine.
Landfills and the presumption of guilt

Do you know what legal amendment Marksová is proposing this time? No, just kidding; this time it isn't Marksová, but Environment Minister Richard Brabec. And how does he intend to enrich our lives? People who have illegal dump sites on their property must prove in court that they didn't dump the waste there themselves, otherwise they will be forced to clean it up; and anyone who fails to do so faces a fine of up to one million crowns. The initial, glaring absurdity of this law will hit anyone right between the eyes: How on earth are you supposed to prove that you didn't leave a mess somewhere (at any point) in the past?! One of the main reasons the presumption of innocence exists is precisely the practical impossibility of proving you didn't do something if the alleged act spans an extended period; on the other hand, after the old communist cop Huml wiped his ass with this principle by pushing through strict owner liability for vehicles, other thugs cannot afford to be left behind.

Yet I consider the far more pressing aspect of the entire matter to be the fact that the state interferes at all in who creates a landfill on their own land. The very term "illegal dump" should evoke someone dumping trash on someone else's land, but that isn't the case here: it applies to the owner as well if they lack a permit from the relevant authority. And we aren't talking about radioactive or extremely toxic waste, or anything that endangers health or emits an unbearable stench into the surroundings—other legal statutes exist for all of that, having nothing to do with landfills. The state simply dictates whether you may keep a dump on your own property, even when it causes zero pollution to the surroundings. Now they have merely upgraded existing filth so that a landowner can be penalized even when someone else dumps trash on his property and he cannot prove his innocence; and that, dear friends, is how the state protects our property and property rights.
Marksová versus stress

I thought we had heard enough about this woman, but I just can't resist; guess what amendment she has come up with now! Employers will supposedly be legally mandated not only to provide safe working conditions for their employees, but also to actively protect them against stress. How? By introducing "anti-stress rooms," "anti-stress corners," or mandatory workplace breaks—supposedly left to the employer's discretion. Which ties into the funniest part of the entire proposal: there are zero penalties for violating this law. Staring in disbelief? Comrade Marksová explains it like this: "We rather mean to convey that employers shouldn't forget about it. We envision this as a dialogue between the labor inspectorate and the company. If an employer neglects it, we will remind him. [...] I don't understand why this should be missing from a modern labor code." In other words, everyone can safely not give a flying fuck about it.

Unlike the issues I dissected here over the past three days, this one is rather laughable; you can take it as light relief following those other horrors. In any case, I think it provides a wonderful probe into the woman's mindset: "I don't understand why this should be missing from a modern labor code." Marksová simply suffers from a certain obsession that can be observed among some internet-debating socialists: they need to have absolutely every fart regulated by law; the only difference is that while internet commenters spam us with forum posts, the comrade spams us directly with legislation. Why else—apart from a compulsive urge—would anyone push a law carrying zero penalty for non-compliance? Some readers of the D-FENS blog call me a graphomaniac because I enjoy writing; Marksová must be in the same boat, except she doesn't indulge in her free time, but on citizens' extorted money—and her outputs usually can't be simply ignored... though fortunately, this one can.
Marksová versus property owners

Marksová, a hot topic in the Sewers for the third day in a row: first home office regulations, then wage inequality, and now she is proposing a ban on renting out real estate without neighbors' permission—and whenever that goose gets an idea into her head, property rights go right out the window. Her justification? The so-called "poverty merchants" (as the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs calls them) supposedly buy up apartments and rent them to low-income tenants, who cause mayhem in the buildings and trash them, which naturally upsets the neighbors. But why does this situation arise in the first place? First and foremost because it is Marksová's ministry that subsidizes housing for those individuals. The solution is straightforward: stop subsidizing their rent! In one fell swoop, you would get rid of both the "poverty merchants" and the reckless trashing of apartments by ungrateful recipients, while saving money to boot. But that would also expose how utterly useless Marksová and her entire glorious ministry are, so the time-tested playbook was chosen instead: the state created a problem so that it can subsequently "solve" it.
Marksová versus the labor market

Yesterday in the Sewers, we discussed Marksová meddling with home office work; unfortunately, that isn't the only sphere of our lives she believes she can run better than we can. She discovered that Czech women earn 22 percent less than men, which she naturally identified as a golden opportunity to raise her profile and stage some performative bureaucratic activity. And what do you think she intends to do about it? For starters, she will launch a monstrous campaign called "22 Percent Toward Equality," then blow 400 million crowns of looted taxpayer money on subsidies for NGOs and other outfits that pledge to "solve" the "problem" (for example, by encouraging men's greater involvement in childcare; eat your heart out, social engineering). But above all—and here is the real outrage—she will begin dispatching labor inspectors to track down and penalize those who pay men "unjustifiably" more (yes, she will use other people's money to punish those who handle their own money "without authorization").

It is also worth examining the actual reasons women's wages are lower than men's. A significant share undoubtedly belongs to that socialist monstrosity called maternity leave, where the state decreed that employers may not dismiss female employees absent for extended periods, thereby degrading the position of all women on the labor market by attaching a negative externality to employing them; another non-negligible factor is that certain sectors with high female representation (education, healthcare...) have essentially been taken over by the state, meaning those women can kiss market valuation goodbye, as their reality is rigid government pay scales. And in light of these facts, that silly hen will send inspectors after us using money stolen by the state, or stage equality PR campaigns with it? The whole thing is so absurd that I cannot find adequate words to convey the horror; and unfortunately, I cannot find the money the state robbed me of to fund it either.
Marksová versus the home office

The Minister of Labor and Social Affairs—the socialist Marksová—is acting once again as if she knows what's best for us better than we do; I know, doing so is practically her job description, but that doesn't make such behavior any less infuriating. This time, she came up with another amendment (what else) to the Labor Code (which would best be abolished altogether), imposing new obligations on employers regarding remote employees. Those obligations, of course, are nothing but a mountain of utter nonsense (mandating organized socialization with colleagues, covering home internet bills, and the like), topped off by the ultimate stupidity: occupational safety training and ensuring a safe working environment (yes, inside the employee's own home; having an unsafe pad is perfectly fine until you want to write code for your employer there—then doom ensues!). At this point, I honestly don't know whether to laugh at the cow or go weep in a corner.

The consequences of this law "protecting employees" will likely follow the usual pattern whenever someone invents such schemes: it will primarily harm the very people it purported to protect. Total crap? Absolutely. I can readily imagine employers having zero interest in dealing with Marksová's whimsical moods, so they will simply stop offering home office arrangements altogether, just to prevent the damned state from dragging them through the mud if someone hurts themselves at home during working hours where proper Marxist-Marksovian conditions weren't ensured. Another possibility is that restricting remote work is not a side effect, but the deliberate goal of the bill: the woman in question reportedly remarked (I only heard this second-hand) that working from home creates inequality in the labor market, because companies in industries that do not require employees' physical presence on-site gain an unfair advantage over the rest.
The Chinese 'Miracle'

Chinese comrades built the Pentagonal Mart—a gargantuan shopping mall shaped like the Pentagon; if you look it up, you'll see the likeness is quite uncanny and the concept is intriguing. Could the state have actually done something well for once? No; there are a few "catches." Minor details, really... for example, the entire structure cost over two hundred million dollars and was completed back in 2009, yet its interior layout is utterly labyrinthine; but that still isn't the primary problem—the mall sits in an area where nobody lives, ergo nobody goes there, which means nobody sells anything there either. Since its opening, it has stood as a ghost mall, merely decaying while waiting for potential customers to eventually populate the surrounding area. This is precisely why metrics like GDP are completely misleading: constructing an entirely pointless, expensive building clearly helped no one; on the contrary, it consumed resources and has been utterly useless for years, yet it boosted GDP.

Not only that—it serves as a textbook demonstration of the inefficiency of central planning, illustrating that merely pouring money into something does not make it useful. Crucially, however, absolutely all state projects suffer from this exact same defect; it just isn't always quite so glaringly obvious. When the state subsidizes something (literally anything) because it couldn't turn a profit on its own, it means the subjective utility derived from that thing is lower than its cost (if it were otherwise, it would pay for itself); fundamentally, this is the exact same case as the Pentagonal Mart, differing only in degree. When subsidies target something that functions at least partially—people visit, but it doesn't cover its operating expenses—people often tend to judge the project differently because it offers some tangible benefit to consumers; while true, total costs exceed whatever utility anyone derives from it (otherwise, people would willingly pay the full price).
The Earth is round, we need a state

"Members of The Flat Earth Society are all around the globe." Funny? Yes; and true. Seriously. Even the most absurd conspiracy theory has its adherents; what's more, rapper B.o.B. recently thrust them into the spotlight during a debate with astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, prompting iDNES and other Czech outlets to run pieces on The Flat Earth Society (TFES). That naturally sparked discussions—which I enjoy, because one learns a great deal of interesting things from them (more about human nature than the topic itself). But why am I writing about this? What caught my attention? Far more fascinating than TFES's arguments were the reactions to them: the most prevalent response was mockery, of course, yet it frequently came from individuals who demonstrated in the comments that they personally know virtually nothing about physics; they could not refute TFES theories, nor did they even understand the reasons why the Earth must be round—they simply believe the contrary because authorities say so and they don't want to look like fools.

Anyone who holds certain (even erroneous) theories they actually thought about is labeled an idiot and mocked by people who merely adopted the "correct" view of authority without ever bothering to understand it. How many mockers know Kepler's laws, or can explain why a full moon can be observed during the day (one of TFES's main talking points)? TFES cannot convince such people of anything—not because TFES is right, but because their opponents happen to be correct purely by accident (in the Middle Ages, that same personality type burned people at the stake for the reverse), and no rational discussion can be had with them, as they know nothing about the issue and make no effort to comprehend anything; there are many of them, and instead of thinking, they simply reassure one another that "they are right," which "everyone knows except those lunatics in the TFES." To which libertarian does this not ring a bell? The good news is that regarding the shape of the Earth, the truth eventually prevailed; the bad news is that it took centuries.
'Camping' in line

Every now and then, something appears in the world that makes it worthwhile for some people to camp out in line for an entire day; it might be the launch of long-awaited video games (or expansion packs), or perhaps new iPhones. Who are the people waiting? Well, mostly enthusiasts who simply cannot wait—they must get their hands on their beloved hobby as early as humanly possible; they could easily buy it a few days later without waiting, but that wouldn't be the same experience, and they would miss out on chatting with others about their shared passion. During the iPhone 6 launch, queues were drastically shortened or eliminated altogether thanks to an online reservation system. Lines for those who want to wait, open retail sales shortly after for everyone else, and nobody misses out—because that is how capitalism works. Quite unlike lines for meat or bananas under socialism... or, say, lines for state boiler subsidies today!

What are boiler subsidies? Well, the state decided to subsidize people who want to upgrade their heating boilers in a manner that current rulers deem appropriate. And what about those who don't want to wait in line? Can they just show up a few days later to get it without waiting? Of course not, are you out of your minds, wretched subjects?! Only a limited number of applicants will be approved, so tough luck: go camp out in line like good little serfs, beg and scrape, and be grateful to the state for returning at least a fraction of what was stolen from you before—for that is the fundamental nature of subsidies. As the old expropriator and socialist Masaryk once proclaimed in this pernicious line: "In the Czechoslovak Republic, there will no longer be room for the old charity, which was always regarded as an act of mercy, humiliating the poor recipient and dulling his human dignity. In place of humiliating mercy, we establish social obligation today." And there you have it!
A fee for not having money

The bandits at the Ministry of the Environment have teamed up with their cronies at the Ministry of Industry and Trade in pursuit of a common interest: unsurprisingly, the hunt for loot. This time, they came up with an additional tax on owning an older car, alongside an increase in an existing one (for cars meeting the EURO 2 emissions standard, owners will now pay five thousand crowns, and three thousand for EURO 3). The official justification for this particular plundering raid is the alleged goal of "rejuvenating the vehicle fleet"; and first of all, I ask myself whether rejuvenating the vehicle fleet is truly desirable in all circumstances, given that this tax will, for example, apply to my own beloved car—which I maintain at considerable expense in better technical condition than the vast majority of newer vehicles, not to mention that its driving characteristics make it far safer.

All right, I concede that most people don't drive a ten-year-old car out of pure affection for it (not that anyone has the right to tax me for that either); they simply can't afford a new one. Enter the heroic state, which will provide these people with the missing money... no, sorry, an error crept in: it won't give them anything... it will take (...and it isn't a giant, it's Prince Brighteyes). Pure logic. The futility (or rather perverse counterproductivity) of such a measure must be obvious at first glance to anyone who isn't a total idiot, but even if it isn't, we can look at how the exact same scheme played out last time: the vehicle fleet didn't get any younger; on the contrary, it aged slightly (hardly surprising when poor people with older cars had to pay a tax out of their poverty). So are our bandits from the two ministries mentally deficient? Well, they're hardly a beacon of genius, but they aren't that stupid either; it's just that the state couldn't give a dog's shit about the age of the car fleet—the main goal is extorting more cash for the state coffers.
On freedom and necrophilia

Last month in the Sewers, you could read "On Freedom and Incest" as well as "On Freedom and Zoophilia"; to round out this unplanned miniseries, let us look to Sweden, where Liberal People's Party politicians are proposing to legalize necrophilic sex, provided that the deceased gave explicit written consent during their lifetime. This proposal naturally outraged Czech "decent citizens," according to whom the Swedish politicians behind the push to legalize necrophilic desires have gone completely insane, are bleeding-heart do-gooders, and are leading our civilization to ruin. But I ask: what is actually wrong with it? If two people enter into an agreement that one may have sex with the other after death, is that not purely their own business? Why should anyone else interfere, least of all legislators? Unlike zoophilia, where one can (however feebly) argue regarding animal suffering, in the case of necrophilia nothing of the sort makes any sense.

The entire transaction typically involves two participants: one deceased person who, for whatever reason during their lifetime, consented to their future corpse being used for another person's sexual gratification; whether they agreed because they were eccentric, for money, or for entirely different reasons, they evidently derived some subjective utility (material or otherwise). The other person is alive and presumably aroused by sex with a corpse, so they get what they desire as well; this transaction clearly benefits both parties, otherwise they would not have voluntarily entered into it. Why ban a contract that indisputably benefits all parties involved (otherwise they wouldn't have agreed) and harms nobody? And why does it outrage so many Czechs that somewhere in Sweden, a necrophiliac they don't even know will enjoy the corpse of a person who consented to it and whom they don't know either? Well, according to their demented religion, it's their business too. And what religion is that? Why, the biggest and most dangerous of all: statism and democracy.
Dump dumb Trump

Not long ago, I was singing praises here for Apple because its management refused to build a backdoor into iOS for the FBI; I was not at all surprised when, shortly afterward, DJ Trump called on his fellow citizens to boycott Apple products (what real impact that call will have illustrates the gulf between capitalist actions and democratic posturing), given that surveillance and the police state are precisely his goals. What did surprise me, however, was the number of surprised libertarians; and in general, the stance of many of them toward DJ Trump left me somewhat disappointed. Sure, he is endorsed by Molyneux, who once openly advocated against voting for Ron Paul; yes, even now he doesn't explicitly say "Vote Trump," but speaks of him on his shows in ways that paint him as an anti-establishment warrior—which is about the best possible advertisement among libertarians. Yet from Molyneux, I always expect the worst; but what about the others?

DJ Trump is essentially an American Babiš combined with Konvička and Hampl. While he may not fit into the established political machinery and current elites fear him and feel lost on how to deal with him, social engineers rarely get along among themselves anyway—they all want to dictate how people should live, just in different ways. DJ Trump possesses Babiš's lust for power and state snooping, Konvička's hatred of Muslims, and Hampl's raw statism. His platform isn't merely a wall on the Mexican border, but also populist tax hikes on the rich and extreme protectionism, particularly "protecting American jobs" from foreigners (not to mention forcibly deporting people from the US and stripping birthright citizenship from immigrants' children). Not that Sanders would be a better candidate—it's jumping out of the frying pan into the fire—but that is hardly a reason to glorify Trump.
Ministry of Transport versus river boaters

Virtually every paddler has noticed that while some hazardous weirs are marked with "No Boating" signs, signs explicitly permitting navigation are practically nowhere to be found. Most weirs have thus historically borne no signage at all, which for decades meant boating over them was legal. But the Ministry of Transport is on a rampage, redefining road and waterway signs, and Minister Ťok is acting completely unhinged; their latest demented regulation outlaws running unmarked weirs. This creates the absurd situation where even a weir equipped with a canoe chute (specifically designed for boats to pass through) cannot legally be navigated without a permit sign—even though the chute's very existence speaks for itself! And the fine? Up to two hundred thousand crowns. Yes, you read that right—Ťok has lost his mind completely. To all self-described "right-wing" ANO voters, congratulations on electing such a creature (and it isn't just weirs; the Ministry of Transport has been running wild across the board lately).

What are the likely practical consequences? Anyone familiar with boaters knows that the vast majority won't even notice this decree, and the rest will simply ignore it. And police posting cops by weirs? I wouldn't rule it out, but I don't expect it either. At most, leaders of children's paddling clubs will face hassles: to maintain peace of mind, they will likely phone weir administrators (if they can track down contacts) to request individual permits (which the law has always allowed). In any case, it's just another bureaucratic nuisance for everyone involved—something Ťok couldn't care less about if he tried. And the reason behind it all? Probably importing the good old "Ordnung muss sein" into Czech waters; or a bureaucrat needing to show performative activity; or perhaps some cops lobbied for it to collect easy fines (doubtful, but who knows); or... dear state, government, bureaucrats, and Mr. Ťok: you know where you can shove it.
State surveillance in Germany

The German government has given its cops the green light to deploy malware (viruses, Trojan horses) to spy on suspects; so on top of countless other cyber threats, the biggest parasite of all—the state—will now be spreading this filth across networks. And when I say "our networks," I refer to the fact that the Internet knows no national borders. That the government has legalized conduct for which it imprisons others is nothing new under the sun (wars, taxes, classroom propaganda, and jailing anyone who defies it), so I don't intend to dwell on that; I find the technical execution far more intriguing. Because how does malware spread? Viruses replicate and propagate through various files, worms spread across networks, and Trojans are software with advertised functionality (such as screensavers, but far beyond that) that users voluntarily download, while secretly performing other actions (such as spying for the state).

The logical question is: how will government malware isolate and locate its target? Will cops infect clouds of computers before hitting the right one? Surely we can trust them not to abuse data harvested from other machines, right? And once this type of state surveillance becomes routine, will antivirus vendors be accused of obstructing justice? And no, this isn't entirely sarcastic, considering that Apple was already coerced by the US government to build an iOS backdoor for the FBI, ISPs are legally obligated to spy under court orders, and server hosts are forced to hand user data over to cops. Is there any reason why things should unfold differently for developers fighting state malware? Personally, I see none... and so I ask myself: when and where does this end? But beyond asking questions, I'll leave you with a few parting tips...
A public affair: raising children

Who knows best what is optimal for children? Their parents? Not at all; that idea has supposedly been thoroughly discredited. The Ministry of Education will take the best care of our kids—using our money. And Minister Kateřina Valachová naturally knows best of all, having decided to push for the inclusive education of disabled children. This particular social engineer decided that too many pupils attend special-needs schools, so together with her bureaucrats, she devised a "solution" to a problem of her own invention: school counseling facilities (ŠPZ) issue recommendations on whether an individual child should attend a mainstream school or a special-needs school. If parents choose to enroll their child in a standard school despite a recommendation for a special-needs one, everything is peachy; but reverse the situation, and all bets are off. If parents enroll their child in a special-needs school contrary to an ŠPZ recommendation, child welfare services can harass them to their heart's content—in extreme cases, escalating to the complete removal of the children.

At this point, one cannot even trot out that tired—and completely demented—trope that parents aren't "experts" in education while state employees hold official credentials; social workers aren't required to be (and typically aren't) experts in special-needs pedagogy, which renders the whole thing utterly nonsensical. The entire policy is nothing but naked state tyranny: a regime with zero remaining inhibitions, whose politicians, bureaucrats, and enforcers consider it entirely normal to dictate whatever crosses their minds. Some apparatchik at the ministry gets a whim, and eager functionaries at child welfare don't hesitate to tear families apart just to indulge her fancy. Excuse my bluntness, but this is simply sickening; and I don't care whether the woman is an idiot who means well, merely bored, or needing to demonstrate bureaucratic activity—the consequences are horrific either way.
Nanny state, vintage 2016

Once upon a time, beyond nine mountains and nine rivers in the Italian town of Sonnino—land of the finest cars—lived an absolute lunatic who was dissatisfied with how his wife (failed to) attend to the household chores and his manhood. And because he was also a spiteful whiner, he went and reported her to the police station. Lounging around the precinct were uniformed apes unable at that moment to cruise around in their police Alfa Romeos, presumably bored out of their minds; so instead of putting the snitch firmly in his place, they charged his wife with "domestic abuse," carrying a potential two to six years behind bars. Whether the court finds her guilty or not (hopefully not), the state will at minimum harass her by dragging her to hearings and forcing her to endure proceedings. And for what?! For not cleaning, cooking, or putting out? Seriously? What world are we living in?

Italian media criticize the case as sexist, arguing that we have gender equality and domestic chores should not be exclusively a woman's responsibility; but is that really the core of the issue? Has the notion that each household should function according to whatever its members mutually agree upon—without an arbiter on the public payroll—truly become absurd today? Does the state really need to intervene even in—literally—washing dirty laundry? And if anyone breathes a sigh of relief that this didn't happen in the Czech Republic, don't celebrate too soon: under the new Civil Code, concealing extramarital affairs from one's spouse is actually illegal. A forty-year-old woman from Pardubice is already suing her husband over this: having caught him with a mistress, she is now demanding that the state compel him to surrender exhaustive details about her, including their future plans together. In light of this, I ask: Can anyone still wipe their own ass without state assistance? And does anyone even want to?
The French government versus property rights

Many supermarkets in France have long observed an informal custom: unsold food is given away free in the evening for people to take. While it may not be peak freshness, homeless people (or poor Czech exchange students xD) hardly turn their noses up at it, and supermarkets save money on waste disposal. A while ago, word reached me that French lawmakers were attempting to outlaw this practice (citing hygiene regulations), though in practice they didn't quite manage; and because the state simply cannot leave anything alone—everything must be either banned or mandated—it has now slapped French supermarkets with an obligation to donate all unsold food to charities (with transport costs seemingly borne by the donor). President Hollande is so thrilled by the mandate that he wants to expand it to restaurants and cafeterias, while pressuring Juncker to implement it EU-wide—naturally including the Czech Republic.

Why is this completely wrong? First and foremost, because property rights should be inviolable. It is simply immoral to violently coerce someone into giving their property away against their will—after all, how would champions of this law enjoy being legally required to sort their trash and haul parts of it elsewhere at their own expense? Supporters claim this solves the problem of supermarkets wasting food; but what drives their incentive to waste in the first place? Exactly: farm subsidies artificially driving down food purchase prices. How about ending agricultural subsidies and letting market mechanisms work? The frequent outrage over food waste also completely ignores the costs (such as logistics and transport) required to salvage that food; those costs (partly inflated by nonsensical subsidies) are often higher than the value of the discarded food itself. The free market minimizes waste best, as no superior mechanism for resource allocation exists; every state distortion of it is a road to hell.
Equality at all costs, even if there's no bread on the table

Socialist Jiří Dienstbier, minister without portfolio (what a made-up job) in charge of human rights and equal opportunities, discovered that among the top 250 Czech companies by turnover, women make up only 13 percent of board members. Because the man is a dyed-in-the-wool social engineer, he decided this isn't enough—and how did he arrive at that conclusion? Instead of humbly acknowledging that the most successful market actors—upon whom Dienstbier, by the way, parasitizes—might actually know what they're doing, he concluded that he knows better. Thirteen percent is simply inadequate because a political parasite decrees it so. In his own words, this isn't about giving preference to less qualified women or men, but about establishing "fair rules" enabling both men and women to succeed in executive hiring. Why is this sheer lunacy?

This entire premise rests on the assumption that leading corporations cannot select executive talent as competently as Dienstbier—a man who produces zero economic value that anyone would voluntarily pay for, parasitizing via the state on those who do. Did these companies not choose the most qualified candidates available? Nobody has barred women from pursuing careers for decades; yet our society has far more households where the husband works while the wife manages the home than the reverse. The underlying reasons don't matter—whether tradition, biological predispositions, or personal preferences—the logical outcome is that more men than women are willing to sacrifice their entire lives to career advancement, ergo more of them succeed. Forcing companies through state coercion to appoint different leaders than they choose for themselves only damages their efficiency and distorts the market.
The Ministry of Transport is on a rampage

It wasn't long ago that Minister Ťok and his henchmen redefined the "No Trucks" sign for us; and here they are again, baring their fangs with proposals for fresh highway harassment. First on the agenda is authorizing uniformed apes to confiscate vehicle registration certificates on the spot if they deem tires too worn, exhausts damaged, windshields cracked, bodywork dented, rims scuffed, brake pads thin, or countless other nitpicks. And since the authority on the scene holds all the cards—acting as both prosecutor and judge—the driver can only appeal after the fact, while being stranded without a vehicle in the moment. It represents a sublime instrument of police extortion: "No administrative proceedings, pay the fine on the spot, or else..." And as D-FENS rightly observes: "The moment a police officer, municipal cop, or bureaucrat receives any power, he immediately abuses it, exercising it disproportionately whenever and wherever he can."

Furthermore, they are introducing "two strikes" and "three strikes" systems based on absurd escalations in penalty points; fines are spiking yet again (as if ours weren't already several times higher relative to average wages than in Germany, Austria, and most of Europe): driving without a seatbelt 1,500 crowns (I fail to see why that is an offense at all); speeding up to 25,000 crowns (irrespective of what car you drive, as if driving any car is identically hazardous); driving under the influence will be taxed up to 75,000 crowns (even without an accident), just like driving without a license (the law mandating state permission to operate motor vehicles is inherently backward to begin with), and many more. And by long tradition, once such laws pass, nobody ever repeals them—at most, they tighten them further. Not that it achieves anything, aside from making clear who is master and who is the dog.
Apple to the US government: Fuck off!

All right, for diplomatic reasons it wasn't literally "fuck off," but something along the lines of: "We have no sympathy for terrorists, we respect FBI professionals, the government has good intentions, we will cooperate... but we will not compromise iOS security for them." Let us recap from the beginning: a married couple of terrorists attacked a center for people with disabilities in San Bernardino a few months ago; both were subsequently shot dead, leaving their motives murky, along with any possible ties to wider terror networks. The only actionable lead was their iPhones, so the FBI began leaning on Apple for assistance and data. Apple initially cooperated, handing over everything they possessed; but that wasn't enough for the spooks—not to mention the prospect of exploiting the situation for broader precedents—which culminated in a court order directing Apple to write a specialized iOS update containing a backdoor for the FBI.

Tim Cook, the company's CEO, flatly refused, laying out his reasoning to customers in an open letter. He earns my utmost respect for that move—as does anyone who stands up to the state. What makes this especially encouraging is that Apple is no defenseless minnow the government can effortlessly crush. The question is: what next? How will the court respond? Will it levy compounding daily fines that Apple must pay until bowing to the rulers' will, much like the case of Larry Flynt? Or will the whole affair quietly blow over? Judging by Cook's stance, Apple genuinely intends to stand its ground; otherwise, rather than penning dramatic open letters, they would have left backchannels open. And since Cook is no fool, flanked by armies of seasoned legal and technical minds he undoubtedly consulted, yet still chooses defiance, I suspect a genuine chance of victory exists. What do you think?
Quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi

Member of Parliament Štěpán Stupčuk, belonging to the iron-fisted, driver-harassing party ČSSD, got dead drunk and crashed into a guardrail or traffic sign on the D7 highway; when the cops arrived on the scene, he informed them that although he stood alone beside the wrecked car, he hadn't been driving; furthermore, despite being visibly smashed, he refused to blow into a breathalyzer. Witnesses exist who say they saw him behind the wheel, yet the police are still "investigating"; one eyewitness was right there on the scene, offering testimony to the uniformed apes confirming that the MP had indeed been driving, but they told him to watch his tongue and consider what he might get dragged into, reportedly turning down his business card.

Honestly, I couldn't care less whether Stupčuk is punished; in principle, I wouldn't give a damn even if he had killed himself, provided he harmed no one else and merely damaged infrastructure—ideally, the entire matter would remain strictly between him, his insurer, and whoever repairs the road. What infuriates me is that these exact same Social Democratic thugs are the foremost champions of laws enabling traffic harassment by police (beginning with the penalty points system). They are the ones who brand the exercise of constitutional rights "the close-relative loophole," clamor for harsher crackdowns on drunk drivers, and draft laws enabling cops to harass law-abiding motorists. And why? Because they engineer laws "for the little people"; when it impacts them personally, they resort to the very tactics they otherwise denounce as "pathetic excuses."
Another police whip over decent people

The Ministry of Transport has redefined the "No Trucks" road sign; it no longer applies merely to vehicles over 3.5 tons, but now also covers light vans, pickups, or station wagons with a cargo partition. Through a mere stroke of a bureaucrat's pen, countless reasonably logical restrictions—originally designed to keep overly heavy vehicles off roads not built for them—have been turned into a glorious tool of harassment, the dream of every uniformed ape. Beyond bans on entering certain zones, this also affects passing lanes on highways where truck overtaking has long been prohibited; now, anyone driving a standard station wagon with an interior cargo partition mesh is barred from passing as well—which makes profound sense, of course, because an interior wire mesh works miracles on a car's driving dynamics!

The Ministry of Transport no longer even pretends these signs serve a useful purpose. If they did, officials could hardly rewrite their meaning on a whim, decreeing that wherever it was previously "proper" to exclude vehicles over 3.5 tons, lighter cars are now banned too based purely on how their cabin space is partitioned from cargo space. The real motive behind such nonsense is police harassment and extorting fines for victimless actions. Clouds of pointless signs clutter the Czech Republic (especially some completely brain-dead STOP signs: in Kralupy, for instance, I drive past one every week whose net contribution to safety is negative, leading drivers to ignore it, which is why uniformed apes constantly camp there collecting fines). But the cops naturally welcome every additional pretext to justify their headcounts (with one cop per 250 citizens, the Czech Republic ranks near the top globally, rivaled only by a handful of totalitarian regimes).
Stropnický and Stropnický

Babiš's lackey Martin Stropnický entered the elections on the ANO ticket with a billboard declaring: "So our children won't be ashamed of us"—a slogan that took on an ironic dimension the moment his son, Matěj Stropnický, pursuing a career with the Greens (who had reproached him for getting elected to Prague City Council solely through the patronage of his father and his father's master, Babiš), needed to score political points. Junior promptly branded ANO (from whom he had gladly received pre-election backing, which he hadn't hesitated to solicit from Babiš personally and via his father) a fraudulent scam, and its members mindless puppets incapable of independent thought who can't do anything right. Martin Stropnický declined to comment, but I suspect mutual pride reigns between father and son: both behave like true politicians—groveling, cronyism, betrayal, no comment—and their moral standards must have them bursting with pride.

And because the Greens are a similar crowd, the gambit worked like a charm: they elected Stropnický Jr. as party chairman; after all, his outburst made him a media darling, so what more could they want? As an aside, the clan has not only father and son, but also mom in politics—how touching. In any case, while Martin Stropnický plays second fiddle to his overlord Babiš, Matěj Stropnický has adopted Václav Havel's moralizing rhetoric: in his first major interview as Green chairman, he declared himself opposed to motoring, only to proclaim minutes later that it is abnormal for eighty percent of Czech citizens to afford vacation flights—right after admitting that he flies himself. The plebs, apparently, should get around by bicycle and train. The whole circus would be hilarious if it weren't so tragic. Why? Because people vote for both of them; and I ask: why on earth should I obey laws enacted by such spineless swine?
EET approved

For roughly a week now, I've worked on nothing other than VAT control statements for our Czech clients. Beside myself, another developer, a financial analyst, and a project manager are scrambling around it—our combined billing for just one week across those few companies comes to around two hundred thousand crowns, completely squandered thanks to the state as we scramble to put out fires caused by its mandatory reporting (most of our clients are abroad, where Babiš's tentacles cannot reach). Every time such a scheme is introduced, we are treated to politicians' drivel about how seamlessly everything will roll out, with zero friction and negligible costs; I always recall those promises when I'm left cleaning up the mess—at no small expense. And right now, as I kicked off a code compilation and glanced at online news... lo and behold: comrades Babiš and Sobotka shut down opposition filibusters and rammed through the Electronic Registration of Sales (EET). I can already foresee how "technically flawless" that rollout will be.

Beyond implementing EET on the side of reporting merchants, another hilarious saga will be the state's technical implementation on the receiving end. The Ministry of Finance initially tried to keep the technical specifications top-secret (I wonder why), but once the full uncensored draft began leaking across the Internet (for example, it has been downloadable from my repository for several months), they finally published it too (just google "EET specifikace"). Anyone with even a passing understanding of IT systems can have a good laugh (gallows humor, really)—the project architecture is an absolute joke. But what else would anyone expect from the state? While the technical execution is arguably the least fundamental issue, I have already written plenty about the moral bankruptcy of EET; now that the law has passed (the opposition claims it will challenge it before the Constitutional Court, though I wouldn't hold my breath), it will be fascinating to watch the incompetent state attempt to get this contraption off the ground.
The Ministry of Health puts on a show

Svatopluk Němeček and his backup band at the Ministry of Health need to step into the limelight and demonstrate some performative activity again, since they haven't made much noise since their totalitarian ban on smoking in private pubs; how else can one explain the thoroughly idiotic bill they've just unveiled? First, alcohol sales would be banned at events intended for children—and mind you, not just to minors (which is already law), but banned from being sold altogether, even to parents. Second, sporting events would be forbidden from selling beverages exceeding four percent alcohol by volume: so a 10-degree light lager is permissible, but a 12-degree beer is contraband; forget about mulled wine, let alone anything stronger. And the justification? Well, that is the million-dollar question! Frankly, I cannot conceive of a single coherent reason: the state isn't officially attempting to ban alcohol sales generally, so why these arbitrary carve-outs?

It is nothing more than inventing legislation for the sake of legislating, churning out activity for activity's sake, with zero actual benefit—banning things simply because it's been "too long" since the last ban. Unfortunately, this is precisely how totalitarianism creeps in: not just via the devil Babiš and his calculating master plans, but through bored apparatchiks like Němeček who feel compelled to tinker because "it's their job" and somehow expected of them. Countless citizens—befuddled by democracy—even applaud this nonsense on the grounds that they dislike alcohol, parents don't need to drink at their kids' events, and they don't do it themselves, so why not outlaw it? Their opponents typically counter that having a beer isn't harmful. But someone addressing the crux of the issue—not whether one drinks or abstains, but state prohibitions that amount to indefensible threats of physical violence against merchants—is nowhere to be found. It truly depresses me.
A raped schoolgirl?

A thirteen-year-old German girl of Russian descent failed to show up for school one day, didn't return home, and only resurfaced the following day; when she finally came back, she claimed she had been raped by African refugees. The Russian Foreign Minister kicked up a storm, alleging German media were covering up the case; but the Internet has long reach, so the story exploded anyway—anti-Islam crusaders staged rallies, whipped up passions, and politicians scrambled to capitalize on the outrage. A few days later, however, the girl reportedly retracted her statement, confessing she had skipped school over academic troubles and that the sexual encounter was consensual. The public reactions followed a predictable script: pro-migrant progressives attacked anti-Islam activists for spreading hoaxes, while many activists remained convinced the girl had indeed been raped, claiming the retraction was merely a cover story orchestrated by police because rapist refugees contradict the politically correct media narrative.

In this post, I don't intend to arbitrate what actually happened—while I subscribe to George Carlin's first rule, "I don't believe anything the government tells me," that doesn't mean blindly believing the exact opposite either, so in principle I acknowledge both versions could be true (though after examining the available details, one appears distinctly more plausible). What is far more revealing, however, is the public's reaction: I have read posts from dozens of anti-Islam activists who "know with absolute certainty" that the girl was raped, alongside posts from progressives who "know" with identical certainty that she fabricated the entire story. The catch is that from the publicly available evidence, neither conclusion can be asserted with confidence. What is truly disheartening is how many people jump to conclusions simply because it reinforces their preconceived biases; most debates on this subject reveal that logic and evidence have been abandoned, as discussions surrounding migration have become almost entirely emotional shouting matches.
Opencard, Lítačka, money and politics

We all likely remember former Prague Mayor Pavel Bém's magic trick: "I will make seven hundred million crowns vanish, and I'll even guess which card you're thinking of." A few years have passed since then, and on top of that already outrageous acquisition price (nearly three-quarters of a billion), over another billion has been drained in operational costs. Remember all the hype about how it would be a multi-functional card, storing your library card, micro-payments, and whatever else? Wealth inequality

Oxfam, which incessantly bombards us with reports on what percentage of global wealth is held by what fraction of the population, announced that a long-hyped milestone has been crossed: the richest one percent now owns more than the rest of humanity combined. Accompanying this came the usual clarion call for politicians to "fight inequality." Economists at Deloitte pushed back against Oxfam's findings; how? By challenging the flawed methodology that calculates an individual's net wealth as total assets minus debt—a metric that renders a fifth of Americans and Europeans living in prosperity with, say, student debt, statistically "poorer" than starving children in Africa with zero assets and zero liabilities. Yet even Deloitte conceded that wealth inequality is "too high" and that "something must be done about it."

That is what I call half-assed argumentation: getting bogged down in technical minutiae while endorsing the demented premise. What is the fundamental flaw in such studies? First and foremost, the obsessive fixation on relative wealth ratios and total blindness to the fact that absolute wealth continues to rise at a rapid pace. Even the poor are growing richer, so what does it matter if the wealthy accumulate riches faster? It is constantly framed as though the rich prosper at the direct expense of the poor; in reality, it is a mutually beneficial exchange (an entrepreneur produces value, becoming very wealthy, while everyone who purchases their goods improves their own living standard). Furthermore, critics overlook that "the rich" and "the poor" are not static castes—people move between these tiers over time. But most importantly: while taxation may compress relative wealth disparities, overall wealth creation is unequivocally choked by state redistribution! Thus, what might offer short-term crumbs to today's poor harms tomorrow's poor far more.
