What Is Capitalism?

Yesterday I wrote about what capitalism is not, and didn't miss the opportunity to debunk some delusions of its critics. Today I would like to write a few lines about what capitalism is. To start off, allow me to quote a man whom I consider the greatest thinker of the twentieth century and probably of all time—Murray Newton Rothbard:
Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism; anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. The true anarchism will be capitalism; and the true capitalism will be anarchism.
If anyone happens to want a translation, that capitalist creation Google Translate handles it quite well (with one's eyes squinted).
So what does the term capitalism mean? It is a free market without state intervention. Yes, of course, capitalists can be ruthless businessmen motivated by their own selfishness and greed, which poses a huge problem when combined with the state—corruption, laws tailored to their businesses, subsidies, monopolies (which, by the way, do not arise without the state). In a free-market environment, however, that very same profit-seeking and greed drives those same people to satisfy the needs of others—how else could they obtain money without the state other than by persuading people to use their services and buy their products?
And what is the best way to persuade someone to buy something from you? Naturally by offering them something that person needs! Some might say that while this is a lovely theory, in practice things work quite differently. Yes, of course, you're right, in practice things work differently, but why? Because of the state, of course! In a free market, it genuinely works exactly as I describe; just look at places where the state doesn't interfere as much—Singapore, Hong Kong, and others—look at how they flourish! But what about socialist Sweden? Couldn't there be another way? No; just take a look at history: Sweden acquired its wealth during periods of wild capitalism; socialism was installed only after the country had already become immensely wealthy (and that growth was significantly slowed down as a result).
Capitalism is freedom and abundance; capitalism means the free market that took us from horse carriages to cars, from typewriters to computers, from empty pantries to full refrigerators, from hard toil in the fields to the freedom to choose a career in countless fields, from food being enormously expensive to negligible, from an occasional wash in a creek to luxurious bathrooms, from one outfit per person to overflowing closets, from an outhouse to a flush toilet, from journeys taking days or weeks to hours—in short, from poverty to riches! Make no mistake: this is not the work of a bureaucrat; behind it was greed, personal gain, and the pursuit of wealth... the very same qualities that the state turns into a catastrophe, the market harnesses for our benefit.
What Capitalism Is Not

In recent years, I've observed that criticizing capitalism has become immensely trendy and popular, especially among young people (though by no means only among them). Well, fair enough, let everyone define themselves against whatever they see fit. What I find very sad and alarming, however, is that the vast majority of those who rail against capitalism typically have no clue what capitalism actually is. And the problem isn't simply that they "define it differently"—which wouldn't matter in itself if they adhered to such definitions consistently—but rather that they mostly criticize some grotesque monstrosity, while wanting to use the law to restrict real capitalism.
First, allow me to list a few examples of what capitalism is definitely not: Capitalism is certainly not Agrofert and Babiš—those are the products of socialist subsidies and regulations (biofuels...); capitalism is not private schools strictly hamstrung by state regulations; capitalism is seriously not private health insurance companies when health insurance is mandatory; capitalism is definitely not a (non-state) company that the state grants a monopoly on anything (water supply, for example). Where there is no free market, there cannot be capitalism; and if the state intervenes, then it is not a free market.
Some people argue that when big companies have non-market privileges, it's not the state's fault, but the corporations', because they bribe civil servants and politicians. Regardless of the outcome of academic debates over who is more to blame, it is completely evident how the problem definitely cannot be solved: by granting more power to the state. Even if it were absolute truth that it's solely and exclusively the fault of large corporations that corrupt politicians write custom-tailored laws for them, one cannot argue that the state will fix it (since the problem arose precisely because it does not); if states are corrupted by major market players, then regardless of who is to blame, the consequence of expanding state power can be nothing other than more corruption!
You can blame businessmen for corrupting politicians; but as long as there are businessmen operating in a market environment and politicians possessing the power to distort that environment, corruption will inevitably occur (after all, records of it are thousands of years old—it has evidently never been otherwise, nor could it be). The only solution, therefore, is either to strip businessmen of the ability to do business, or to strip politicians of the power to make decisions; and surely anyone who either remembers the first option or at least theoretically understands why it is a road to hell should also realize that the problem cannot be eliminated in any way other than by abolishing political power (increasing it will achieve the exact opposite). And for those who still don't realize it, I have one such picture...
Who Is the Real Threat?

I constantly hear people around me saying that immigrants are our greatest threat and that something urgently "needs to be done" about it; when I ask further, in 99% of cases that "needs to be done" means that politicians, the government, the police—simply the state—ought to act. Although direct statistics are inaccessible due to political correctness, in many countries one can observe a rise in crime that correlates with the arrival of migrants, which in my eyes is a sufficient argument (further strengthened by the concealment of direct statistics) for stating that immigrants are a statistically more dangerous group in our society. But are they really what threatens us the most?
An incomparably more dangerous group that initiates orders of magnitude more violence than all migrants combined consists of our nation-states and the European Union. Not citizens, not ordinary people, not "all of us," no "society," but states—which means politicians, bureaucrats, police officers, and other parasites living off our money, which they take from us under the threat of violence and call taxes. These people rob us, impose their will upon us, and if we do not submit, they haul us off by force and lock us behind bars in prison (even when we haven't harmed anyone; for example, merely because we refuse to pay them or don't want to let them meddle in our transactions); they are people who commit more violence in a single day than immigrants manage in an entire year. I am not saying that mass migration poses no threat; I am merely calling for reflection on whether it is wise, in addressing this problem, to expand the powers of a state that generates more evil and violence than all immigrants combined.

Snow White and the Black Man

A wave of indignation was stirred up by Miroslav Donutil's piece recently broadcast on Czech Television (ČT)—a remake of Snow White in which the prince was a black man. Intrigued, I went to listen to the fairy tale, and it truly was dreadful, although the black prince was about the least of its problems in my eyes. Yes, of course, there were some mildly racist quips—for example, pointing out the drawbacks of Snow White's fair skin—but the hell with that, I personally am not overly sensitive to racism. What struck me far more, however, was the utter mental (and indeed spiritual, though I could forgive that) emptiness of the whole tale: not only was the struggle between good and evil removed, but so were all hardships; the protagonists simply faced no obstacles whatsoever. Snow White found the dwarves, cooked for them, they mined gold, she headed into town, met the black prince there, they got married, and had children. I'm really not exaggerating: there wasn't the slightest hint of a plot, of overcoming hardship or peril.
This complete toothlessness is no accident; it is a common hallmark of many modern fairy tales—above all, avoid taking a stand; the battle between good and evil is "out," and courage or problem-solving are likewise tossed aside. The main protagonist must show no initiative or influence over the events that simply drift past him (take Harry Potter, for instance: sure, things happen, but the main character exhibits no foresight or drive to take matters into his own hands—quite the contrary), because we must protect children from getting the impression that each of us is the master, driver, and engineer of our own destiny; things just sort of happen regardless of our actions. Whoever thrives was just "lucky," and otherwise "bad luck" is to blame—never the person himself. The motto of many modern fairy tales is: "He who does nothing makes no mistakes; so above all, don't stand out." How will such stories shape the generation raised on them? Compared to that, a black prince is seriously an entirely unproblematic character.

After all, by not publishing communist articles in my Sewers, I certainly don't deprive them of the freedom to express themselves on their own turf and on their own dime; but if I forcibly prohibited them from publishing on their own servers (whether on my own or through the state), that would unequivocally be an attack on freedom of speech.

Murray Newton Rothbard; requiescat in pace

Today marks exactly twenty-one years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers, and geniuses of the twentieth century—and in my opinion, of all time—departed this world just shy of his 69th birthday: Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism." The significance of his work lies in the astonishingly consistent unification of two seemingly unrelated schools of thought: the Austrian School of economics and anarchism. While his teacher, the brilliant economist Ludwig von Mises, proved the impossibility of economic calculation under central planning—thereby demonstrating beyond a shadow of a doubt the superiority of a free-market economy over a socialist one—he still assumed that the free market would be secured by the state. On the other hand, various anarchists pointed out the ethical indefensibility of the state as a monopoly on violence, yet their proposed solutions were typically various communist utopias devoid of any economic foundation.
In his life's work, Murray Newton Rothbard consistently merged these two currents into consistent anarcho-capitalism, recognizing that the state is the obstacle to both anarchy and the free market, while the absence of a monopoly on violence constitutes both anarchy and a free market. As he put it: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." He was a man of keen analytical intellect with an absolute sense of logic, yet simultaneously deeply emotional; an unrelenting hatred of evil—whose greatest modern embodiment is the state—permeated his entire body of work. He passed away before I was even ten years old; later, however, what he created profoundly shaped my life and opened my eyes. Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
China, 1984: Sesame Credit

The Chinese government has launched the Sesame Credit app (if you Google it, beware of confusing it with Credit Sesame, which is different software), whose purpose is to assess how good a citizen someone is and assign people a score accordingly. This score will subsequently be taken into account when dealing with authorities and the state in general, but it could also affect things like loan accessibility, pension amounts, and the like. From the sources I reviewed, I wasn't able to pin down precisely how the scoring system works—or rather, my search yielded conflicting reports (some claim the app will track virtually everything, including social media activity: sharing pro-government posts earns you points, while sharing anti-government posts loses them; the app's developers, however, deny this). Over time, people will come to see it as completely normal, just like the Czech census has droves of defenders. And just as Babiš argues in favor of introducing EET by pointing out that Croatia has it too, I wonder whether I will live to see the first Czech politician justify the rollout of Sesame Credit by arguing that it produces wonderful results in China.

The Worse, the Better?

Not only from libertarians, I occasionally read reflections along the lines of "the worse, the better," which generally assume that the current establishment (the bloated state, the EU) must soon collapse under its own weight because what politicians are doing is unsustainable. Yes, that's true: it isn't sustainable in the long run, and if socialism keeps expanding, it will eventually not only stifle our society's prosperity but could halt it altogether, so that we begin growing poorer, which will ultimately lead to collapse. But when? It took the Soviet Union nearly three generations, and it had far better conditions for collapse than what we have now. Why? First, it was genuinely completely centrally planned, whereas we are only partially so; second, the overall level of wealth back then was lower, ergo the road to absolute destitution was shorter; third, personal freedom (speech, religion, etc.) was lower; fourth, a positive example of "the West" existed (even if talking about it was forbidden).
The power of the market is fascinating: despite all the regulations and the massive ball and chain of the public sector, the private sector still manages to generate wealth. Historical precedent tells us that even once that ceases to be the case, it can take three generations for change to happen; if we factor in the time before we even start growing poorer, we are talking at best about our great-great-grandchildren being affected. I'm not saying the EU can't collapse sooner; on the other hand, it would easily be replaced by another variety of socialism. That's why I wouldn't pin too much hope on the slogan "the worse, the better." Supporting things that ridicule or cause infighting within the establishment while carrying minimal real danger is another matter (right now, for instance, the premier Czech clown named Zeman). So what is our only—albeit slim—chance? Tirelessly explain the benefits of liberty to people. Another year is here, and with it new armies of school-indoctrinated statists... so we've got work to do xD

To Protect and Serve... and Crash

In 2014 (we don't have this year's statistics yet), 1,327 official vehicles driven by uniformed monkeys and 84,532 cars driven by normal people were involved in traffic accidents; in total, at the start of that year, 8,282 monkey vehicles and 7.8 million human vehicles were registered. It follows that during that period, about 1% of humans crashed, compared to 16% of the monkeys who were supposed to protect and serve those humans. Can a sixteen-fold accident rate be explained by higher mileage? The average human car travels fifteen thousand kilometers a year; while there are no exact statistics for police cars, to make up for the aforementioned disparity, the ape-squad would have to clock a quarter of a million kilometers a year, which would basically require replacing the entire fleet every single year—and according to the police department's financial reports, that isn't happening by a long shot.
Not to mention that even if mileage did explain such a staggering number of crashes, by the state's very own logic, that excuses nobody—or does the penalty point system somehow take into account who drives more kilometers? No. Are points wiped away based on crash-free kilometers? No. Why then should the cops be judged by a different standard? They simply crash sixteen times more often than everyone else and cause chaos on the roads.
Someone might argue that the uniformed monkeys are involved in so many accidents because they're chasing criminals and "road hogs"; but does a pursuit give them the right to endanger others? No. Not even the state grants them such a right, because under the law, while they may violate traffic rules, they may only do so without endangering anyone. Out of the 1,327 accidents they were involved in, they caused 661 and were deemed not at fault in 666 (and that assumes their colleagues and the courts aren't biased in their favor, which I highly doubt); thus, one cannot even claim that the monkeys are innocent victims being rammed by criminals.
And the moral of the story? Cops are aggressive, dim-witted brutes, dangerous to themselves (which is the absolute least of my concerns) and to everyone around them. The state tells us they are on the roads to protect and serve us, but in reality they are pests. And whenever I hear politicians talk about piles of corpses on the roads and "road pirates," I think they ought to sweep their own doorstep first, because the only real pirates are their own henchmen.
Is Multiculturalism the Root of Evil?

Especially lately, particularly in connection with the migrant crisis, we can read from many commentators that multiculturalism is evil, that it has failed, never worked, and will lead to our downfall; and I cannot disagree that if politicians continue forcing multiculturalism down our throats as they have done so far, nothing good will come of it. However, I get the distinct impression that authors of such pieces often suffer from a fairly fatal misunderstanding of the actual root problem, which in my opinion simply isn't multiculturalism; it is state-enforced multiculturalism.
What would multiculturalism look like without state backing? Well, lunatics like Kohout would probably continue going to the ghetto to kiss Gypsies, all sorts of left-leaning students would keep preaching it to us, writing articles about it, and a few might even take some refugees into their own homes; and my personal guess is that this move alone would cure quite a few of them of their multiculturalism. But what would be the real impact on an ordinary person? Practically none: we could all simply ignore Kohout, and the number of #welcomed refugees would likely be in the single digits or low dozens.
Why, then, is multiculturalism a problem? Because the state forces it upon us under the threat of violence. We are not suffering because of deranged eccentrics kissing Gypsies, but because of anti-discrimination laws, mandatory EU refugee quotas, expensive detention camps, forced integration programs, and NGOs hooked up to the state money pipeline—in short, because of politicians and bureaucrats paid with public funds who need to justify their own existence. Multiculturalism on its own, without state sponsorship, would be nothing more than a fairly harmless hobby of a few café-dwelling leftists (and without access to public money, there would be vastly fewer of them).
So we have two problem factors here: the state and multiculturalism. What would the state do without multiculturalism? Bureaucrats would simply find another pretext to prey on decent people. And what would multiculturalists do without the state? At most, they would draw pitying smiles from those around them. Unfortunately, I arrive at the exact same conclusion as so many times before: the primary cause of the problem is, once again, the state. And as so often happens, the situation looks different at first glance, leading many to actually see the solution in further state intervention (just in the opposite direction), when all it would take is for the government to leave people the hell alone.

A Few Tweaks for the Sewers

I've pushed a few changes to the codebase of the Sewers, but I've already received several follow-up or confused questions about what's going on, so allow me to comment briefly: first, I added an RSS feed—nothing much to explain there, whoever uses RSS readers can add my feed; second, I made a few theme tweaks that might not be entirely obvious at first glance. Unregistered visitors have it easy: a new menu item has simply appeared (» appearance «) where they can choose how the Sewers should look for them; the setting will be saved in browser cookies. Registered users have it slightly more intricate: in addition to the » appearance « option, they also have » edit account details «, where they can make the same choice, but this setting will be stored in the database with their user accounts rather than in cookies.
What's the difference? Whatever you set in the » appearance « menu will be saved only in that specific browser; conversely, through » edit account details «, you can set the appearance that the Sewers will have wherever you log in from. In the event of a conflict between settings, the user profile setting ("edit account details") wins, although it contains an option (the very first one) that can override this (i.e., the user's theme will match whatever was chosen in the » appearance « menu). You can use this, for instance, to mute the sounds of the Sewers while at work (the black-and-white imageless theme is also soundless), which some readers asked for. And as I just verified theory in practice, giving a website a makeover via CSS is remarkably easy, so if anyone has an idea or request for another theme, feel free to write to me; if several similar suggestions come together, or if I like something, I'll implement it.

Social Dynamics

What goes around comes around; and when it comes to collective guilt, that holds twice over. If we divide people into "us" and "them" (based on anything other than the actions of specific individuals) in order to curtail the liberties of "the others" because of the wrongdoing of some of "them," we hand brilliant ammunition to "their" populists, who preach collective guilt as well. And the more we act that way, the more "they" will perceive things the same way, which in turn vindicates the rhetoric of "our" populists, and the whole dynamic can escalate ad absurdum. Applying this to refugees, we find that by restricting their liberties, we genuinely drive them into the arms of various terrorist organizations. But beware! There is no good idea that cannot be distorted and abused; and unfortunately, that is what the bleeding hearts are doing: they divide society into "us" and "them" in the exact same manner, but curtail "our" liberties for "their" benefit, boldly claiming that if they don't, "they" will become radicalized.
Do you know what German bleeding-heart politicians are calling for right now? They want to ban New Year's Eve fireworks, allegedly so as not to traumatize refugees, because consumer fireworks might remind them of war; and they justify restricting our freedoms by claiming we must yield so as not to radicalize anyone. But don't they realize that this is precisely what they are doing? After all, the principle cuts both ways, and who started it is completely irrelevant. How is it that the bleeding hearts understand this principle clearly in one direction, while the anti-Islam crowd understands it in the other, yet neither group can pause to reflect that there isn't the slightest reason why the exact same thing wouldn't apply to both sides? Social Networks Are Not for Minors

Bureaucrats in the European Union are drafting legislation according to which social networks would be banned for anyone under thirteen, while youths aged thirteen to sixteen would only be allowed access with parental consent. What can one say to that? First, surely we can all see what an outrage this is, as the state once again declares its intention to raise children in place of parents; if this continues, in a few generations it will be the norm that raising children is the domain of the state, and if anyone dares suggest that parents should do it, they will be branded an extremist. Second, I hope it is also clear to everyone what absolute bullshit this is, given that we can all imagine how enforceable such a law is in practice.
There are essentially two ways this can turn out if the bill passes (it hasn't been approved yet): Either there will be some state-run registry of parental consents or a similar madness, or the law could be deftly wielded as a stick to beat inconvenient dogs—which would be a disaster in either case; or it will simply boil down to adding another checkbox for parental consent alongside the terms-and-conditions box—in which case it will be comically toothless, further cementing the notion that breaking the law is the norm, which would be just fine. We thus have three possibilities: (a) the bill doesn't pass, (b) the bill passes and someone actually starts enforcing it, or (c) the bill passes and becomes a complete joke. Option (b) is horrifying, but strikes me as unlikely; personally, I'd bet on (a). Readers' guesses are warmly welcome in the comments.
Compulsory Voting?

I recently heard Miloš Zeman speaking again on the topic of compulsory voting, of which he has long been an ardent proponent. Because only about half of the electorate participates in this democratic process, the ruling elite finds that insufficient and wants more; and when they want something, nothing is easier than simply ordering the people to do it. The reality of the matter, however, is that only the president truly wants it, and he lacks the power to push it through; ergo, we will most likely not see compulsory voting in the foreseeable future. That said, it cannot be ruled out entirely down the road, as there are countries where citizens have this obligation (paying a fine if they refuse to participate).
At first glance, of course, such an idea struck me as monstrous, since such a law is morally indefensible; the question is, what would the practical repercussions be? First of all, it would undoubtedly turn people against the ruling class, which is always a positive. Furthermore, in my view, such a law would create fertile ground for ridiculing democracy more effectively. In Germany, for example, there is a political party called "The Party" (in the original, "Die PARTEI"), which has a single plank in its platform: "We will do nothing." Understandably, it doesn't enjoy huge support, but mandatory voter turnout could change that.
Not to mention that one could potentially exploit compulsory voting by founding a party whose primary promise would be the repeal of compulsory voting; beyond that, it could also run on a libertarian platform, ideally smuggled in Trojan-horse style: the official platform would simply be repealing mandatory voting, but in the event of electoral success, it could pursue some liberalization in parliament, or at least use media attention to spread libertarian ideas. The question, of course, is how many of the roughly 50% who abstain do so out of pure laziness versus principle, which would greatly determine where those votes would go if forced to the ballot box.
So while we can certainly be glad that voting isn't mandatory here (one less potential bureaucratic nuisance), personally I wouldn't dread its introduction that much. Our situation couldn't deteriorate significantly as a result (aside from yet another idiotic government edict, of course); on the other hand, such a law could ultimately yield some liberalization, or at least weaken the state in the eyes of its voters and further stoke their anger. The question, of course, is how much that would actually change things. What do you think, dear readers?

The Future of Bitcoin?

How Do We Lose Our Freedom?

Some time ago, I dumped a comment into the Sewers that several people wrote to me suggesting I should publish as a full-fledged "article." Since I felt it was rather long for the Sewers, here I outline its core point (in slightly more general terms): how we lose our freedom.
Phase One:
We possess a certain freedom (of speech, movement, enterprise, bearing arms, etc.); people are not (yet) willing to give it up, and anyone who tries to restrict it for the sake of some bureaucratic nuisance gets told to get lost, begins losing voters, and is shunned by his peers. If someone were somehow to pass a law abolishing this freedom out of the blue, anyone who promises to repeal the legislation will score gains in the next election.
Phase Two:
The prohibitionists present a powerful emotional pretext to curtail this freedom (a terrorist attack, mass child abuse, radiation, biological weapons, and so forth—basically anything that stirs strong emotions, even if its connection to the freedom in question is utterly marginal). If it represents a major intrusion into our lives, they promise the change is only temporary. I presume we are all familiar with arguments like "after all, during wartime this and that is allowed or done" (using war as a benchmark of moral high ground is laughable in itself). Hysteria completely drowns out any reasoned debate, and the ban passes.
Phase Three:
Once people have grown accustomed to the freedom being somewhat restricted, social engineers propose reducing the number of murders, rapes, robberies, and the like by curtailing this freedom just a little bit more. While these attempts occasionally fail, over time they eventually succeed (notice that once a regulation is introduced, practically no one ever repeals it). Once that happens, with the public no longer paying much attention, that freedom starts being chipped away over every petty triviality and bureaucratic whim. Although initially unthinkable, by this point it leaves virtually everyone indifferent (aside from a few crazy libertarians).
Phase Four:
Processes (in both the public and private sectors), services, goods, and norms emerge that are predicated upon that freedom being restricted in some way. These are then used as arguments for why that freedom must remain suppressed. Even when the original pretext disappears, or proves to have been nonsense from the very beginning, in reality it no longer matters. Nobody cares about the freedom anymore; moreover, "everyone knows" it must be restricted, because otherwise "things wouldn't work" (due to all the established processes that rely on that restriction).

The Ministry of Health amended the Public Health Protection Act (yes, we have such a law too, because our bodies belong to the state) so deftly that students in schools are not allowed to come into contact with motor fuels (greetings to apprentice auto mechanics) or weak acids and ethanol (cheers, chemistry students), meaning that chemistry Olympiads are completely done for as well. Like true consummate professionals, Minister Němeček and Minister Valachová first and foremost bicker over who is to blame: according to Valachová, Němeček screwed it up with an idiotic amendment, while he defends himself by claiming she had the draft in advance and should have commented on it. As for the problem itself, that can naturally wait, because one can always set up an interdepartmental committee, draft a proposal, and send it to public health officers, who also have plenty of time. Can you imagine acting like this at your job?
Yet this tragicomic incident is merely the tip of the iceberg, a symptom of something far deeper. Beyond the existence of such blatant filth as the Public Health Act undoubtedly is (by which the state declares that we don't own our health—and therefore not even our own bodies—but rather politicians do, usurping the right to decide), we face yet another issue: the entire concept of our legal system is turned on its head. A law took effect that is blatantly wrong, as everyone knows, including those who drafted it; yet everyone is forced to obey it, because if a teacher were now to conduct experiments with students using prohibited substances (the very same ones allowed just a month ago), he'd end up behind bars. Someone might argue that it has to be this way, because otherwise, every instance of unlawful conduct would require evaluating whether the violated law happened to be nonsensical in that specific situation. Gollum, Erdoğan, and Freedom of Speech in Turkey

A Misguided Debate

Sometimes I put on the talk show "Máte slovo" on my second monitor (mostly as background noise) if there's a political topic in that episode. Today, they discussed an amendment to the already totalitarian "Significant Market Power Act," tightening the law even further. The show's hot topic was supermarkets securing discounts from food manufacturers leveraging their strong market position; however, the law states that an entity possessing "significant market power" may not demand a lower price without "just cause" (that's actually in there). The debate then unfolded with proponents of regulation accusing retail chains of buying food at low prices from a dominant market position, while supermarket representatives denied it—and everyone implicitly assumed that this must be wrong.
Why is this dreadful? Well, for the same reason the debate on smoking bans in restaurants was atrocious, centered entirely on whether cigarettes harm health and how badly smoke smells (the single key takeaway from that debate that I still remember to this day was that smoke in a pub spreads just like urine in a swimming pool). And that is precisely how virtually everything is debated (far beyond just that talk show): whenever adopting a regulation on anything is discussed, the debate is essentially reduced to whether that "anything" causes harm or not; if the answer is yes, regulation is automatically assumed to be justified, ergo right. And that is why, dear libertarians, we must tirelessly point out the heart of the matter: liberty, property rights, and the true cost of regulatory laws (not merely economic, but above all moral)—because no one else is going to do it for us.

The State as a House

In connection with migration, we often hear the comparison that a state is like a house: just as a property owner decides whom to welcome into his home and whom not to, the state should supposedly decide who is allowed across its borders and who stays out. While such a comparison might seem intuitive at first glance, in reality it is one of the falsest analogies I have ever encountered; what makes it especially unique is that the claim being compared actually contradicts the very premise it draws from.
How so? Well, if the state determines who is permitted to cross the border, it simultaneously prevents me from inviting into my home whomever I see fit (since in some cases it keeps them out of the country entirely). Isn't that paradoxical? The analogy rests on the premise that it is good for me to decide for myself whom I let into my house, yet this very principle, used as the benchmark, would be overridden by the principle the analogy seeks to justify: I can hardly invite whoever I want into my home if that person isn't even allowed across the border.
Another flaw with this analogy is that while a house typically has a rightful owner who makes the decisions, the state does not. A far more accurate analogy would be an apartment building in which I own an apartment: Can my neighbors, by majority vote, forbid me from having a guest over whom they happen to dislike? Hmm... suddenly that's not quite so clear-cut, is it? Not that they couldn't establish such an agreement in advance, but if no such rule existed when I purchased the apartment, it suddenly becomes a rather murky matter, and I highly doubt anyone would still use the analogy in that form (even though it is more accurate in every respect).
Yet even more than a house, a state resembles a city; and here we find ourselves on very thin ice indeed, as having the residents of a city vote on who is allowed to come there to work, for example, is virtually unheard of. By no means take this text as a defense of EU refugee quotas—because even more absurd than neighbors telling me who can visit my home would be them ordering me whom I must take in; I am merely pointing out that comparing national borders to private property boundaries makes virtually no sense, and in fact contradicts itself.

A rather unpleasant nuisance has spread around here: Prague cops are bragging to the media about how, after a multi-month operation, they caught wicked taxi drivers. And what did these villains do? The state, however, violently mandates that all exchanges take place according to its own (moronic) rules. Six cabbies and one bureaucrat who tipped them off about inspections have been charged, with the uniformed monkeys even boasting about tailing them around the clock, requiring ten detectives and dozens of decoys per target just to prove each victim broke the law by at least five thousand CZK, since anything below that threshold is merely an administrative infraction rather than a felony (and not every sting worked, as the drivers rarely offered that kind of deal).
Even leaving aside the moral dimension—namely the disgrace of the state interfering in voluntary exchanges—what actually happened here? A detective (counting a fresh recruit) makes about 25,000 CZK a month; let's conservatively say the multi-month sting lasted two months; let's assume the decoys worked for free; let's ignore equipment and cab fare expenses. We find that the state blew 3.5 million CZK (a conservative lower estimate) on detective salaries alone, just to—holy shit, to do what!? To convict six people of offering someone a ride at a mutually agreed (albeit steep) price, and one guy for covering for them. Bravo! Three and a half million to charge seven people with a victimless crime—and the bastards even brag about it in the media!? Are you wondering if they've completely lost their minds? Well, Google it and read how the press kisses their asses for it, followed by ecstatic comments from the moronic mob... because why wouldn't we blow millions just to stop someone from making a 98% margin? And that, dear children, is democracy: rule of the people!
Mini-Marx

Whoever cannot generate that much value (plus all the taxes) for an employer simply won't be hired by anyone, as the employer would lose money. Nazi-Islam

The perennial comparison of Islam to Nazism and Muslims to Nazis is among the most popular Islam-bashing arguments; not that such a comparison doesn't make sense in certain special situations—some of the smarter crusaders against Islam use it mostly sensibly—but in the vast majority of cases it is nothing more than brainless parroting of these opinions by dumber folks who are capable of nothing more than rewriting completely random texts simply by substituting occurrences of the corresponding words. One could even write software in half an afternoon that could do this automatically, and the output would be roughly just as stupid. Where, then, do such comparisons fall short?
First of all, although Islam shares some features with Nazism, it also has a number of entirely different characteristics. The main difference lies above all in the fact that while Nazism is a very young and specific ideology, Islam is nothing but one huge mess, a religion many hundreds of years old with countless interpretations and a holy book with loads of translations (six 'major' ones and heaps of others). In reality, Islam encompasses a whole range of different currents (from aggressively totalitarian Salafists to benevolently frivolous Sufis), which Nazism simply does not have. For that reason, it is completely absurd, for instance, to compare 'moderate Muslims' to 'moderate Nazis' (since there were in fact no Nazi factions preaching anything diametrically opposed to the teachings of Hitler himself; had they existed, then such a comparison would make sense).
Moreover, even in cases where the comparison does make sense, abominations often stem from it. This typically happens when someone tries to push through a ban on Islam by arguing that Nazism is also banned. The problem here lies, first and foremost, in the fact that banning a totalitarian ideology is itself a totalitarian practice; one simply cannot defend against totalitarianism with totalitarianism (meaning not even Nazism should be banned). If we sacrifice freedom of speech, expression, the press, or religion, we ourselves become those whom we want to ban! The argument that bans on totalitarians are not themselves totalitarian practices is completely absurd; there is no objective yardstick to determine what ought to be banned, ergo someone must exist who decides—and that is precisely where totalitarianism lies.
I am definitely not claiming that comparing Nazism and Islam is necessarily wrong under all circumstances; political Wahhabism, for instance, truly does resemble Nazism. But one cannot indiscriminately and thoughtlessly claim across the board that they are one and the same thing, because that is plain and simple not true. The differences are sometimes negligible, other times enormous, so before comparing one to the other, it is wise to reflect on what the outcome is supposed to be and whether the comparison doesn't completely lose its meaning in that specific area. Please, let us not blind ourselves to logic in the name of fanaticism.
Illegal Pig Slaughters

Based on an EU regulation from a few years ago, the Czech state forbade its subjects from hosting traditional pig slaughters unless they have a special permit; unfortunately, by all accounts this permit cannot be obtained simply by going down to the authorities; rather, you more or less need to own a slaughterhouse. Conventional neighborhood pig slaughters are simply a thing of the past; and commercial pig slaughters organized by pubs likewise. However, the whole thing also has a silver lining—the state lacks the resources to actively monitor compliance with this law, so the only way it can harass anyone is if somebody snitches on them first.
The downside is that such scumbags can indeed be found among us. In 2014, the state raked in one hundred and twenty thousand crowns in fines, all from natural persons (corporations most likely didn't dare, since you need to advertise it, which increases the risk of being reported), who were probably snitched on by their neighbors. Shame on them! Shame on every bastard capable of ratting out his neighbor for slaughtering his own pig; this can't even be excused by any bullshit about the 'danger to society' of such an act—this is pure, unadulterated filth, for which those involved deserve the utmost contempt.
On the other hand—although I failed to track down the exact number of such snitches—given that a single fine for an illegal pig slaughter can climb up to three hundred thousand and the state collected one hundred and twenty thousand for the whole year, we can assume there were likely just a handful (or a small dozen) of cases; even if the average fine were only ten thousand, that would be twelve people, or one per month, which isn't that many for a population of ten million. Overall, I like the certain indifference of people in this country toward breaking laws; although people mostly consider taxes to be right in the abstract, on a personal level tax evasion and working under the table are not socially condemned all that much (unlike in Germany, for example, where it is viewed similarly to robbing a neighbor).
In any case, it is a downright shame to follow such laws that the state doesn't enforce; it is enough to convince snitches not to snitch. So if you know any such human garbage, be nasty to them, ostracize them, convince those around you to do the same, just teach them a lesson so they think twice next time. And the fewer people collaborate with the police, the better, so spread information around you about all the evil the police have caused or done (for
examples
one doesn't need
to look far
). The state is evil; and whoever is willing to commit dirty deeds for it, let decent people show them that this is not the way.
The War on Drugs Has (Always) Been Failing

The War on Drugs has (always) been failing; Murray Newton Rothbard and other brilliant visionaries predicted this long before this war properly even began, people immune to state prohibitionist propaganda realized it within a few years, others understood it after a few decades, and today basically everyone knows it, including little kids—even former rulers are now admitting it. The Global Commission on Drug Policy assessed the state of affairs in a report in which it found, with surprise, that drug policy costing millions of dollars out of taxpayers' pockets has failed, because while missing its mark entirely, it instead creates organized crime and causes the death of thousands of people; members of this commission include, for example, former UN chief Kofi Annan, former NATO Secretary General and former EU High Representative for Common Foreign and Security Policy Javier Solana, former US Secretary of State George Shultz, and former presidents of Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia. The former powerful, whose power no longer depends on the drug war, have no reason to lie anymore...
Right in the introduction of their report, it states: 'The global war on drugs has failed, with devastating consequences to individuals and societies around the world.' It also says in the same place: 'Political leaders and public figures should have the courage to articulate publicly what many of them acknowledge privately: that the available evidence strongly demonstrates that repressive strategies will not solve the drug problem, and that the war on drugs has not, and cannot, be won.' What matters is that those past leaders, who criticize it today, plucked up that courage; I'd also be curious to know how they guessed what current leaders say in private—could it be rich personal experience? xD
The whole thing belongs to the vast category of things that would be laughable if they weren't so tragic. It's one thing that strictly logical explanations of why the war on drugs simply would not work existed decades ago, but since that was inconvenient, they were quite understandably ignored. Police Scaremongering: 'Drunk Goggles'

The cops have launched another campaign against drunk drivers; it's hard to tell what the goal is this time—it could be media barrage softening up the ground for stricter legislation or another round of bureaucratic harassment, or maybe someone just needed to justify their activity on the taxpayers' dime. In any case, the whole thing played out with the uniformed monkeys having so-called 'alcohol goggles' purchased for them—which make people see double or triple—calling up some subservient journalists, slapping the goggles on them, and having them drive between traffic cones so that they'd write articles about what a horror it would be if pedestrians stood in place of the cones.
I assume the overwhelming majority of readers know what it feels like to be drunk; and who thinks that the only problem in that state is vision? Of course, I'm not claiming one can't get hammered to the point of being practically blind; on the other hand, loss of motor skills, slower reflexes, and other issues that fundamentally impair the ability to drive set in far earlier. Hence the sheer absurdity of the police's claim that the goggles supposedly simulate a 1.5 per mille blood alcohol level—they likely simulate far more in terms of vision, but far less in other respects (or simply just a 1.5 effect on vision and nothing else).
The result is that both the whole test and the 'alcohol goggles' are simply a lie; they do not simulate what they are supposed to simulate. Sure, you can certainly induce a state somewhat equivalent to intoxication by confusing the eyes, but that's highly individual, as alcohol affects different people differently anyway; so aside from a sensationalist PR stunt and fearmongering in the papers, the informational value of such shenanigans is practically nil. And I ask: Who paid for all this? But above all... which of these payers, the taxpayers, would have paid for such nonsense voluntarily if they didn't have to? Imagine how absurd it would be if someone asked people for money so they could buy 'alcohol goggles', put them on journalists, and make them weave between cones... but why ask when you can just take it by force, right?
And finally, purely as an aside, I wonder whether it's illegal to drive with 'alcohol goggles'. Does applicable legislation forbid me from putting on glasses behind the wheel that significantly distort my vision? Of course, if I crash because of it, the situation is clear; but as long as I drive without an accident, can a monkey in uniform slap me with a fine for it? If not, why not? If it really is as equivalent to drunkenness as the cops claim, for what reason is one prohibited while the other is allowed? Does that make any sense at all? I'm afraid this is once again a purely arbitrary decision by politicians who claim a monopoly on knowing what is best for us.
